Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 5, verse 1:

Madaniyya [except verse 3, which was revealed at 'Arafat during the Farewell Pilgrimage] and it has one hundred and twenty verses [revealed after the Conquest]. In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

It is said: wafā bil-ʿahd and awfā bihi (he fulfilled the covenant). [The author said: "It is said: wafā bil-ʿahd and awfā bihi, and from it: 'those who fulfil their covenant' (al-mawfūna bi-ʿahdihim)." Aḥmad said: The Mighty Book has (waffā) with the doubled form in His words, "And Abraham who fulfilled (waffā)" [Q. 53:37], and awfā occurs often, as in "Fulfil the covenants" (awfū bil-ʿuqūd) [Q. 5:1]. As for the triliteral wafā, it occurs only in His words, "And who is more faithful (awfā) to his covenant than Allah?" [Q. 9:111], because the comparative form (afʿal) is built only from a triliteral root, and so it was built from wafā.]] And from it: "and those who fulfil their covenant." The ʿaqd (covenant) is a firm pledge, likened to the tying of a rope or the like. Al-Ḥuṭayʾa said:

A people who, when they make a covenant for their neighbour, / tie the ʿanāj and tie the kurab above it.

A people, they are the nose and the tails, others than them; / and who would equate the tail with the nose of the she-camel?

(These lines are by al-Ḥuṭayʾa.) The ʿanāj (kitāb pattern) is a rope tied to the bottom of the bucket, then to the ʿarāqī, the plural of ʿurqūwa, which is the piece of wood across the mouth of the bucket. The kurab (kasab pattern) is a rope tied to the end of the ʿurqūwa and the ʿanāj to bind them. This is a metaphorical image: their state in securing the covenant in many ways is likened to one who secures a bucket with many ropes. Or the state of their covenant in its extra firmness is likened to a bucket that is securely tied. "The nose of the she-camel" is the epithet of Jaʿfar ibn Qurayʿ: his father slaughtered a she-camel for his wives, and his mother sent him to take her share, but he found only the head. His father said, "Take hold of it," and he began dragging it by the nose, and so he was given that epithet. His tribe was ashamed of that epithet, so the poet borrowed "the nose" to mean the noble and exalted of high rank, by way of explicit metaphor. Or he likened the people to it with eloquent comparison, and likened others to the tail in baseness and lowliness. The interrogative is one of denial, meaning no one equates the nose with the tail in rank, so from then on this epithet became praise.

In it there is a pun (tawriya) of the utmost beauty.

These are the covenants of Allah which He made with His servants and imposed on them, from the obligations of the religious duties. It is also said: they are what they agree among themselves of trust-contracts, what they swear to, and what they conclude in sales and the like. The apparent meaning is that they are the covenants of Allah upon them in His religion, such as making lawful what He made lawful and unlawful what He made unlawful; and that it is a statement stated in general terms and then followed by detail, which is His words, "Lawful for you" and what follows.

Al-bahīma: every four-legged animal, on land and in sea. Its attribution to al-anʿām is for specification, the attribution that carries the meaning of "from," like "a ring of silver." The meaning: the beasts of the cattle, except what is recited to you (illā mā yutlā ʿalaykum), i.e., except what is forbidden by what is recited to you of the Qur'an, such as His words, "Forbidden to you is carrion" [Q. 5:3], and except what is recited to you as a verse prohibiting it. Al-anʿām: the eight pairs. It is also said that "the beast of cattle" means gazelles, wild cows and the like, as if they intended what resembles the cattle and approaches them in the category of beasts in chewing the cud and lacking fangs, so it was attributed to the cattle because of the resemblance. Ghayra muḥillī al-ṣayd is in the accusative as a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in "lakum," i.e., these things were made lawful for you, not as those who make lawful game-hunting. It is reported from al-Akhfash that its accusative is governed by His words, "Fulfil the covenants," and His words "while you are in the state of iḥrām" are a circumstantial clause for "muḥillī al-ṣayd," as if it were said: We made lawful for you some of the cattle in a state where you refrain from hunting while you are in ihram, so that you are not made to suffer hardship. Inna Allāha yaḥkumu mā yurīd: He decrees whatever He wills of rulings, and He knows that it is wisdom and benefit. Al-ḥurum: the plural of ḥarām, which is muḥrim (one in the state of ihram).

The sacred symbols of God (*sha'a'ir*, the rites and markers of worship): the singular is *sha'ira*, meaning whatever is marked out as a sign or emblem of the rites (*nusuk*). These include the stations of the Hajj, the places where the pebbles are thrown, the circumambulation area (*mataf*), the course between Safa and Marwa (*sa'y*), and the acts that are the signs of the Hajj, by which one is recognised as in the state of consecration (*ihram*), circumambulating, running between Safa and Marwa, shaving the head, and sacrificing. The sacred month is the month of the Hajj. The offerings (*hadi*) are what is sent to the House and drawn near to God among the sacrificial animals. It is the plural of *hadiyya*, just as one says *jadi* as the plural of *jadiyya* of the saddle (*jadiyyat al-sarj*). [[The author's remark "as one says *jadi* as the plural of *jadiyya* of the saddle": in *al-Sihah*, *al-jadiyya* (with the *dal* sukun) is a stuffed thing placed beneath the two pommels of a saddle or pack-saddle; its plural is *jadi* and *jadiyyat*. (Commentator's note.)]]

The garlands (*qala'id*): the plural of *qala'ada*, which is what the offering is garlanded with, such as a sandal, the handle of a water-skin, bark of a tree, or other such things.

Those who make for the Sacred Mosque: those who intend it, namely the pilgrims and those performing the minor pilgrimage (*'umra*). To violate (*ihlal*) these things means to be careless about the sanctity of the sacred symbols, to prevent those who observe the rites from them, to create in the months of the Hajj something by which people are turned away from the Hajj, and to interfere with the offerings by seizing them or preventing them from reaching their place of sacrifice. As for the garlands, there are two opinions. The first:

That they are meant to be the animals bearing garlands, which are the camels (*budn*), and they are joined to the offerings as a particular mention and for added emphasis, because they are the most noble of the offerings, like His saying ﴿and Gabriel and Michael﴾ [2:98]. It is as if it were said: "and the garlands from among them, specifically."

The second: that it forbids interfering with the garlands of the offerings, as an intensification of the prohibition against interfering with the offerings themselves, in the sense of: "Do not violate their garlands, let alone violate them yourselves," just as He said ﴿and not to display their adornment﴾ [24:31], forbidding the display of adornment as an intensification of the prohibition against displaying its places. ﴿Nor those making for the Sacred Mosque, seeking bounty from their Lord and His good pleasure﴾, meaning do not violate people who make for the Sacred Mosque. Bounty (*fadl*) is reward, and His good pleasure (*ridwan*) is that He be pleased with them. That is: do not interfere with people who have this description, out of honour for them and as a denunciation of anyone interfering with such people.

It has been said: this verse is *muhkam* (definitive, not abrogated). [[*Muhkam*: a verse whose ruling has not been abrogated. (Translator's gloss.)]] It is related from the Prophet (ﷺ): "Al-Ma'ida is among the last of the Qur'an to be revealed, so make lawful what is lawful in it and unlawful what is unlawful in it." [[Related by al-Hakim through the chain of Jubayr ibn Nufayr, who said: "I entered upon 'A'isha, and she said to me: 'O Jubayr, do you recite al-Ma'ida?' I said: 'Yes.' She said: 'Indeed it is the last surah to be revealed: al-Ma'ida and al-Fath.' al-Tirmidhi indicated that her words 'and al-Fath' refer to 'when the help of God comes.' He said: 'It has been related also from Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with them both.'"]] Al-Hasan said: "There is no abrogated (*mansukh*) ruling in it." [[*Mansukh*: a ruling that has been abrogated; *naskh* is abrogation. (Translator's gloss.)]] It is related from Abu Maysara: "In it there are eighteen obligations, and there is no abrogated ruling in it." It has been said: it is abrogated (*mansukh*). It is related from Ibn 'Abbas: "The Muslims and the polytheists used to perform the Hajj together. So God forbade the Muslims to prevent anyone from the Hajj to the House, by His saying ﴿Do not violate﴾. Then after that there was revealed ﴿The polytheists are only unclean﴾ [9:28] and ﴿It is not for the polytheists to maintain the mosques of God﴾ [9:17]." Mujahid and al-Sha'bi said: "﴿Do not violate﴾ was abrogated by His saying ﴿and kill them wherever you find them﴾" [2:191].

They explained seeking bounty as trade, and seeking good pleasure as meaning that the polytheists used to think of themselves that they were upon the right course of their religion and that the Hajj would bring them closer to God; so God described them by their own assumption. 'Abd Allah read: "wa la a'mi al-bayt al-haram," in the genitive construction. Hamid ibn Qays and al-A'raj read *tabtaghun* with a *ta'* (second person), addressing the believers. ﴿So hunt﴾ is a permission to hunt after it had been forbidden to them, as if it were said: "And when you have come out of the state of consecration, there is no blame on you if you hunt." It is also read with a *kasra* on the *fa'*. It has been said that it is a substitution for the *kasra* of the *hamza* at the beginning. It is also read: *wa idha ahlaltum*. One says *halla al-muhrim* and *ahalla*. *Jarama* functions like *kasaba* in its transitivity to one object and to two. You say *jarama dhanban* (he committed a sin), like *kasabahu*; and *jarramtuhu dhanban* (I made him commit a sin), like *kasabtuhu iyyahu*. It is also said *ajramtuhu dhanban*, by transferring the transitive verb to two objects with the *hamza*, as in their saying *akasbtuhu dhanban*. On this reading, and on the reading of 'Abd Allah, *la yajrimannakum* with a *damma* on the *ya'*, the first object of the two readings is the pronoun of the addressees, and the second is ﴿that you transgress﴾. As for ﴿that they barred you﴾, it is read with a *fatha* on the *hamza*, and it is attached to *shana'an* in the sense of cause; *shana'an* means intense hatred. It is also read with a sukun on the *nun*. The meaning: "Let not hatred of a people, because they barred you, lead you to transgression, nor compel you to it." It is also read *in sadduhum* as a conditional *in*. In the reading of 'Abd Allah: *in yasuddukum*. The meaning of their barring them from the Sacred Mosque: the people of Makka prevented the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and the believers from the minor pilgrimage on the day of al-Hudaybiyya. The meaning of transgression: avenging oneself upon them by inflicting harm on them. ﴿And help one another in righteousness and piety﴾, through pardon and forbearance; ﴿and do not help one another in sin and aggression﴾, through retaliation and the satisfaction of revenge. It is permissible for the meaning to be general, covering every righteousness and piety and every sin and aggression, so that by its generality it includes both pardon and vindication.

The people of the Jahiliyya used to eat these forbidden things: the animal that dies of its own accord (al-bahima allati tamutu hatfa anfiha), and al-fasid, which is the blood in the intestines (al-mabari). Al-mabari are the intestines into which the blood is put after it has been drawn, and then roasted for the guest. Their saying "None has been forbidden to whoever has been made to bleed (fuzida lahu)" runs as a proverb. "Fuzida" is in the passive voice; its original form is "fusida," and its sad was made sakin for lightness and then changed into a zay. End of quote. (Ghayn)

﴿And that over which the name of other than God has been invoked﴾: that is, the raising of the voice for other than God. This is their saying, at the slaughter, "In the name of al-Lat and al-Uzza."

﴿The strangled﴾: the animal they strangled until it died, or that choked to death by itself.

﴿The beaten﴾: the animal they beat to death with a stick or a stone.

﴿The fallen﴾: the animal that fell from a mountain or into a well and died.

﴿The gored﴾: the animal that another animal gored and it died from the goring.

﴿And what a beast of prey has eaten of it﴾: ﴿except what you have slaughtered (dhakkaytum)﴾, that is, except what you reached while it was still alive (its dhakat, its ritual slaughter) and it was convulsing like a slaughtered animal and its jugular veins were gushing blood.

ʿAbd Allah (Ibn Masʿud) read "wa-l-manṭūḥa" (the gored). In a narration from Abu ʿAmr, "al-sabʿu" is read with a sukun on the ba'. Ibn ʿAbbas read "wa-akīlu al-sabʿi" (and what the beast of prey has eaten).

﴿And what is slaughtered on the altars (al-nusub)﴾: they had stones set up around the House (the Kaʿba), upon which they slaughtered and cut up the meat, glorifying them by this and drawing near to them by it. These were called al-anṣab (the altar-stones), and nusub is the singular. Al-Aʿsha said:

*"Do not worship the erected idol (dhā l-naṣbi l-manṣūbi),*
*lest you end in ruin; worship your Lord God instead.*
*Pray at the times of the evenings and the forenoon,*
*do not praise Satan; praise God instead."*

This is of al-Aʿsha. "Nusub" may be read like ḍarb and like shurb; in one dialect like sabab, and in another like ʿunuq. The meaning here may include the one erected as a sign (al-ʿalam al-manṣūb).

What is meant here is the idol, and any one of the stones that were set up around the House, for whose sake they sacrificed the offerings (al-hady) to draw near to them. Dhā is a demonstrative noun in the accusative, governed by a verb that is omitted and explained by the one mentioned, in the manner of al-ishtighal (the construction in which the verb is omitted and the noun is governed by an implied verb). Al-Jawhari took it as meaning "beware of this idol," so it is accusative by way of al-taḥdhīr (warning). It is also related with "lā tansukannahu" in place of "lā taʿbudannahu" (do not perform the rites for it). It is also related "al-muthrīn" (the wealthy) in place of "al-shayṭān" (Satan), meaning the rich.

It is also related for the second half of the verse "wa-llāhu rabbuka fa-ʿbudā," and "li-ʿāqibatin" means "seeking a good outcome." Placing the object first serves to restrict the meaning, and for the added fāʾ. It is also possible that it is governed by an implied "wa-lzam Allāha rabbaka" (and hold fast to God your Lord), in which case it is accusative by way of al-ighrāʾ (urging on), and the fāʾ is conjunctive with the implied element. "Fa-ʿbudā" is emphasized with a nūn that is changed into an alif for pause. "ʿAlā" here means "fī" (in). It is also related "sabbiḥ" in place of "ṣalli" (pray), and the meaning is the same: pray the prayers at the time of the forenoon and the evenings. "Fa-ḥmadā" is like "fa-ʿbudā."

It is said that nusub is a plural, and its singular is niṣāb. It is also read "al-nuṣub" with a sukun on the ṣād.

﴿And that you seek decision by the arrows (al-azlam)﴾: God has forbidden you to seek the apportioning (al-istiqsam) by the arrows, that is, by the lots. When one of them wanted to undertake a journey, a campaign, a trade, a marriage, or some matter of great importance, he cast the lots. On some of them was written "My Lord has forbidden me," on some "My Lord has commanded me," and some were blank. If the one commanding came out, he proceeded with his intention; if the one forbidding came out, he refrained; and if the blank one came out, he shuffled them again. So the meaning of seeking apportionment by the arrows is seeking knowledge of what has been apportioned to him, of what has not been apportioned to him, by means of the arrows. It is also said that it is the gambling game (al-maysir). Their dividing of the slaughtered camel into the known shares was also of this kind.

﴿That is a transgression (fisq)﴾: the reference is to the seeking of apportionment, or to the taking of what was forbidden to them, since the meaning is "forbidden to you is the eating of carrion, and so-and-so."

If you ask: Why was the seeking of apportionment by the arrows, by the traveller and others, to know one's situation, called a transgression? I answer: Because it is an intrusion into the knowledge of the unseen, which God alone has kept to Himself, the Knower of hidden things. He said: ﴿None in the heavens and the earth knows the unseen except God﴾. And the belief that there is a path to it and a way of deducing it (wa-ilā istinbāṭihi) is an error and misguidance. His saying "My Lord has commanded me" and "My Lord has forbidden me" is a fabrication against God, and who can tell whether He commanded him or forbade him? The soothsayers and the astrologers are in this same position. If he meant by "Lord" the idol (for it is related that they used to cast the lots before their idols), then the matter is plain.

﴿Today﴾: it does not mean a particular day. It means the present time together with the times that adjoin it and approach it, of the past and the future. Like your saying, "Yesterday I was young, and today you are grey-haired." You do not mean by "yesterday" the day before your present day, nor by "today" your very day. Similar to this is "now" (al-ān) in the verse:

*"Now that the hair at the middle of my chest has turned white,*
*and I have bitten on a stump from my tooth,*
*I have milked this age through its extremities,*
*and I have come to what comes to one who knows."*

This is of al-Dhuhli. It is also said to be of Abu l-ʿAlaʾ al-Maʿarri. "Al-ān" means the present time. "Al-masruba," with a ḍamma on the rāʾ (and it may be read with a fatḥa), is the thin, lengthy line of hair growing in the middle of the chest down to the navel, and it is the last thing to turn white in a person; so its whiteness is a metaphor for reaching the utmost of greying. As for al-masraba with a fatḥa alone, it is the place of excrement. "Min nābī" is a preceding circumstantial phrase, and "min" is partitive. "Al-jadhm" is the root of a thing, as if his canine teeth had crumbled until only their roots remained. It is also possible that the meaning is that they have fallen out and their place in the flesh remains; this too is a metaphor for what has preceded, and an emphasis on its sense. "Ḥalabtu hādhā al-dahr" means I gathered what it contains of events and tested them. "Ashṭurahu" means its sides and extremities; so he likened time to a place having sides, by way of metaphor (kināya), and affirming the sides is an imaginative depiction (takhyīl). It is in the accusative by way of badal (apposition). Also, "shaṭr" means half the udder of a she-camel: in one half there are two teats, and in the other half two teats. So he likened the age to a she-camel by way of al-makniyya (the implicit metaphor), and affirming the sides is an imaginative depiction, and milking it is a supporting detail (tarshīḥ). This is more apt and closer than the first. "Ashṭurahu" is also in the accusative by way of apposition. It is possible that "ḥalaba" is doubled to make it transitive, not for intensification. The meaning then is: I made the age milk its sides for me, and gather for me what is in them of wonders and marvels. It is said that by "its sides" is meant the kinds of good and evil. "Atayt" means I did; for whoever does a thing must direct his body and heart to it. The meaning: it has become my custom that I do what I do with knowledge in my possession, from the long test I have made of the events of the age.

It is also said: what is meant is the day of its revelation. It was revealed on Friday, and it was the day of ʿArafa, after the afternoon prayer, during the Farewell Pilgrimage.

﴿Those who disbelieve have despaired of your religion﴾: they despaired of annulling it, and of your returning to make lawful these foul things after they have been forbidden to you. It is also said: they despaired of your religion, that they would overcome it, because God, Mighty and Majestic, fulfilled His promise to make it prevail over all religion.

﴿So do not fear them﴾: after the religion has become manifest, and the fear of the disbelievers has gone, and they have turned back defeated and subdued after having been victorious.

﴿And fear Me﴾: and devote to Me your fear sincerely.

﴿Today I have perfected your religion for you﴾: I have sufficed you against your enemy and made the upper hand yours, as kings say: "Today our kingship is complete, and everything we want is complete," when they have been spared from one who disputes their rule and have reached their aims and objectives. Or: I have perfected for you what you need in your obligations, of teaching the lawful and the unlawful, and of the specifying of the laws, and the rules of analogy (qawānīn al-qiyās) and the foundations of independent reasoning (uṣūl al-ijtihād).

﴿And completed My favour upon you﴾: by the conquest of Mecca, and your entering it secure and manifest, and by the demolition of the landmarks and rites of the Jahiliyya, and that no polytheist performs the pilgrimage with you, and no naked person circumambulates the House. Or: I have completed My favour upon you by completing the affair of the religion and the laws, as if He said: today I have perfected your religion for you and completed My favour upon you by that, for there is no favour more complete than the favour of Islam.

﴿And I have approved for you Islam as a religion﴾: that is, I have chosen it for you from among the religions, and I have informed you that it is the only approved religion. ﴿Whoever seeks other than Islam as a religion, it will not be accepted from him﴾. ﴿Indeed this community of yours is one community﴾.

If you ask: With what is His saying ﴿So whoever is compelled﴾ connected? I answer: With the mention of the forbidden things. His saying ﴿That is a transgression﴾ is a parenthetical insertion, by which the meaning of the prohibition is emphasized. Likewise what follows it, because the prohibition of these foul things is part of the complete religion, the perfect favour, and Islam described as approved, to the exclusion of other creeds.

The meaning: whoever is compelled by hunger (fī makhmaṣa), that is, by famine, to eat carrion or other than it, ﴿without inclining to sin﴾, that is, not deviating toward it, like His saying ﴿neither desiring nor transgressing﴾. ﴿Indeed God is Forgiving﴾, He does not hold him to account for that.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 5, verse 4:

The question carries the sense of saying, which is why ﴿what has been made lawful for them﴾ follows it, as if it had been said: "They ask you, 'What has been made lawful for them?'" He did not say "what has been made lawful for us," as a report of what they said, because they asked using the third-person form, as you say "Zayd swore that he would surely do it." Had it been said, "I will surely do it, and what has been made lawful for us," it would have been correct. ﴿Mā﴾ (what) is the subject, and ﴿has been made lawful for them﴾ is its predicate, as in your saying, "What thing has been made lawful for them?" Its meaning is: what of the foods has been made lawful for them? As if they, when he recited to them what had been forbidden to them of foul foods, asked about what had been made lawful for them of them, and so it was said: ﴿The good things have been made lawful for you﴾, meaning what is not foul among them, which is everything whose prohibition has not come in the Book, the Sunnah, or the analogical reasoning of a mujtahid (qualified jurist). ﴿And what you have taught of the hunting animals﴾ is conjoined to ﴿the good things﴾ [[Mahmud, may God Most High have mercy on him, said: "And what you have taught, as a conjunction to the good things... etc." Ahmad, may God Most High have mercy on him, said: He excelled in drawing attention to this hidden secret, except that the state (ḥāl), by its original nature, is transitional and not fixed; and the implication of this formulation is to make it one of the necessary attributes of the trainer of the hunting animals, which are established for him.]], meaning: the good things have been made lawful for you, and the game of what you have taught has been made lawful. The noun has been omitted. Or you may make ﴿mā﴾ conditional, with its response being ﴿then eat﴾.

The ﴿jawāriḥ﴾ (hunting animals) are the predatory ones among the beasts and birds, such as the dog, the leopard, the panther, the eagle, the falcon, the hawk, and the shāhīn. The ﴿mukallib﴾ is the one who trains the hunting animals and makes them ferocious toward the game for their owner, and who tames them for that by what he knows of stratagems and methods of discipline and refinement. Its derivation is from ﴿kalb﴾ (dog), because training is most often done with dogs, so the word was derived from its name because of their prevalence within their kind. Or because the predator is called a dog (kalb). From this is the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ), "O God, set upon him a dog from Your dogs," and a lion ate him. It is also from ﴿kalab﴾ in the sense of ferocity; it is said: "He is a kalib for such-and-such," if he is fierce toward it.

The accusative ﴿mukallibīna﴾ is a state (ḥāl) relative to ﴿ʿallamtum﴾. If you ask: what is the benefit of this state, since it is dispensed with by ﴿ʿallamtum﴾? I say: its benefit is that the one who trains the hunting animals is to be expert in his knowledge, trained in it, and described by making them ferocious. ﴿Tuʿallimūnahunna﴾ is a second state or a resumption. In it there is a sublime benefit [[He continued his words, saying: "And in His saying, ﴿you teach them from what God has taught you﴾, there is a sublime benefit... etc." Ahmad said: The verse is evidence that beasts have knowledge, since their being taught means, linguistically, the acquisition of knowledge by them through its means, contrary to those who deny this.]], namely that everyone who takes knowledge must take it only from the one who is most learned in its people, most skilled in its discernment, and most penetrating into its subtleties and realities, even if he must travel to him on the livers of camels.

How many a taker of knowledge from another, one who has mastered it, has wasted his days and, at the meeting with the experts, bitten his fingers in regret! ﴿From what God has taught you﴾ refers to the knowledge of training; for it is an inspiration from God and also acquired through reason. Or [it means] from what He has shown you that you should teach: following the game upon the release by its owner, its restraint at his rebuke, its return at his call, the holding of the game for him, and that it should not eat from it.

﴿Mukallibīna﴾ is also read with the lightened form (mukallibīna), and afʿala and faʿala are often interchangeable. The "holding on its owner" means that it does not eat from it, based on the Prophet's (ﷺ) saying to ʿAdī ibn Ḥātim: "And if it eats from it, do not eat, for it has held only for itself." [[Agreed upon, from the hadith of ʿAdī ibn Ḥātim.]] And from ʿAlī, may God be pleased with him: "If the falcon eats, do not eat." [[I have not found it.]] The scholars differed: they stipulated abstention from eating for the beasts of prey, because they are disciplined by beating, but did not stipulate it for birds of prey. Some did not consider abstention from eating at all and did not distinguish between holding all of the game and holding part of it. And from Salmān, Saʿd ibn Abī Waqqāṣ, and Abū Hurayrah, may God be pleased with them: "If the dog eats two-thirds and one-third remains, and you have mentioned God's name over it, then eat." [[The hadith of Salmān was transmitted by Ibn Abī Shaybah and ʿAbd al-Razzāq through Qatādah from Saʿīd ibn al-Musayyab from Salmān concerning a dog released upon game: if it eats two-thirds, eat the remaining third. The hadith of Abū Hurayrah similarly was narrated by Ibn Abī Shaybah through al-Shaʿbī from him, who said: "If you release your dog and it eats it, then eat, even if it eats a third of it." The hadith of Saʿd ibn Abī Waqqāṣ was likewise narrated by Ibn Abī Shaybah through Bakr ibn al-Ashajj from Ḥumayd ibn Mālik from Saʿd concerning game upon which a dog is released; he said: "Eat it, even if nothing remains of it but a small piece."]]. If you ask: to what does the pronoun in His saying ﴿and mention the name of God over it﴾ refer? I say: either it refers to ﴿what they have held﴾, meaning, "Name God over it when you reach its slaughter," or to ﴿what you have taught of the hunting animals﴾, meaning, "Name God over it at its release."

The food of those who were given the Book (ahl al-kitab, "People of the Book") is lawful for you. It is said: it means their slaughtered animals. It is also said: it means all their food. All Christians are included in this ruling.

It is related from 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, that he excluded the Christians of the Banu Taghlib, saying: "They are not Christians in the true sense, and they have taken from Christianity only the drinking of wine."[[Ibn Abi Shayba narrated it from the transmission of Ibrahim al-Nakha'i from 'Ali, and it is a broken chain (munqati', a chain with a missing link). al-Shafi'i and 'Abd al-Razzaq narrated it connected (mawsul) from the transmission of 'Ubayda from 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him.]] Al-Shafi'i adopted this view.

It is related from Ibn 'Abbas that he was asked about the slaughtered animals of the Arab Christians, and he said: "There is no harm in them."[[Malik narrated it in the Muwatta' from Thawr from Ibn 'Abbas in these words, and it is a broken chain: Thawr did not meet Ibn 'Abbas, and he took it from 'Ikrima, but Malik omitted him. Ibn Abi Shayba narrated it through 'Ata' ibn al-Sa'ib from 'Ikrima from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "Eat the slaughtered animals of the Banu Taghlib and marry their women."]] This is the view of the majority of the Successors (tabi'un), and Abu Hanifa and his companions adopted it.

According to Abu Hanifa, the ruling on the Sabians is the ruling on the People of the Book. His two companions said: they are of two kinds. One kind reads the Zabur (Psalms) and worships the angels, and another kind reads no scripture and worships the stars. These latter are not among the People of the Book.

As for the Magians (majus), the Sunna has treated them as the People of the Book with regard to collecting the jizya (poll tax) from them, but not with regard to eating their slaughtered animals or marrying their women.

It is related from Abu al-Musayyab that he said: if a Muslim is sick and he orders a Magian to pronounce the name of Allah and slaughter, there is no harm. Abu Thawr said: if he orders him to do so while the Muslim is healthy, there is also no harm, though he has done wrong.

﴿And your food is lawful for them﴾, so there is no blame on you if you feed them, because if the food of the believers were forbidden to them, it would not be permissible for them to be fed by you.

[[Mahmud said: "Its meaning is: there is no blame on you if you feed them..." etc. Ahmad [Ibn al-Munayyir] said: This verse may be cited by those who hold that disbelievers are addressed by the branches of the Sharia, because permissibility is a ruling, and He has attached it to them in His words ﴿And your food is lawful for them﴾, just as He attached the ruling to the believers. This verse is clearer as evidence for this than His words ﴿They are not lawful for them, nor are they lawful for them﴾, because one could say about that verse that negating a ruling is not itself a ruling. One cannot say that about this verse of al-Ma'ida, since the ruling in it is affirmative. And Allah knows best. When al-Zamakhshari sensed that it indicates this, and he is among those who hold that addressing disbelievers with the branches of the Sharia is impossible, he forestalled this by interpreting it as turning the address to the believers, meaning: there is no blame on you, O Muslims, if you feed the People of the Book, as you have seen in his words too.]]

﴿The chaste women﴾ means free women, or women of chastity. Specifying them urges believers to choose carefully for their offspring. The believing slave women may be married by agreement, and likewise the unchaste women among them. As for slave women who are People of the Book, according to Abu Hanifa they are like Muslim women, but al-Shafi'i disagreed. Ibn 'Umar did not hold that marriage to People of the Book was permitted, and he argued from the words "Do not marry idolatresses until they believe," and he said: "I know of no greater polytheism than her saying that her Lord is 'Isa."

It is related from 'Ata': "Allah has made Muslim women plentiful, and they were permitted to them only at that time."

﴿Chaste, not fornicators, nor taking secret lovers﴾, meaning friends. The word khadan (secret lover) applies to both males and females.

﴿Whoever disbelieves in the faith﴾, meaning in the laws of Islam and in what Allah has made lawful and unlawful.

**[Al-Zamakhshari's commentary on Surah al-Ma'idah, verse 6]**

﴿When you rise to prayer﴾ is like His saying: ﴿So when you recite the Qur'an, seek refuge in Allah﴾. [[Mahmud (al-Zamakhshari) said: "His saying 'when you rise' is like His saying 'so when you recite the Qur'an, seek refuge in Allah'..." Ahmad (Ibn al-Munayyir) said: This statement can be accepted from the Sunni as it can be accepted from the Mu'tazili. We say: the act comes into existence through the servant's power, joined to it and accompanying it. The Mu'tazili says it, meaning that it is created by that power and arises from its influence. The expression is used in both doctrines but with different meanings. And Allah is the Granter of success.]] It is also like your saying: "When you strike your slave, then be gentle with him," where what is meant is the intention to perform the act.

If you ask: Why is it permissible to express the intention to perform an act by the act itself?

I answer: Because the act comes into existence through the agent's power over it, his will to do it, his intention toward it, his inclination, and the sincerity of his motive. Just as the capacity to do an act is expressed by the act itself in their saying: "A human does not fly" and "a blind person does not see," meaning they are not able to fly or to see. From this is His saying: ﴿We shall repeat it, a promise upon Us; indeed We are ever doing [it]﴾, meaning: indeed We are capable of repetition. Likewise the intention to perform an act is expressed by the act, because the act is caused by power and will. The effect is therefore placed in the position of the cause because of the connection between them, and for the brevity of speech. Similar to this, placing the effect in the position of the cause, is their saying: "As you judge, so you will be judged," where the initial deed, which is the cause of the recompense, is expressed by the word for the recompense, which is its effect.

It has also been said that the meaning of "when you rise to prayer" is "when you intend prayer," because whoever turns toward something and rises to it is necessarily intending it, so the intention toward it is expressed by rising to it.

If you say: The apparent meaning of the verse requires ablution for every person rising to prayer, whether in a state of minor impurity or not, so what is its justification?

[[He returned to his words: "If you say: the apparent meaning of the verse requires ablution for every person rising to prayer..." Ahmad said: Al-Zamakhshari denied that a homonym (mushtarak) may be understood to mean each of its meanings together. He had already denied this before, and whoever permits the intention of all the possible senses permits that in this verse. Among those who permit that is al-Shafi'i, may Allah have mercy on him. Enough is it that he is the leader and exemplar of the discipline. This holds when it is established that the form "af'il" is shared between obligation and recommendation; then its inclusion in the verse of both groups, those in a state of minor impurity and those who are pure, is valid, and its inclusion of those who are pure is on the basis of recommendation. And Allah knows best.]]

I answer: The imperative may be for obligation, in which case the address is specifically to those in a state of minor impurity; or it may be for recommendation.

It is related from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and the caliphs after him that they performed ablution for every prayer. [[Al-Bukhari reported it through 'Amr ibn 'Amir from Anas, with the wording "at each [prayer]," and added: "I said: How did you used to do it?" He said: "One of us would be sufficed by the ablution as long as he had not broken it." And al-Tirmidhi reported it through Humayd from Anas similarly, and added "whether pure or impure." Muslim has, from the hadith of Yazid: "The Prophet (ﷺ) used to perform ablution for every prayer; but when the day of the Conquest came, he prayed the prayers with one ablution. 'Umar said to him: You did something you did not used to do. He said: I did it, O 'Umar." This will come shortly. Abu Dawud, al-Hakim and Ahmad have, from the hadith of Asma' bint Zayd ibn al-Khattab, from 'Abd Allah ibn Hanzalah ibn al-Ghasil: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) had commanded ablution at every prayer, whether pure or impure. When that became hard upon him, he commanded the siwak." And his saying: "The caliphs after the Prophet (ﷺ) used to perform ablution for every prayer": Ibn Abi Shaybah and al-Tabari reported it through Abu 'Awanah from Muhammad ibn Sirin, who said: "The caliphs Abu Bakr, 'Umar, 'Uthman and 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with them, used to perform ablution for every prayer."]]

And from the Prophet (ﷺ): "Whoever performs ablution upon ablution, Allah records for him ten good deeds." [[The compilers of the Sunan reported it except al-Nasa'i, from the hadith of Ibn 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with them both. Al-Tirmidhi said: its chain is weak.]]

And from him, peace be upon him, that he used to perform ablution for every prayer. [[This was already pointed out, and that Muslim reported it without mention of wiping. Likewise the compilers of the Sunan reported it.]] When the day of the Conquest came, he wiped over his leather socks and prayed the five prayers with one ablution. 'Umar said to him: "You did something you did not used to do." He said: "I did it deliberately, O 'Umar," meaning to show that it is permissible?

If you say: Is it permissible that the imperative includes both those in a state of minor impurity and others, obligatory for the former and recommended for the latter?

I answer: No, because the word bearing two different meanings is a kind of riddle and obscurity.

It has been said: performing ablution for every prayer was obligatory when it was first enjoined, and then it was abrogated (naskh).

"Ila" (until, to) expresses the sense of a limit in general. As for whether it is included in the ruling or excluded from it, this depends on the evidence. Among the examples where the evidence shows exclusion is His saying: ﴿then [let there be] postponement until a time of ease﴾, because hardship is the reason for granting respite; and when ease comes, the cause ceases. If ease were included in it, he would be granted respite in both states, being both in hardship and in ease. Likewise His saying: ﴿Then complete the fast until the night﴾; if the night were included, continuous fasting would be required. Among the examples where the evidence shows inclusion is your saying: "I memorized the Qur'an from its beginning to its end," because the speech is directed to memorizing the whole Qur'an. And from this is His saying: ﴿from the Sacred Mosque to the Farthest Mosque﴾, since it is known that he was not carried to Jerusalem without entering it. As for ﴿to the elbows﴾ and ﴿to the ankles﴾, there is no evidence in them for either of the two matters. So the majority of scholars took the cautious course and ruled that they are included in the washing. Zufar and Dawud took the certain course and did not include them.

It is related from the Prophet (ﷺ), peace and blessings be upon him and his family, that he used to turn the water around his elbows. [[Al-Daraqutni reported it from the hadith of Jabir: "The Prophet (ﷺ) when he performed ablution turned the water around his elbows," and its chain is weak.]]

﴿And wipe over your heads﴾: the intended meaning is to attach the wiping to the head. Whether one wipes part of it or all of it, both attach the wiping to the head. Malik took the cautious course and required the wiping of all of it or most of it, according to the differing reports. Al-Shafi'i took the certain course and required the least that falls under the name of wiping. Abu Hanifah took the explanation of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), which is what is reported: that he wiped over his forelock. [[Muslim reported it from the hadith of al-Mughirah ibn Shu'bah in a story in which: "He wiped his forelock, the turban, and his leather socks." And al-Tabarani has from his hadith: "The Prophet (ﷺ) performed ablution and wiped over his forelock."]]

The measure of the forelock is a quarter of the head.

A group read ﴿and your feet﴾ in the accusative. [[Mahmud said: "A group read ﴿and your feet﴾ in the accusative..." Ahmad said: He did not give a satisfactory justification for the genitive reading. The reason is that washing and wiping are close, in that each of them is touching the limb, so it is easy to conjoin the washed with the wiped on this basis, as in the poet's words: "Girded with a sword and a spear... and I fed them chaff and cold water," and its parallels are numerous. The skilled scholars took this line. Then it is said: What is the benefit of this conjoining by reason of closeness? Why not attach to each of them its own verb in its proper sense? It is said: its benefit is brevity and conciseness. Confirming the benefit with what al-Zamakhshari mentioned, and its verification, is that the original form would be, for example: "Wash your feet with a light washing, without excess," as is customary. These meanings were condensed by conjoining the feet with the wiped members, and this conjoining, which occurs only in a single act or two very close acts, indicates that the washing required for the feet is a light washing close to wiping, and that its inclusion with it under one form is good. This is a complete establishment of this intended meaning. And Allah knows best.]], which indicates that the feet are washed. If you ask: What do you do with the genitive reading and its inclusion under the ruling of wiping? I answer: Of the three washed members, the feet are washed by pouring water over them, so they are prone to the blameworthy excess that is forbidden. Therefore they were conjoined with the third, the wiped member, not so that they be wiped, but to draw attention to the obligation of moderation in pouring water over them.

It has been said: ﴿to the ankles﴾ was mentioned with the limit to remove the suspicion of one who supposes they are to be wiped, since wiping has no limit set for it in the Shari'ah.

It is related from 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, that he came upon some young men of Quraysh and saw excess in their ablution. He said: "Woe to the heels from the Fire." When they heard this, they began washing them thoroughly and rubbing them vigorously.

It is related from Ibn 'Umar: "We were with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and a people performed ablution while their heels were white and shining. He said: 'Woe to the heels from the Fire.'" [[Agreed upon (Bukhari and Muslim), through the route of Yusuf ibn Mahak from 'Abd Allah ibn 'Amr, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) fell behind us on a journey, and we caught up with him..." and he mentioned it; in it: "and their heels were shining." In Muslim: "We returned with the Prophet (ﷺ) from Makkah to Madinah." In Abu Nu'aym's al-Mustakhraj: "and their heels were white and shining." (Note): I have not seen it from the hadith of Ibn 'Umar, and it seems to have been garbled for the author of the book or for one of those who took it from him.]] In the narration of Jabir: "Woe to the 'araqib." [[Reported by Ibn Majah, Ahmad, Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ishaq and Abu Ya'la, through Abu Ishaq from Sa'id ibn Abi Kurayb from Jabir. It is in Muslim from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah. For al-Nasa'i it is in the hadith of 'Abd Allah ibn 'Amr mentioned above, and for Abu Ya'la from the hadith of 'A'ishah, and for Sa'id ibn Mansur from the hadith of Abu Dhar, may Allah be pleased with him.]]

It is related from 'Umar that he saw a man performing ablution and leave the sole of his foot untouched, so he commanded him to repeat the ablution. This was to make the ruling stricter for him. [[Ibn Abi Shaybah and 'Abd al-Razzaq reported it through Abu Qilabah: "'Umar saw a man performing ablution and a spot the size of a fingernail remained on his foot. He said: Repeat the ablution." It is disconnected (munqati'). Al-Bayhaqi reported it connected through al-Thawri from al-A'mash from Abu Sufyan from Jabir: "'Umar saw a man..." and mentioned it with the wording "a patch (lum'ah)." It has also been reported as marfu' (traced to the Prophet): Ahmad and Abu Dawud reported it through Khalid ibn Ma'dan from some Companions: "The Prophet (ﷺ) saw a man who had a patch the size of a dirham on the top of his foot which the water had not reached, so he commanded him to repeat the ablution and the prayer." Al-Athram said from Ahmad: its chain is good. Abu Dawud said: it is mursal. Ibn Daqiq al-'Id answered him that the non-mention of the Companion's name is a defect, and that Khalid is described as frequently reporting mursal narrations. (Note): The phrase "to make the ruling stricter" is from the words of the author of al-Kashshaf, and there is something to examine in it, since it is possible that what is meant by "repeat the ablution" is "wash your feet," by way of mentioning the whole and intending the part. As for what is in the marfu' report, it is possible that the command mentioned was after the man had broken his ablution.]]

It is related from 'A'ishah, may Allah be pleased with her: "Indeed, for my feet to be cut off would be dearer to me than that I wipe over my feet without leather socks." [[Ibn al-Jawzi reported it in al-'Ilal al-Mutanahiyah through the route of al-Qasim from her, without the phrase "without leather socks." Its chain includes Muhammad ibn Muhajir al-Baghdadi, whom Ibn al-Jawzi criticized as a fabricator.]]

It is related from 'Ata': "By Allah, I do not know that any of the Companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) wiped over the feet." [[I have not found it.]]

Some people have gone to the apparent sense of the conjunction and required wiping.

It is related from al-Hasan that he combined the two matters (washing and wiping).

It is related from al-Sha'bi: "The Qur'an was revealed with wiping and washing as a sunnah."

al-Hasan read ﴿and your feet﴾ in the nominative, meaning "and your feet are washed or wiped, up to the ankles."

It is also read ﴿so purify yourselves﴾, meaning: purify your bodies; and likewise ﴿that He may purify you﴾. In the reading of 'Abd Allah: ﴿then head for clean earth﴾.

﴿Allah does not intend to place upon you any hardship﴾ in the matter of purification, so that you are not granted leave for tayammum; ﴿but He intends to purify you﴾ with the dust when water is unavailable to you for purification; ﴿and to complete His favor upon you﴾, and to complete His grace upon you by His permissions along with His obligations; ﴿that you may be grateful﴾ for His favor, so that He rewards you.

"And remember the favour of Allah upon you," namely the favour of Islam, "and His covenant with which He bound you" — that is, He made you enter a firm pact with it. It is the covenant that He took from the Muslims when the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) pledged them to hearing and obeying, in ease and hardship, in eagerness and in reluctance, and they accepted and said: "We hear and we obey." It was said: it is the covenant of the night of 'Aqaba and in the Pledge of Ridwan.

The verb *yajrimannakum* (﴿يَجْرِمَنَّكُمْ﴾) is construed with the preposition *ʿalā* ("upon"), by implicit transitivity: the verb is taken to carry the sense of a verb that takes that preposition, as if it were said: *wa-lā yaḥmilannakum* (and let not ... bring you to). It is also permissible that His saying ﴿أَنْ تَعْتَدُوا﴾ ("that you transgress") means ﴿عَلَى أَنْ تَعْتَدُوا﴾ ("upon that you transgress"), so that *ʿalā* is omitted together with *an*, as in the saying of the Prophet, peace be upon him: "Whoever is referred (*ittibaʿa*) to a wealthy person, let him accept (the referral)," because it means *uḥīla* (was referred). The reading *shanaʾun* is also recited with a sukūn (*shanaʾn*), and its parallel among verbal nouns is *layyān*. The meaning is: let not your hatred of the polytheists lead you to abandon justice, so that you transgress against them by taking revenge on them and by satisfying yourselves with what is in your hearts of rancour, through committing what is not lawful for you, such as mutilation (*muthla*), slander, killing their children or women, breaking a covenant, or the like.

﴿اعْدِلُوا هُوَ أَقْرَبُ لِلتَّقْوَى﴾ ("Be just; that is nearer to God-consciousness (*taqwā*)"). He first forbade them to let enmity drive them to abandon justice, then went on to state the command to be just explicitly, as emphasis and intensification. Then He went on to mention the reason for the command to be just, which is His saying ﴿هُوَ أَقْرَبُ لِلتَّقْوَى﴾, meaning: justice is nearer to God-consciousness and more suited to it. Or: it is nearer to God-consciousness because it is a means of grace (*luṭf*) toward it. In this there is a great admonition: if justice is required of them even with the disbelievers, who are the enemies of God, to this degree of strength, what then is to be assumed about its obligation with the believers, who are His friends and beloved?

﴿لَهُمْ مَغْفِرَةٌ وَأَجْرٌ عَظِيمٌ﴾ ("For them is forgiveness and a great reward") is an explanation of the promise, after the completion of the preceding speech, as if He said: He first gave them a promise; so it is asked, what did He promise them? And it is answered: ﴿لَهُمْ مَغْفِرَةٌ وَأَجْرٌ عَظِيمٌ﴾. Or it may be by intending the sense of saying, i.e., He promised them and said to them, ﴿لَهُمْ مَغْفِرَةٌ﴾. Or by treating "promised" as though it were "said," since it is a kind of speech. Or the promise may be taken to govern the sentence ﴿لَهُمْ مَغْفِرَةٌ﴾ itself, just as "We left (*tarakna*)" governs ﴿سَلَامٌ عَلَى نُوحٍ﴾ ("Peace upon Noah"). It is as if it were said: He promised them this statement, and when He who does not break the promise promises them this statement, He has promised them its content of forgiveness and great reward.

This statement is one with which they will be greeted at death and on the Day of Resurrection; so they rejoice in it, find ease through it, and it alleviates for them the agonies and terrors before they reach the reward.

The meaning is: let not your hatred of the polytheists lead you to abandon justice, so that you transgress against them by taking revenge on them and by satisfying yourselves with what is in your hearts of rancour, through committing what is not lawful for you, such as mutilation (*muthla*), slander, killing their children or women, breaking a covenant, or the like.

﴿اعْدِلُوا هُوَ أَقْرَبُ لِلتَّقْوَى﴾ ("Be just; that is nearer to God-consciousness (*taqwā*)"). He first forbade them to let enmity drive them to abandon justice, then went on to state the command to be just explicitly, as emphasis and intensification. Then He went on to mention the reason for the command to be just, which is His saying ﴿هُوَ أَقْرَبُ لِلتَّقْوَى﴾, meaning: justice is nearer to God-consciousness and more suited to it. Or: it is nearer to God-consciousness because it is a means of grace (*luṭf*) toward it. In this there is a great admonition: if justice is required of them even with the disbelievers, who are the enemies of God, to this degree of strength, what then is to be assumed about its obligation with the believers, who are His friends and beloved?

﴿لَهُمْ مَغْفِرَةٌ وَأَجْرٌ عَظِيمٌ﴾ ("For them is forgiveness and a great reward") is an explanation of the promise, after the completion of the preceding speech, as if He said: He first gave them a promise; so it is asked, what did He promise them? And it is answered: ﴿لَهُمْ مَغْفِرَةٌ وَأَجْرٌ عَظِيمٌ﴾. Or it may be by intending the sense of saying, i.e., He promised them and said to them, ﴿لَهُمْ مَغْفِرَةٌ﴾. Or by treating "promised" as though it were "said," since it is a kind of speech. Or the promise may be taken to govern the sentence ﴿لَهُمْ مَغْفِرَةٌ﴾ itself, just as "We left (*tarakna*)" governs ﴿سَلَامٌ عَلَى نُوحٍ﴾ ("Peace upon Noah"). It is as if it were said: He promised them this statement, and when He who does not break the promise promises them this statement, He has promised them its content of forgiveness and great reward.

This statement is one with which they will be greeted at death and on the Day of Resurrection; so they rejoice in it, find ease through it, and it alleviates for them the agonies and terrors before they reach the reward.

The commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 5, verse 11:

It is narrated that the polytheists saw the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and his Companions standing to perform the noon prayer together, and that was at Usfan during the campaign of Dhat al-Anmar. When they had prayed, the polytheists regretted that they had not fallen upon them, and said: "They have another prayer after this one which is dearer to them than their fathers and their sons," meaning the afternoon prayer, and they intended to attack them when they stood for it. Then Gabriel descended with the Prayer of Fear (salat al-khawf) [[Al-Tabari narrated it from the transmission of al-Nadr ibn Umar, from Ikrimah, from Ibn Abbas, with some variation in it, and its wording says: "The Messenger of God (ﷺ) went out on a military expedition. He met the polytheists at Asqalan. When he prayed the noon prayer, they saw him bowing and prostrating, and some of them said to others: 'It was an opportunity for you. If you had raided them, they would not have been able to do anything to you.' A speaker among them said: 'Indeed they have another prayer,'" and the rest is similar. Its origin is in Muslim, from the transmission of Abu al-Zubayr, from Jabir: "We campaigned with the Prophet (ﷺ) against a people from Juhayna, and they fought us a severe fight. When we prayed the noon prayer, the polytheists said: 'If we had charged upon them, we would have cut them off.' They said: 'Indeed a prayer is coming to them which is dearer to them than the first,' so Gabriel informed the Prophet (ﷺ), and the Messenger of God (ﷺ) related that to us. When the afternoon prayer came, we formed two rows..." (the hadith continues). In al-Tirmidhi and al-Nasai, from the transmission of Abd Allah ibn Shaqiq, from Abu Hurayra, there is something similar.]]. It is also narrated that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) went to the Banu Qurayza, with Abu Bakr, Umar and Ali (may God be pleased with them), seeking from them the blood-money (diya) of two Muslims whom Amr ibn Umayya al-Damri had killed by mistake, thinking them to be polytheists. They said: "Yes, O Abu al-Qasim, sit until we feed you and lend you." So they seated him in a porch and intended to kill him treacherously. Amr ibn Jahhash set out to a large millstone to drop it upon him, but God restrained his hand, and Gabriel descended and informed him, so he went out [[Ibn Ishaq narrated it in al-Maghazi, and through him al-Bayhaqi and Abu Nuaym in al-Dala'il. He said: "My father Ishaq ibn Yasar ibn al-Mughira ibn Abd al-Rahman ibn al-Harith ibn Hisham, and Abd Allah ibn Abi Bakr ibn Muhammad ibn Amr ibn Hazm, and others of the people of knowledge, told me: Abu Baraa Amir ibn Malik ibn Jafar ibn Kilab came to the Messenger of God (ﷺ)," and he mentioned it at length. In it he said: "Then the Messenger of God (ﷺ) went out to the Banu al-Nadir seeking their help regarding the two slain men whom Amr ibn Umayya al-Damri had killed, as Yazid ibn Rumán told me, saying: There was a covenant and alliance between the Banu al-Nadir and the Banu Amir. When the Messenger of God (ﷺ) came to them seeking their help, they said: 'Yes, sit, O Abu al-Qasim,' and he sat by the side of a wall of their houses. Then some of them withdrew privately to others and said: 'Who will climb onto this house and drop a rock upon him, killing him with it, so that he relieves us of him?' Amr ibn Jahhash ibn Kab volunteered for that, and he climbed up to drop a rock as they had said, while the Messenger of God (ﷺ) was with a group of his Companions, among them Abu Bakr, Umar and Ali. Gabriel came to him from heaven with what the people intended, so he stood up and went out returning to Medina. Then he ordered war against them and marching towards them, and the people set out." (Note) In the words of the author of al-Kashshaf: "They were both Muslims," but I did not find that in any of its transmissions. Rather, Musa ibn Uqba in al-Maghazi explicitly stated that they were both disbelievers, and they had a covenant. In Abu Nuaym's al-Dala'il, from the hadith of Ibn Abbas: "Amr ibn Umayya met two men from the Banu Kilab who had a safe-conduct, but he did not know of it, and he killed them."]]. It is said: He stopped at a station and the people scattered among the thorn trees seeking shade in them. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) hung his sword on a tree, and a Bedouin came, drew the sword of the Messenger of God (ﷺ), then approached him and said: "Who will protect you from me?" He said: "God," and he said it three times. Then the Bedouin sheathed the sword [[The phrase "fasha'a al-a'rabi al-sayf" (the Bedouin sheathed the sword) is in al-Sihah: shamtu al-sayf means I sheathed the sword, and shamtuhu means I drew it, and it is one of the words with opposite meanings. (Ayn)]], so the Messenger of God (ﷺ) called out to his Companions and informed them, and he refused to punish him [[Agreed upon (Bukhari and Muslim), from the transmission of Abu Salama, from Jabir, similarly. Al-Bukhari has it through another channel.]]. It is said: "He extended his tongue against him" when he insulted him, and "he extended his hand against him" when he seized him with violence. The meaning of "extending the hand" is stretching it out toward the one being seized. Do you not see their saying: "So-and-so is broad-armed (basit al-ba')" and "long-armed (madid al-ba')," with the same meaning?

"So He restrained their hands from you," meaning He prevented them from extending them toward you.

When the Children of Israel had settled in Egypt after the destruction of Pharaoh, God commanded them to set out for Jericho (Ariha), in the land of Syria, which was inhabited by the Canaanite giants. He said to them: "I have written it for you as a dwelling place, so go forth to it and fight those who are in it, and I will be your helper." Moses, peace be upon him, was commanded to take from each tribe a chief (naqib) who would be a guarantor over his people for fulfilling what they had been commanded, as a binding pledge upon them. He chose the chiefs and took the covenant from the Children of Israel, and the chiefs undertook it on their behalf. He then set out with them. When he drew near the land of Canaan, he sent the chiefs to spy on it. They saw huge bodies, strength and might, so they were afraid, returned, and reported to their people, although Moses, peace be upon him, had forbidden them to report to them. So they broke the covenant, except for Caleb son of Jephunneh of the tribe of Judah, and Joshua son of Nun of the tribe of Ephraim son of Joseph, and both of them were among the chiefs.

The naqib is the one who searches out the condition of the people and investigates it, just as he is called an arif (overseer), because he knows (ya'rifuha) their condition.

﴿Indeed I am with you﴾, that is, your helper and supporter.

﴿You have supported them﴾, that is, you have aided them and protected them from the hands of the enemy. From this comes ta'zir, which means punishing and preventing a return to corruption. It is also read with a light pronunciation (ʿazzartumūhum, with the shadda omitted). One says: "azzarat al-rajul" when one lowers and humbles him. Ta'zir and ta'zir (with alif) are from one root. From the same root comes: ﴿We will surely support you with powerful support﴾, that is, strong. It has also been said that the meaning is: "We took their covenant to faith and tawhid (the oneness of God), and We sent from among them twelve kings who would establish justice among them, command them to what is right, and forbid them what is wrong."

The lam in ﴿Surely if you establish﴾ is a preface to an oath, and the lam in ﴿I will surely expiate﴾ is its response. This response takes the place of both the response to the oath and the response to the condition together. ﴿After that﴾, after that firm condition, attached to the great promise. If you say: "Whoever disbelieved before that also strayed from the right way." I say: Indeed, but the straying after it is clearer and greater, because disbelief's ugliness is magnified by the greatness of the blessing that is denied. So when the blessing increases, the ugliness of disbelief increases and it persists.

﴿We cursed them﴾, that is, We drove them away and expelled them from Our mercy. It has been said: We transformed them (into apes). It has been said: We imposed the poll tax (jizya) upon them. ﴿And We made their hearts hard﴾, that is, We forsook them and withheld from them the subtle graces, until their hearts hardened. Or: We gave them respite and did not hasten punishment upon them until they hardened.

Ibn Mas'ud read: qasiyah (قسية), that is, debased and adulterated. From the saying: "dirham qasiy" (a debased dirham). It comes from qaswah (hardness), because pure gold and silver are soft, while the adulterated one is dry and hard. Al-qasi and al-qasih (with the letter ha') are close in meaning, both indicating dryness and hardness. It is also read qasiyah with a kasra on the qaf, for the sake of harmony (ittiba').

﴿They distort the words﴾ is an explanation of the hardness of their hearts, for there is no harder hardness than fabricating lies against God and altering His revelation. ﴿And they have forgotten a portion﴾, that is, they have left a large share and a full measure of ﴿what they were reminded of﴾ from the Torah. The meaning is that their abandonment of the Torah and their turning away from it amounts to neglecting a great portion. Or: their hearts hardened and became corrupt, so they distorted the Torah, and some things were removed from their memory.

It is related from Ibn Mas'ud, may God be pleased with him: "A person may forget some knowledge through sin he commits." Then he recited this verse. It has also been said: they left aside their own share of what they were commanded regarding belief in Muhammad, may God bless him and grant him peace, and the description of him.

﴿And you will not cease to discover﴾, that is, this is their habit and their constant practice, and their forefathers were upon it: they betrayed the messengers, and these betray you. They break your covenants, support the polytheists against your fighting, and intend to assassinate you. ﴿Except a few of them﴾ means betrayal, or an act involving betrayal, or a soul, or a treacherous group. It is said: "a man who is khā'inah (very treacherous)," like their saying "rajul rāwiyah lil-shi'r" (a man who is a great transmitter of poetry) for emphasis. The poet says:

"You told yourself of fidelity, but you were not
One who is treacherous in betrayal, the misleading finger."

This is by al-Kilabi, addressing a guest who stayed with him and then coveted his slave girl. The hamza is for address, and "Amāyatayn" is the name of two mountains, and "Ṣalfa'" is the name of a place. The meaning: O companion, if you had seen my horsemen at these two mountains extending to the sides of Ṣalfa', you would have told yourself of fidelity to the covenant out of fear of me, as is obligatory for you, and you would not have been treacherous for the sake of the enemy. Or: and you would not have been made a betrayer for treachery, the reading being that this is a predicate after a predicate, meaning one who is much given to betrayal, and the ta' is for emphasis, like "rāwiyah." Perhaps he had gestured to the slave girl with his finger, so he named the gesture with it a betrayal that misled him.

It is also narrated as "mughl al-usba'" with a ghayn, and "ghull" and "aghall," when one steals something trivial, as if he made his finger a thief, that is, a stealer, through the gesture.

It is also read ﴿upon treachery﴾ from them, ﴿except a few of them﴾, and they are those among them who believed. ﴿So pardon them﴾ is an incitement to oppose them. It has been said that this is abrogated (mansukh) by the verse of the sword. It has also been said: pardon their believers and do not hold them accountable for what has passed from them.

﴿أَخَذْنا مِيثاقَهُمْ﴾: We took their covenant. We took the covenant of those among the Christians who came before them, from the people of Moses, meaning a covenant like theirs, to believe in God and His messengers and to do good deeds. We also took the covenant of the Christians themselves to that effect. If you say: "Why was it not said: *min al-Nasara*" (from the Christians)?

[[Mahmud said: "If you say: why was it not said *min al-Nasara*... etc." Ahmad said: There remains a subtle point in specifying this place by attributing Christianity to their claim, and this did not occur in any other place. Do you not see the words of the Exalted: ﴿وَقالَتِ الْيَهُودُ وَالنَّصارى نَحْنُ أَبْناءُ اللَّهِ وَأَحِبَّاؤُهُ﴾ (The Jews and the Christians said: "We are the sons of God and His beloved.")? The correct view in this, and God knows best, is that since the purpose of this verse is to censure them for breaking the covenant taken from them concerning supporting God, it was fitting that the statement begin with what indicates that they did not support God and did not fulfil what they pledged regarding support. Their whole affair was nothing but uttering the claim of support and saying it, without doing it. And God knows best.]]

I say: Because they named themselves thus only as a claim to supporting God. They are the ones who said to Jesus: "We are the helpers of God" (*ansar Allah*). Then they differed afterwards into: Nestorians (*Nasturiyya*), Jacobites (*Ya'qubiyya*), and Melkites (*Malkaniyya*), as helpers of Satan. [[His words "and Melkites, helpers of Satan": in al-Khazin there is a fourth sect, namely the Marqusiyya. (ʿ)]]

﴿فَأَغْرَيْنا﴾: We stirred up, that is, We attached and bound. The verb *gharā* is used when someone *lazima* (clings to) a thing and *lasiqa bihi* (sticks to it), and *aghraahu ghayrahu* (another made him cling to it). From it comes *al-ghirā'* (glue), which sticks to things.

﴿بَيْنَهُمُ﴾: between them, that is, among the differing sects of the Christians. It was also said: between them and the Jews.

Similar to this is the verse ﴿وَكَذلِكَ نُوَلِّي بَعْضَ الظَّالِمِينَ بَعْضاً﴾ (Thus We make some of the wrongdoers allies of others), and ﴿أَوْ يَلْبِسَكُمْ شِيَعاً وَيُذِيقَ بَعْضَكُمْ بَأْسَ بَعْضٍ﴾ (or confound you into sects and make some of you taste the violence of others).

O People of the Book, this is addressed to the Jews and the Christians: concerning what you used to conceal, such as the description of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and such as the stoning (rajm). And He pardons much of what you conceal: He does not make it clear when there is no religious benefit requiring it, and there is no purpose in it except that a ruling or its description [[His saying "illa iqtida' hukm wa-sifatihi" (except the requirement of a ruling and its description): there is perhaps a omission or a distortion here that caused the meaning to be obscure, so let it be examined. (A)]] that must be made clear. Likewise the stoning, for in it is the revival of a Sharia and the extinction of an innovation. From al-Hasan: "and He pardons much of you," He does not hold you to account. ﴿There has come to you from Allah a light and a clear Book﴾: He means the Qur'an, because it dispels the darknesses of polytheism and doubt, and because it makes clear what was hidden from people of the truth. Or because it is manifestly inimitable. ﴿By it Allah guides whoever follows His good pleasure to the paths of peace﴾: whoever of them believes in it; the paths of peace are the ways of safety and deliverance from the punishment of Allah, or the paths of Allah.

Their saying "Indeed, Allah is the Messiah" means that they uttered the statement outright, holding that the true reality of God is the Messiah and nothing else. It has been said:

There were people among the Christians who said this. It has also been said that they did not state it explicitly, but that their doctrine leads to it, since they believed that he (the Messiah) creates, gives life, causes death, and governs the affairs of the world. "Who then has any power against Allah" means who can prevent anything from His power and will, "if He wished to destroy the Messiah, son of Mary, and his mother, and all those on earth." This is evidence that the Messiah is a created servant like the rest of the servants. By coupling "all those on earth" with "the Messiah, son of Mary, and his mother," He intends that they are of the same kind as them, with no difference between them and others in humanity. "He creates what He wills," that is, He creates from a male and a female, creates from a female without a male as He created Jesus [[The phrase "as He created Jesus" in al-Nasafi reads: "creates from a male without a female, as He created Eve from Adam." (ʿ)]], and creates without a male or female as He created Adam. Or, "He creates what He wills" may mean creating as with the birds shaped by the hand of Jesus as a miracle for him, and as with the raising of the dead, the healing of the blind and the leper, and other such things. Therefore it is necessary that this be attributed to Him, and not attributed to a human being through whose hand it occurs.

﴿The sons of Allah﴾ means the followers (ashyaʿ) of the two sons of Allah, Uzayr and al-Masih, just as the followers of Abu Khubayb, who was ʿAbd Allah ibn al-Zubayr, were called "al-Khubaybun." Musaylima's company used to say, "We are the prophets of Allah," and the kinsmen, relatives and retainers of a king say, "We are the kings." For this reason the believer of Pharaoh's family said: ﴿The kingdom is yours today﴾ (40:29). If it is true that you are the sons of Allah and His beloved, then why does He ﴿punish you for your sins﴾ and ﴿you be transformed and the Fire touch you for a number of days﴾, by your own claim? If you were sons of Allah, you would be of the kind of the Father, neither committing abominations nor deserving punishment. If you were His beloved, you would not disobey Him, and He would not punish you. ﴿Nay, you are human beings, among those He has created﴾, ﴿He forgives whom He wills﴾, and they are the people of obedience, ﴿and punishes whom He wills﴾, and they are the disobedient.

[[Mahmud said: "That is, the people of obedience (﴿and punishes whom He wills﴾): he said, that is, the disobedient."
