The Messenger makes it clear to you. There are three possible readings of its object. First, one may posit that the object is *al-mubayyin* (the thing made clear), namely the religion and the laws (*al-shara'i'*), and that it is omitted because what the Messenger was sent to clarify is already evident. Second, one may posit that the object is *ma kuntum tukhfun* (what you used to conceal), and that it is omitted because it has already been mentioned. Third, one may posit no object at all, so that the meaning is: he gives you clarification. In that case its position is the accusative of circumstance (*al-hal*), meaning "making it clear to you," that is, *mubayyinan lakum*.

*ʿAla fatratin* is connected to *jāʾakum* ("has come to you"), meaning: it has come to you during a lull in the sending of messengers and a break in revelation.

*An taqūlū* means "lest you say," that is, out of fear that you would say. *Fa-qad jāʾakum* is connected to an omitted element, meaning: do not offer excuses, for it has come to you.

It has been said that between Jesus and Muhammad, may Allah's blessings be upon them both, there were five hundred and sixty years. It has also been said six hundred, and it has been said four hundred and some sixty. From al-Kalbi: between Moses and Jesus there were one thousand seven hundred years and one thousand prophets, and between Jesus and Muhammad, may Allah's blessings be upon them all, there were four prophets.

Three of them were from the Children of Israel, and one was from the Arabs: Khalid ibn Sinan al-ʿAbsi.

The meaning is a favour bestowed upon them, and that the Messenger was sent to them at the time when the traces of revelation had been obliterated and they were most in need of him, so that they would rejoice at him, regard him as the greatest blessing from Allah, and as an opening of a door to mercy, and so that the proof would be binding upon them, and they could not plead on the Day of Resurrection that no one had been sent to them to warn them of their heedlessness.

**Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on Surah 5, verses 20–24:**

﴿He made among you prophets﴾, because no nation was ever sent as many prophets as the Children of Israel. [[Mahmud said: "No nation was sent as many prophets as the Children of Israel..." etc. Ahmad said: What led to interpreting *mulk* (kingship) in these ways is that God, in the apparent meaning of the speech, informed that He made all of them kings, by His saying ﴿and made you kings﴾, and He did not say "made among you kings" as He said "made among you prophets." So when He generalized kingship to them, and there is no doubt that kingship as commonly known, which is general dominion, did not belong to each one of them, it is necessary to take *mulk* to mean what was established for all of them or most of them, from the mentioned parts.

This is what motivated the interpretation of *mulk* in this way, and God knows best. Although this meaning was not established for each one of them individually, it was established for their kings, and they were from among them, since Israel, the father, is the nearest common ancestor who unites them. Since their kings were from them, and they were their relatives, their partisans, and connected to them, it was permissible to bestow this favor upon them, and the meaning is understood. This is exactly the statement mentioned earlier in the saying of the Jews and Christians, ﴿We are the children of God and His beloved﴾, and what came before it of antiquity. If you ask: Why did He not say "when He made you prophets," since prophets were from among them just as you said about kings? I say: Prophethood is a distinction different from kingship. Ordinary people share in many of the things by which kingship becomes kingship, but this is not so with prophethood, for its rank is too high for one who has not been granted it to share with one who has been granted it in its distinction, its specificity, and its description. This is the secret of distinguishing the prophets and generalizing the kings, and God knows best.]] ﴿and made you kings﴾, because He made them kings after the kingship of Pharaoh, and after the tyrants (*jabbarun*) had ruled over them, and because kings multiplied among them just as prophets did. It was also said: they were enslaved in the hands of the Copts (*al-Qibt*), so God rescued them, and their rescue was called kingship. It was also said: *al-malik* is one who has a wide dwelling in which there is running water. It was said: one who has a house and servants. It was said: one who has wealth that does not require him to undertake labors and bear hardships. ﴿and gave you what He had not given anyone among the worlds﴾, namely the splitting of the sea, the drowning of the enemy, the shading of the clouds, the sending down of manna and quail, and other great matters. It was said: he meant the worlds of their time. ﴿The Holy Land﴾, meaning the land of Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem). It was said: Mount Sinai (*al-Tur*) and what surrounds it. It was said: al-Sham (Greater Syria). It was said: Palestine, Damascus, and part of Jordan. It was said: God named it for Abraham as an inheritance for his offspring when he was lifted up on the mountain, and it was said to him, "Look, all that your eye can reach is yours." Bayt al-Maqdis was the dwelling place of the prophets and the abode of the believers. ﴿which God has prescribed for you﴾, meaning He allotted it to you and named it for you, or He inscribed in the Preserved Tablet (*al-Lawh al-Mahfuz*) that it is yours. ﴿and do not turn back on your heels﴾, meaning do not retreat or turn back on your heels fleeing in fear of the tyrants, out of cowardice and panic. It was said: when the chieftains (*al-nuqaba'*) informed them of the condition of the tyrants, they raised their voices weeping and said, "Would that we had died in Egypt." They also said, "Come, let us appoint over us a leader who will lead us back to Egypt." It is also permissible that it means: do not turn back on your heels in your religion, by opposing the command of your Lord and disobeying your Prophet, so that you return as losers of the reward of this world and the Hereafter.

*Al-jabbar* is on the pattern *fa'al*, from *jabara* in the sense of *ajbara* (to compel someone to do something); it is the tyrant who compels people to do what he wants. ﴿Two men said﴾, namely Caleb and Joshua, ﴿from among those who feared﴾, meaning from among those who fear God and are mindful of Him, as if it were said: two men from among the God-fearing. It is also permissible that the *waw* (in *alladhina yakhafun*) refers to the Children of Israel, and the relative pronoun's returning pronoun is omitted, its estimated form being: "from among those whom the Children of Israel fear," and they are the tyrants, and these two were men from among them. ﴿upon whom God had bestowed favor﴾, by faith, so they believed. They said to them: the Amalekites (*al-'Amaliqa*) are bodies without hearts, so do not fear them, and advance upon them, for you will surely overcome them, encouraging them to fight them.

The reading of one who reads *yakhafun* with a *damma* (*yukhafun*, i.e., "those who are made to fear") supports this: ﴿and thus God bestowed favor upon them both﴾, as if it were said: from among the two who feared. It was also said: it is from *al-ikhafa* (causing fear), and its meaning is: from among those who are made to fear by God through reminder and admonition, or whom the threat of God's punishment frightens. If you ask: What is the position (*mahall*) of ﴿upon whom God bestowed favor﴾? I say: If it is connected with ﴿those who fear﴾ in the sense of a description of the two men, it is in the nominative case (*marfu'*). If it is taken as an interjected independent clause, it has no place in the sentence (*la mahalla lahu*). If you ask: How did they know that they would be victorious? I say: From the report of Moses concerning that. And the words of God, the Exalted, ﴿which God has prescribed for you﴾. It was also said: from the strength of their assumption (*ghalabat al-zann*), from what they had observed of God's custom in supporting His messengers, from what they knew of God's dealing with Moses in subduing his enemies, and from what they knew of the condition of the tyrants.

The gate: the gate of their town. ﴿We will never enter it﴾: a negation of their entering it in the future, in an emphatic manner that brings despair. ﴿so long as they are in it﴾ is an explanation of "forever" (*abadan*), which is a suspension of the emphatic negation by a long span of time, and ﴿so long as they remain in it﴾ is an explanation of the eternity.

﴿So go, you and your Lord, and fight﴾. It is possible that they did not intend the literal meaning of going [[Mahmud said: "It is possible that they did not intend the literal meaning of going, but..." etc. Ahmad, may God have mercy on him, said: Al-Zamakhshari means that they asked to see God openly, which is impossible by reason, out of obstinacy. This has already been mentioned, and we have explained that their persistence in this was due to their not understanding faith in Him specifically, as a demand and a shirking of the truth in His saying, ﴿We will never believe you until we see God openly﴾.]], but rather as one says, "I spoke to him, so he went to answer me," meaning the sense of intention and purpose for the answer; as if they said, "Intend to fight them." The apparent meaning is that they said this out of contempt for God and His Messenger, lack of concern for them, and mockery, and they intended their literal going by their ignorance, their harshness, and the hardness of their hearts, by which they worshipped the calf and by which they asked to see God, the Mighty and Majestic, openly. The evidence for this is the contrast of their going with their sitting. It is related that Moses and Aaron, peace be upon them, fell prostrate on their faces before them because of the severity of what came upon them, and they (the Children of Israel) intended to stone them. For a particular reason God linked the Jews with the polytheists and placed them before them in His saying, ﴿You will surely find the most intense of people in enmity toward those who believed to be the Jews and those who associated partners with God﴾.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 5, verses 25–26:

When they disobeyed him, rebelled against him, opposed him, and uttered what they uttered of the word of disbelief, and no obedient companion remained with him whom he could trust except Harun, he said: ﴿My Lord, I have no power except over myself and my brother﴾. [Continuation of his words. Mahmud said: "He said, 'My Lord, I have no power except over myself...' etc." Ahmad said: And in the words of Musa, peace be upon him, on the night of the Isra' to our Prophet, peace be upon him: "I have tested the Children of Israel and experienced them, so return to your Lord and ask Him for a reduction, for your community cannot bear that." His repeating this statement many times is a confirmation of what al-Zamakhshari mentioned. As for if the intended meaning of the two men is other than Yusha' and Kalib, who were from the Amalekites whom the Children of Israel feared, so that "yakhafun" means that the Children of Israel feared them, then the pronoun in this case refers to the Children of Israel, and the returning pronoun (al-'a'id) is omitted, which is the object. According to this, there is no doubt that these two men were not from the Children of Israel upon whom fighting the Amalekites was prescribed. Musa, peace be upon him, meant only: "I have no power over the Children of Israel upon whom fighting is obligated, except over myself and my brother," and Allah knows best.] This is an expression of distress, grief, complaint to Allah, sorrow, and tenderness of heart, by the like of which mercy is attracted and victory is sent down. Similar is the saying of Ya'qub, peace be upon him: ﴿I only complain of my anguish and my grief to Allah﴾.

And from 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, that he used to call people from the pulpit of Kufa to fight the rebels (al-bughat), but none answered him except two men, so he heaved a deep sigh (fatanaffasa al-su'da'). [His words "fatanaffasa al-su'da'": in al-Sihah: "al-su'da' with a damma and a long vowel is a long breath," end. (Editor's note: 'a'.)] He prayed for them and said: "Where do you stand in relation to what I desire?"

Several grammatical analyses are mentioned for the word akhi ("my brother"): it may be in the accusative as a conjunction (ataf) upon nafsi ("myself") or upon the pronoun in inni ("indeed I"), meaning: "and I have no power except over myself, and my brother has no power except over himself." It may be in the nominative as a conjunction upon the position (mahall) of inna and its subject, as if it were said: "I have no power except over myself, and Harun likewise has no power except over himself," or upon the pronoun in la amliku ("I have no power"), and this is permitted because of the separation. It may be in the genitive as a conjunction upon the pronoun in nafsi, but this is weak because of the ugliness of conjoining upon a pronoun of the genitive except by repeating the preposition.

If you say: Were not the two men mentioned with him?

I say: It is as if he did not trust them completely nor felt at ease with their steadfastness, because of what he had tasted over a long period and continuous companionship of his people's conditions, their fickleness, and the hardness of their hearts. So he mentioned only the infallible Prophet about whose matter there is no doubt.

It is also permissible that he said this out of extreme impatience when he heard from them, to minimize those who would agree with him. It is also permissible that he meant: "and whoever brings me into brotherhood upon my religion." ﴿So separate﴾, i.e., judge between us and them by giving us what we deserve and giving them what they deserve, and this is in the sense of a curse upon them. For this reason was joined to it his saying: ﴿for it is forbidden to them﴾ by way of causation, or: "so set us apart from them and deliver us from their companionship," like his saying: ﴿and deliver me from the wrongdoing people﴾. ﴿For it is forbidden to them﴾, i.e., the holy land is forbidden to them; they will not enter it nor will they possess it.

If you say: How can this be reconciled with His saying: ﴿which Allah has prescribed for you﴾?

I say: There are two aspects. The first: that it is meant that He prescribed it for you on condition that you fight its people, so when they refused to fight, it was said: "for it is forbidden to them." The second: that it is meant that it is forbidden to them for forty years, and when the forty years passed, what was prescribed came to pass. It is narrated that Musa set out with those who remained of the Children of Israel, with Yusha' at their vanguard, and he conquered Jericho (Arihaa') and remained there as long as Allah willed, then he died, may Allah's blessings be upon him. It was also said: when Musa died, Yusha' was sent as a prophet, and he informed them that he was the prophet of Allah and that Allah had commanded him to fight the tyrants, so they believed him and pledged allegiance to him, and he went with them to Jericho, killed the tyrants and expelled them, and all of Syria became the Children of Israel's. It was also said: none of those who said ﴿We will never enter it﴾ entered the holy land, and they perished in the wilderness of Tih, and their descendants grew up and fought the tyrants and entered it. The governing element of the adverbial phrase (zarf) is either (muharramah, "forbidden") or (yatihuna, "they wander"). The meaning of ﴿yatihuna fi al-ard﴾ is that they travel in it bewildered, not guided to any path. Al-tih is the desert in which one gets lost. It is narrated that they remained forty years in a region of six farsakhs, walking every day in earnest, until when they tired and in the evening found themselves in the place from which they had set out. The cloud shaded them from the heat of the sun, a pillar of light appeared to them at night illuminating them, and manna and quail were sent down upon them, their hair did not grow long, and whenever a child was born to them, it had a garment like a fingernail that grew with its growth. If you say: Why were they blessed with the cloud's shade and other things while they were being punished? I say: Just as some calamities descend upon the disobedient as a rubbing (ʿarkan) of them, and upon them together with that is manifest blessing. This is like a compassionate father who strikes his child and hurts him so that he may be disciplined and refined, and does not cut off his kindness and benevolence from him. If you say: Were Musa and Harun, peace be upon them both, with them in the wilderness?

I say: This is disputed. It was said they were not with them, because it was a punishment, and Musa had asked his Lord to separate them and the people. It was also said: they were with them, but that was a comfort and safety for them, not a punishment, like the fire for Ibrahim and the angels of torment. It is narrated that Harun died in the wilderness, and Musa died there a year after him.

Yusha' entered Jericho three months after his death. The chiefs (naqaba') died suddenly in the wilderness, except Kalib and Yusha'. ﴿So do not grieve﴾, i.e., do not sorrow over them, because he regretted having prayed against them. It was said: they deserved punishment for their wickedness, so do not grieve or regret.

The two sons of Adam, by his loins: Qabil and Habil. God revealed to Adam that each of them should marry the twin of the other. Qabil's twin was the more beautiful, and her name was Iqlima, so he envied his brother for her and was enraged. Adam then said to them, "Offer a sacrifice, and whichever of you is accepted, I will marry her to him." Habil's offering was accepted, when a fire came down and consumed it, and Qabil's envy and rage increased, and he threatened him with killing. It was also said: they were two men from the Children of Israel. ﴿Recite to them the account truthfully﴾: a recitation accompanied by truth and accuracy. Or: recite to them an account that is true and agrees with what is in the books of the earlier peoples. Or: with the correct purpose, which is to condemn envy, because the polytheists and the People of the Book all used to envy the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and act with hostility toward him.

Or: recite to them while you are sincere and truthful. The phrase ﴿when they offered a sacrifice﴾ is in the accusative, governed by "the account", meaning their story and their news at that time.

It is also permissible for it to be a substitute (badal) for "the account", meaning: recite to them the account, the account of that time, with an elided genitive (mudaf) understood.

The qurban (sacrifice) is the name of what one draws near to God with, whether a sacrificial animal or charity, just as the ḥulwān (gift) is the name of what is given as a gift.

It is said: he offered charity (qarraba ṣadaqatan) and drew near by it (taqarraba bihā), because taqarraba is the intransitive form (muṭāwaʿa) of qarraba. Al-Aṣmaʿī said: "They drew near as the ḥarf (?) ... " [The text reads: "taqarrabū qarf al-qamaʿ"], and it is transitive with bi so that it has the meaning of qarraba. If you ask: how is His saying ﴿God accepts only from the God-conscious﴾ a reply to His saying ﴿I will surely kill you﴾? I say: since the envy of his brother over the acceptance of his offering was what led him to threaten him with killing, he said to him: "You were only brought to this by your own self, through its stripping off the garment of God-consciousness, not by me; so why do you kill me?"

And why do you not reproach yourself, nor compel it to God-consciousness, which is the cause of acceptance? He replied to him with wise, concise speech comprehensive of meanings. In it there is evidence that God does not accept an act except from a believer who is God-conscious, and so how few of those who do deeds have their deeds accepted. It is related from ʿĀmir ibn ʿAbd Allāh that he wept when death approached him. He was asked, "What makes you weep, when you were such-and-such?" He said: "I hear God saying ﴿God accepts only from the God-conscious﴾."

﴿I shall not stretch out my hand toward you to kill you﴾. It was said: he was stronger than the killer and more capable of seizing him, but he abstained from killing his brother and submitted to him out of fear of God, because defending himself was not permissible at that time. This is what Mujāhid and others said.

﴿I want you to bear my sin and your sin﴾: that you should bear the sin of my killing, if I killed you, and the sin of your own killing of me. If you ask: how can he bear the sin of his killing him, when ﴿no bearer of burdens bears the burden of another﴾? I say: the meaning of "the like of my sin" is an extended usage, as you would say: "I read the recitation of so-and-so," and "I wrote the writing of so-and-so," meaning "the like of," and this is a widespread and familiar extension that is hardly ever used otherwise.

Similar to this is His peace and blessings be upon him saying: "The insulting of two people is on the one who starts it, as long as the wronged one does not exceed the limit." (Muslim related it from Abū Hurayra, and al-Bukhārī in al-Adab al-Mufrad related something similar from Anas.) This means that the one who starts it bears the sin of his insulting, and the like of the sin of insulting his companion, because he was the cause of it. However, the sin is removed from his companion and pardoned, because the latter is retaliating and defending his honour. Do you not see His saying "as long as the wronged one does not exceed the limit," because if he goes beyond the limit of retaliation and transgresses, he is not safe?

If you ask: when Habil refrained from killing his brother, submitted, and abstained from what was forbidden in his law of defence, where is the sin, so that his brother should bear its like, and the two sins be combined upon him? I say: it is assumed (muqaddar), so he bears the like of the assumed sin, as if he said: "I want you to bear the like of my sin, had I stretched out my hand to you." It was also said: "my sin" means the sin of my killing, and "your sin" is the one for which your offering was not accepted.

If you ask: how is it permissible that he should wish the wretchedness and punishment of his brother by the Fire? I say: he was a wrongdoer, and the recompense of the wrongdoer is good and permissible to intend.

(Note from the author: "because he does not intend except what is good." This is the doctrine of the Mu'tazila [the rationalist school]. By "the sin" is meant the burden (wabāl) of the killing and what it drags with it of deserving punishment. I say: it is to convey that he does not do what would earn him this shameful description. For this reason he emphasised it with the particle of emphatic negation.

﴿So his soul made the killing of his brother easy for him﴾: it made it spacious and facilitated it for him, from "the pasture was spacious for him" (ṭāʿa lahu al-martaʿ) when it became wide. Al-Ḥasan recited "fa-ṭāwaʿat" (it submitted). In it there are two possibilities: that it is of the type where a form with alif means the same as a plain form, and that it means that the killing of his brother was as if his self called him to undertake it, and it obeyed him and did not refuse. The lām in "lahu" is for added connection, as in your saying: "I preserved for Zayd his wealth."

It was said: he killed him when he was twenty years old, and the killing took place at the Ḥirāʾ ascent (ʿaqabat Ḥirāʾ). It was also said: in Basra, at the site of the Great Mosque.

﴿Then God sent a crow﴾: it is reported that he was the first person killed on the face of the earth among the children of Adam. When he killed him, he left him in the open, not knowing what to do with him. He feared for him from wild beasts, so he carried him on his back in a bag for a year, until he became putrid and the beasts gathered around him. Then God sent two crows, which fought, and one killed the other. It dug a hole for it with its beak and feet, then threw it into the hole.

﴿He said: "Woe is me! Am I unable to be like this crow, and so hide the corpse of my brother?"﴾ It is reported that when he killed him, his body turned black, though it had been white. Adam asked him about his brother, and he said, "I was not a guardian over him." Adam said: "No, you killed him, and that is why your body has turned black."

It is also reported that Adam remained after his killing for a hundred years without laughing, and that he lamented him in verse. That is an utter lie, and poetry is only spurious and corrupted (manḥūl malḥūn). It is well established that the prophets, peace be upon them, are protected from composing poetry.

﴿to show him﴾: to show him, meaning God shows him. Or: to show him, meaning the crow shows him, that is, to teach him, since it was the cause of his instruction; so it is as if its intention was to teach him, by way of metaphor.

﴿the shame of his brother﴾: the nakedness of his brother and what must not be exposed of his body. The word "sawʾa" means disgrace because of its ugliness. A poet said:

"O people, for the great disgrace..."

That is, for the great scandal, and so it is used as a metaphor for it. ﴿that I might hide it﴾ is in the subjunctive as an answer to the interrogative. It is also read with the sukūn (fa-uwārī), as "fa-anā uwārī" (so I hide it), or with sukūn in the place of the accusative for lightness.

﴿from among those who regret﴾: regretting the killing, because of the toil he endured in carrying him, his bewilderment about the matter, the revelation of his incapacity, his being taught by the crow, the blackening of his colour, and his father's anger. But he did not regret with the regret of those who repent.

﴿Because of that﴾: because of that matter and its cause. It was said: its origin is from "min ajl sharr," when one commits it and brings it about, ajala yaʾjulu ajlan. From it is the saying of a poet:

"And the people of a good tent, whose mutual relations are good, have fought over a hasty evil whose instigator I am." 

(These lines are by Khawwāt ibn Jubayr, describing himself as one who stirs up evil and war. He says: "And many a household, that is, close houses as though one house; or it is a metaphor for the closeness of their kinship. It is said: 'ajala al-sharr ajalan' when he committed it and stirred it up, so their fighting was because of it and by its cause. The rebels were then defeated by the evil. So I came asking about them, like your asking about the matter of which you are ignorant." By the simile he indicates that he was not ignorant of them when asking, but was showing them that he was with them and loved them, not their enemies.)

This is shown by the saying "from your doing I did it," meaning: from your having dragged it, that is, committed it. ﴿Because of that﴾ refers to the mentioned killing: that is, because of that killing which they committed and dragged, ﴿We prescribed for the Children of Israel﴾. The "min" here is for the starting point of the action: it began, and the prescription arose because of that.

It is said: "I did such-and-such for such-and-such a reason," and it may be said "ajl such-and-such" with the preposition elided and the verb connected directly, as in the saying: "ajl that God has preferred you." It is also read "min ijl dhālika," with the hamza elided and the nūn given a fatḥa by transferring its vowel to it. Abū Jaʿfar read "min ijl dhālika," with a kasra on the hamza, which is a dialect form; when it is lightened, the nūn takes a kasra, transferring the kasra of the hamza onto it.

It was also said: it means highway robbery. ﴿Whoever gives life to it﴾: whoever rescues it from one of the causes of destruction, whether killing, drowning, burning, demolition, or other things.

If you ask: how did He liken the single one to the whole, and make his ruling like their ruling? I say: because every person has the same claim to honour before God and the inviolability of his sanctity. I say: to magnify the killing of a soul and the giving of life to it in hearts, so that people recoil from boldness against it, and eagerly protect its sanctity. Likewise, when you kill one person, after that, after what We prescribed for them, and after the coming of the messengers with clear signs, ﴿you are indeed extravagant﴾," meaning in killing, not caring for its enormity.

"O people, for the great disgrace..."

It is said: "I did such-and-such for such-and-such a reason," and it may be said "ajl such-and-such" with the preposition elided and the verb connected directly, as in the saying: "ajl that God has preferred you." Or: with the correct purpose, which is to condemn envy, because the polytheists and the People of the Book all used to envy the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and act with hostility toward him.

﴿I shall not stretch out my hand toward you to kill you﴾. It was said: he was stronger than the killer and more capable of seizing him, but he abstained from killing his brother and submitted to him out of fear of God, because defending himself was not permissible at that time. This is what Mujāhid and others said.

﴿I want you to bear my sin and your sin﴾: that you should bear the sin of my killing, if I killed you, and the sin of your own killing of me. "And the people of a good tent, whose mutual relations are good, have fought over a hasty evil whose instigator I am." 

(These lines are by Khawwāt ibn Jubayr, describing himself as one who stirs up evil and war. He says: "And many a household, that is, close houses as though one house; or it is a metaphor for the closeness of their kinship. Their mutual condition is good, yet they have fought because of a hasty evil whose instigator I am, that is, I stirred it up before the battle. There is in this an antithesis. It is said: 'ajala al-sharr ajalan' when he committed it and stirred it up, so their fighting was because of it and by its cause. The rebels were then defeated by the evil. So I came asking about them, like your asking about the matter of which you are ignorant." By the simile he indicates that he was not ignorant of them when asking, but was showing them that he was with them and loved them, not their enemies.)

It is as if, when you say "because of you I did such-and-such," you mean that from your conduct he committed the deed and made it obligatory. This is shown by the saying "from your doing I did it," meaning: from your having dragged it, that is, committed it. ﴿Because of that﴾ refers to the mentioned killing: that is, because of that killing which they committed and dragged, ﴿We prescribed for the Children of Israel﴾. The "min" here is for the starting point of the action: it began, and the prescription arose because of that.

It is said: "I did such-and-such for such-and-such a reason," and it may be said "ajl such-and-such" with the preposition elided and the verb connected directly, as in the saying: "ajl that God has preferred you." It is also read "min ijl dhālika," with the hamza elided and the nūn given a fatḥa by transferring its vowel to it. Abū Jaʿfar read "min ijl dhālika," with a kasra on the hamza, which is a dialect form; when it is lightened, the nūn takes a kasra, transferring the kasra of the hamza onto it.

﴿without a soul﴾: without killing a soul, not by way of retaliation. ﴿or corruption﴾ is coordinated with "soul," meaning: or without corruption on earth, which is polytheism.

It was also said: it means highway robbery. ﴿Whoever gives life to it﴾: whoever rescues it from one of the causes of destruction, whether killing, drowning, burning, demolition, or other things.

If you ask: how did He liken the single one to the whole, and make his ruling like their ruling? I say: because every person has the same claim to honour before God and the inviolability of his sanctity. So when someone is killed, what God has honoured is humiliated and its sanctity violated, and the reverse also holds. So there is no difference, then, between the one and the whole in this respect.

If you ask: what is the benefit of mentioning this? I say: to magnify the killing of a soul and the giving of life to it in hearts, so that people recoil from boldness against it, and eagerly protect its sanctity. For whoever contemplates killing a soul, when he imagines it as the killing of all people, that weighs heavily on him and restrains him; and likewise the one who intends to save it.

It is related from Mujāhid: "The recompense of one who kills a soul is Hell, and the wrath of God, and a tremendous punishment. Even if he killed all people, he would gain nothing more than this." It is related from al-Ḥasan: "O son of Adam, do you think, if you killed all people, you could hope for a deed that would balance that, so that you would be forgiven by it? No, it is a thing your self and Satan have made attractive to you. Likewise, when you kill one person, after that, after what We prescribed for them, and after the coming of the messengers with clear signs, ﴿you are indeed extravagant﴾," meaning in killing, not caring for its enormity.

The two sons of Adam, by his loins: Qabil and Habil. God revealed to Adam that each of them should marry the twin of the other. Qabil's twin was the more beautiful, and her name was Iqlima, so he envied his brother for her and was enraged. Adam then said to them, "Offer a sacrifice, and whichever of you is accepted, I will marry her to him." Habil's offering was accepted, when a fire came down and consumed it, and Qabil's envy and rage increased, and he threatened him with killing. It was also said: they were two men from the Children of Israel. ﴿Recite to them the account truthfully﴾: a recitation accompanied by truth and accuracy. Or: recite to them an account that is true and agrees with what is in the books of the earlier peoples. Or: with the correct purpose, which is to condemn envy, because the polytheists and the People of the Book all used to envy the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and act with hostility toward him.

Or: recite to them while you are sincere and truthful. The phrase ﴿when they offered a sacrifice﴾ is in the accusative, governed by "the account", meaning their story and their news at that time.

It is also permissible for it to be a substitute (badal) for "the account", meaning: recite to them the account, the account of that time, with an elided genitive (mudaf) understood.

The qurban (sacrifice) is the name of what one draws near to God with, whether a sacrificial animal or charity, just as the ḥulwān (gift) is the name of what is given as a gift.

It is said: he offered charity (qarraba ṣadaqatan) and drew near by it (taqarraba bihā), because taqarraba is the intransitive form (muṭāwaʿa) of qarraba. Al-Aṣmaʿī said: "They drew near as the ḥarf (?) ... " [The text reads: "taqarrabū qarf al-qamaʿ"], and it is transitive with bi so that it has the meaning of qarraba. If you ask: how is His saying ﴿God accepts only from the God-conscious﴾ a reply to His saying ﴿I will surely kill you﴾? I say: since the envy of his brother over the acceptance of his offering was what led him to threaten him with killing, he said to him: "You were only brought to this by your own self, through its stripping off the garment of God-consciousness, not by me; so why do you kill me?"

And why do you not reproach yourself, nor compel it to God-consciousness, which is the cause of acceptance? He replied to him with wise, concise speech comprehensive of meanings. In it there is evidence that God does not accept an act except from a believer who is God-conscious, and so how few of those who do deeds have their deeds accepted. It is related from ʿĀmir ibn ʿAbd Allāh that he wept when death approached him. He was asked, "What makes you weep, when you were such-and-such?" He said: "I hear God saying ﴿God accepts only from the God-conscious﴾."

﴿I shall not stretch out my hand toward you to kill you﴾. It was said: he was stronger than the killer and more capable of seizing him, but he abstained from killing his brother and submitted to him out of fear of God, because defending himself was not permissible at that time. This is what Mujāhid and others said.

﴿I want you to bear my sin and your sin﴾: that you should bear the sin of my killing, if I killed you, and the sin of your own killing of me. If you ask: how can he bear the sin of his killing him, when ﴿no bearer of burdens bears the burden of another﴾? I say: the meaning of "the like of my sin" is an extended usage, as you would say: "I read the recitation of so-and-so," and "I wrote the writing of so-and-so," meaning "the like of," and this is a widespread and familiar extension that is hardly ever used otherwise.

Similar to this is His peace and blessings be upon him saying: "The insulting of two people is on the one who starts it, as long as the wronged one does not exceed the limit." (Muslim related it from Abū Hurayra, and al-Bukhārī in al-Adab al-Mufrad related something similar from Anas.) This means that the one who starts it bears the sin of his insulting, and the like of the sin of insulting his companion, because he was the cause of it. However, the sin is removed from his companion and pardoned, because the latter is retaliating and defending his honour. Do you not see His saying "as long as the wronged one does not exceed the limit," because if he goes beyond the limit of retaliation and transgresses, he is not safe?

If you ask: when Habil refrained from killing his brother, submitted, and abstained from what was forbidden in his law of defence, where is the sin, so that his brother should bear its like, and the two sins be combined upon him? I say: it is assumed (muqaddar), so he bears the like of the assumed sin, as if he said: "I want you to bear the like of my sin, had I stretched out my hand to you." It was also said: "my sin" means the sin of my killing, and "your sin" is the one for which your offering was not accepted.

If you ask: how is it permissible that he should wish the wretchedness and punishment of his brother by the Fire? I say: he was a wrongdoer, and the recompense of the wrongdoer is good and permissible to intend.

Do you not see His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿and that is the recompense of the wrongdoers﴾? If it is permissible for God to intend it, it is permissible for the servant to intend it, because he does not intend except what is good.

(Note from the author: "because he does not intend except what is good." This is the doctrine of the Mu'tazila [the rationalist school]. As for the Ahl al-Sunna [People of the Sunna], God wills every existent thing, whether good or ugly, as is established in the science of divine unity (tawḥīd). — ʿ)

By "the sin" is meant the burden (wabāl) of the killing and what it drags with it of deserving punishment. If you ask: why did the condition come with a verb form while the consequence came with an active participle form, ﴿if you stretch out your hand﴾ and ﴿I am not one who stretches out...﴾? I say: it is to convey that he does not do what would earn him this shameful description. For this reason he emphasised it with the particle of emphatic negation.

﴿So his soul made the killing of his brother easy for him﴾: it made it spacious and facilitated it for him, from "the pasture was spacious for him" (ṭāʿa lahu al-martaʿ) when it became wide. Al-Ḥasan recited "fa-ṭāwaʿat" (it submitted). In it there are two possibilities: that it is of the type where a form with alif means the same as a plain form, and that it means that the killing of his brother was as if his self called him to undertake it, and it obeyed him and did not refuse. The lām in "lahu" is for added connection, as in your saying: "I preserved for Zayd his wealth."

It was said: he killed him when he was twenty years old, and the killing took place at the Ḥirāʾ ascent (ʿaqabat Ḥirāʾ). It was also said: in Basra, at the site of the Great Mosque.

﴿Then God sent a crow﴾: it is reported that he was the first person killed on the face of the earth among the children of Adam. When he killed him, he left him in the open, not knowing what to do with him. He feared for him from wild beasts, so he carried him on his back in a bag for a year, until he became putrid and the beasts gathered around him. Then God sent two crows, which fought, and one killed the other. It dug a hole for it with its beak and feet, then threw it into the hole.

﴿He said: "Woe is me! Am I unable to be like this crow, and so hide the corpse of my brother?"﴾ It is reported that when he killed him, his body turned black, though it had been white. Adam asked him about his brother, and he said, "I was not a guardian over him." Adam said: "No, you killed him, and that is why your body has turned black."

It is also reported that Adam remained after his killing for a hundred years without laughing, and that he lamented him in verse. That is an utter lie, and poetry is only spurious and corrupted (manḥūl malḥūn). It is well established that the prophets, peace be upon them, are protected from composing poetry.

﴿to show him﴾: to show him, meaning God shows him. Or: to show him, meaning the crow shows him, that is, to teach him, since it was the cause of his instruction; so it is as if its intention was to teach him, by way of metaphor.

﴿the shame of his brother﴾: the nakedness of his brother and what must not be exposed of his body. The word "sawʾa" means disgrace because of its ugliness. A poet said:

"O people, for the great disgrace..."

That is, for the great scandal, and so it is used as a metaphor for it. ﴿that I might hide it﴾ is in the subjunctive as an answer to the interrogative. It is also read with the sukūn (fa-uwārī), as "fa-anā uwārī" (so I hide it), or with sukūn in the place of the accusative for lightness.

﴿from among those who regret﴾: regretting the killing, because of the toil he endured in carrying him, his bewilderment about the matter, the revelation of his incapacity, his being taught by the crow, the blackening of his colour, and his father's anger. But he did not regret with the regret of those who repent.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 5, verses 33–34:

﴿Those who wage war against Allah and His Messenger﴾: they wage war against the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). Waging war against the Muslims is in the ruling of waging war against him. ﴿and strive upon the earth, spreading corruption﴾: they are corrupters. Or, because their striving upon the earth was along the path of corruption, it was placed in the position of ﴿and they cause corruption upon the earth﴾, so فسادا (fasadan, "corruption") is in the accusative on the basis of the meaning. It is also permissible for it to be a مفعول له (maf'ul lahu, the accusative of purpose), meaning "for corruption."

It was revealed concerning the people of Hilal ibn Uways, between whom and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) there was a covenant. A group who were seeking the Messenger of Allah passed by them, and they intercepted them. It was also said that it was revealed concerning the 'Uraniyyin. So it was revealed to him that whoever combines killing with taking property is to be killed and crucified, and whoever commits only killing is to be killed. Whoever commits only taking property, his hand is cut off for taking property and his foot for terrorizing the road. Whoever commits only terrorizing is exiled from the land. It was also said that this is the ruling for every highwayman, whether he is a disbeliever or a Muslim.

Its meaning is: ﴿that they be killed﴾ without crucifixion, if they commit only killing; ﴿or crucified﴾ along with killing, if they combine killing and taking. Abu Hanifa and Muhammad, may Allah have mercy on them both, said: he is crucified alive and stabbed until he dies. ﴿Or their hands and feet be cut off on alternate sides﴾ if they take property, ﴿or they be exiled from the land﴾ if they do not exceed terrorizing.

From a group of scholars, including al-Hasan and al-Nakha'i, it is reported that the ruler has a choice among these punishments for every highwayman, without detail. Exile (al-nafy) is, according to Abu Hanifa, imprisonment; according to al-Shafi'i, it is banishment from one city to another, so that he is always sought, fleeing in fear. It was also said that he is banished from his own land. They used to exile them to Dahlak, a land at the farthest end of Tihama, and Nasi', which is a land of the lands of Abyssinia.

﴿Disgrace﴾: humiliation and scandal.

﴿Except for those who repent﴾: an exception from those punished with the punishment of highway robbery specifically. As for the ruling on killing, wounding and taking property, it rests with the victims' heirs: if they wish they may pardon, and if they wish they may exact the full retribution.

It is reported from 'Ali (may Allah be pleased with him) that al-Harith ibn Badr [[Ibn Abi Shayba transmitted it from the narration of Mujalid from al-Sha'bi. He said: Harithah ibn Badr al-Tamimi had caused corruption upon the earth and waged war, and he mentioned the story of this in it.]] came to him repentant after he had been committing highway robbery, and he accepted his repentance and averted the punishment from him.

The wasila: everything by which one seeks nearness (yatawassal), i.e., draws near, through kinship, a favour, or otherwise. It was borrowed for that by which one seeks nearness to God Most High, namely performing acts of obedience and abandoning acts of disobedience. He recited [a verse] by Labid:

[[Do you not ask the man what he is striving for: is it a vow to be fulfilled, so it is granted, or is it error and falsehood?

I see people not knowing the worth of their affair; surely every man of intellect is one who seeks nearness to God.

Surely everything other than God is false, and every blessing is inevitably transient.

And every people, a calamity will surely enter among them, from which the fingertips will tremble.]]

This is by Labid ibn Rabi'a al-Amiri. The interrogative hamza followed by a negation is for urging (tahdid) to action, meaning: ask him and say to him: what is it that you want and exert yourself to attain? He used the third-person form, considering the apparent wording of "I see" (ara). Addressing a dual is a customary usage among the Arabs, even though another is intended. His words "anahb" (is it a vow) replace "ma" (what). Al-nahb means a vow, a determination, and haste, just as al-na'b, with an 'ayn, means haste. That is: is it a sound aim, so that it is granted to him, or is it false, so that it is not befitting? Or the meaning is: is it something he has obligated upon himself, so he strives to fulfil it, or is it error?

In any case, it is not befitting. His words "what is the worth of their affair" mean: what is it that they are engaged in of worldly concerns, and the swiftness of their perishing? "Alā" is an introductory particle. "Every man of intellect" means one with reason, "seeking nearness" to God and not to other than Him, i.e., one who takes refuge in Him and seeks protection with Him from the evil of this world and the evil of one who has no reason, or who draws near to Him by what benefits him. It is also related as "bala kull," which is stronger in meaning, because it is a rejection of the claim of generalization in the preceding line. It is also related as "wasil" with a ṣād, meaning one who proceeds or turns wholly (toward Him). It is permissible to interpret both this and "wasil" as meaning one who draws near to God through obedience, not one occupied with the transient world like other ignorant people. "False" is the predicate of "everything," and "transient" is the predicate of "every blessing." "La mahala" is an emphatic parenthetical clause.

"Al-duwayhiya" is the diminutive of "al-dahiya," which is death (al-maniyya), as indicated by what follows. Its diminutive form is for magnification and terror, or for belittling, according to the assumption of the heedless and the negligent.

To ransom themselves with it: that is, so that they may make it a ransom for their own souls. This is a metaphor for the inescapability of punishment for them, and that there is no way at all for them to be saved from it.

It is narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ): "It will be said to the disbeliever on the Day of Resurrection: 'Had you the whole earth full of gold, would you ransom yourself with it?' He will say: 'Yes.' It will be said to him: 'You were asked for something far easier than that.'" [[Agreed upon (Bukhari and Muslim), from the narration of Qatada from Anas, may Allah be pleased with him.]] The phrase "law" (if) together with what it governs is the predicate of "inna" (indeed).

If you ask: why is the pronoun in His words ﴿ليفتدوا به﴾ singular, when two things have been mentioned? I answer: it is like the words of the poet:

*Desire and longing called you when the cooing dove sang sweetly among the branches in the morning, ...*
*The doves answered one another, and they listened to her voice, so each one responds to and answers the other.*
*Whoever has his camel-saddle in Medina at evening, as for me and Qayyar, we are strangers there.*

This was said by Dabi' ibn al-Harith al-Barjumi when Uthman ibn Affan (may Allah be pleased with him) imprisoned him for satirizing the Banu Nahshal. "Tarannuh" means swaying. It is also narrated as "tarannumat," meaning she sang beautifully. "Hatafat" means the dove cooed when she warbled, so "hatuf" means alone. "Bayna" is an adverbial complement of "tarannuh." "Tarub" is an intensive form of "tarab" (joy), used of both masculine and feminine, like "hatuf." It is the subject, and "hatuf" is a circumstantial clause; its annexation does not make it definite in meaning. It is permissible to put it in the nominative as the subject, and "tarub" is its adjective, since it is a descriptive phrase that is annexed and so has no definiteness in form either.

"Al-warq" is the plural of "waraa," a type of dove. "Asakhna" means they inclined and listened. It is also narrated as "ar'an," but I have not found "ra'ana" in the lexicons except with the meaning of growing and increasing, so perhaps its meaning is "they became active" in a figurative sense. It is also narrated as "wa-man yak" with a waw. The pronoun in the nominative for "amsa" refers back to "man."

The clause "bil-Madina rahluhu" (his saddle is in Medina) is its predicate, and the clause is the predicate of "yakun." It is permissible that the nominative of "amsa" is "rahluhu" itself, and the answer to the condition is omitted, meaning: whoever has his saddle in Medina at evening, his condition is good, unlike my condition, for I am a stranger, because my saddle (that is, my dwelling) is not there; there is only me and my horse. "Qayyar" is the name of his horse. It has been said it is his camel, and it has been said his servant. It is either a subject, or it is conjoined to the position of the noun of "inna," whose predicate is omitted for brevity since what is mentioned indicates it. So the conjunction is a conjunction of sentences or of single words. In it there is conjunction before the completion of what is conjoined, but it is on the intention of fronting and postponement. It is a transmitted usage, and one may not analogize from it. It is not permissible to make "gharib" (stranger) the predicate of both, lest two governors act upon one governed element, nor to make it the predicate of Qayyar, because the lam of the initial particle does not enter upon a postponed predicate. The verse is grammatically a statement, but in meaning it expresses lament and sorrow, because he is a stranger and alone.

Or the pronoun is treated like a demonstrative, as if it were said: "to ransom themselves with that." It is also permissible that the waw in ﴿مثله﴾ (its like) means "with," so the referent is singular.

**Al-Zamakhshari's commentary (al-Kashshaf) on Surah 5, verses 38–40:**

﴿وَالسَّارِقُ وَالسَّارِقَةُ﴾ — he (al-Zamakhshari) says: "Their being in the nominative (*raf'ahuma*) is because they are the subject of a nominal sentence (*al-ibtida'*), with the predicate omitted." [[He says: "Their being in the nominative is because they are the subject of a nominal sentence (*al-ibtida'*), with the predicate omitted, according to Sibawayh, as if it were said:" ... etc.]] Ahmad (Ibn al-Munayyir) says: "What is deduced from the various readings is that the common readers never agree upon deviating from the more eloquent form. It is fitting for the Qur'an to proceed according to the most eloquent of the possibilities, and not to be devoid of the most eloquent and what the speech of the Arabs includes, none of whom reached the peak of its eloquence or clung to its fringes."

And Sibawayh is too exalted to be thought to hold that the poets of the Qur'an deviate from the most eloquent form, or that it includes the anomalous (*shadhdh*) which is not counted as Qur'an. We shall cite the passage from Sibawayh's words on this verse so that its hearer may see Sibawayh's freedom from responsibility for this transmission. He said, in the section heading on the imperative and prohibition, after mentioning the places where the accusative is preferred: "In summary, whenever the noun is built upon an imperative verb, that is a place where the accusative is preferred." Then he said, as an indication of what distinguishes this verse from those in which the accusative is preferred: "As for the saying of the Mighty and Majestic: ﴿And the male thief and the female thief, cut off their hands﴾ ... and His saying: ﴿The adulteress and the adulterer, flog them﴾, this is not built upon the verb, but came on the pattern of His saying: ﴿The parable of the Garden which the God-fearing have been promised﴾, then after ﴿in it are rivers﴾, [he says] 'in it is such-and-such' ..."

I say: Sibawayh intends to distinguish these verses from the places in which the accusative is preferred, and the basis of the distinction is that where the accusative is preferred the noun is built upon the verb; but in these verses it is not built upon it, so the accusative is not required here. Sibawayh's speech continues: "The parable was only placed for the narrative mentioned after it, so he mentioned reports and stories, as if he had said: 'and among the stories is the parable of the Garden,' so it is carried on this omission, and God knows best." Likewise, "the adulteress and the adulterer": when He, Mighty is His praise, said: ﴿A surah which We have sent down and made obligatory﴾, in the list of obligations He said ﴿the adulteress and the adulterer﴾, then ﴿flog them﴾ came after the nominative had already been established in it.

I say: Sibawayh intends that the noun was not built upon the verb mentioned afterwards; rather it was built upon an earlier omitted element, and the verb came incidentally. His speech continues: "as in the line of verse:

*And a speaker of the tribe of Khawlan said: 'Marry their girl.'*

So the verb came after the implied element had governed it. Likewise ﴿And the male thief and the female thief﴾, meaning, 'and in what is obligated upon you is the male thief and the female thief,' for these nouns entered after stories and narratives."

Some people read ﴿al-sariqu wa al-sariqatu﴾ with the accusative, and it is, in Arabic, as strong as I have mentioned to you; but the common readers refused except the nominative. I say: Sibawayh means that in the accusative reading the noun is built upon the verb, not dependent on an earlier element, so the accusative is strong relative to the nominative in that the noun is built upon the verb rather than upon an earlier element. He does not mean that it is stronger than the nominative in the case where the noun depends on an earlier omitted element, for he has made clear that this removes it from the category in which the accusative is preferred. How, then, is his preference of it over that understood, when the category differs between the two readings? Preference only occurs after equality within the category: the accusative is preferred over the nominative where the noun is built upon the verb and the nominative is obligatory. I do not say it is preferable where the noun is built upon an earlier speech. Then Sibawayh confirmed this assumed element by saying that the speech occurs after stories and reports. Had it been as al-Zamakhshari supposed, Sibawayh would not have needed an assumption, but would have put it in the nominative as a subject with the imperative as its predicate, as al-Zamakhshari parsed it. So the summary on this basis is: the accusative has one way, namely building the noun upon the imperative verb; the nominative has two ways: one weak, namely the subject (*al-ibtida'*) with the speech built upon the verb, and the other strong and complete, like the accusative way, namely its being in the nominative as predicate of an omitted subject indicated by the context. Whenever two nominative possibilities conflict for us, one strong and the other weak, the reading must be taken as the strong one, as Sibawayh parsed it, may God be pleased with him. And God the Exalted knows best.

﴿fa-qta'u aydiyahuma﴾ — "then cut off their hands." He (al-Zamakhshari) says: The second possibility is that they are in the nominative as the subject (*mubtada'*), and the predicate is ﴿fa-qta'u aydiyahuma﴾, and the particle *fa'* enters because they include the meaning of a conditional, since the meaning is: "the one who stole, male, and the one who stole, female, cut off their hands," and the relative pronoun includes the meaning of the condition.

ʿIsa ibn ʿUmar read it with the accusative, and Sibawayh preferred it over the reading of the common readers because of the imperative, since "Zaydan fa-iḍribhu" ("Zayd, so strike him") is better than "Zaydun fa-iḍribhu."

﴿aydiyahuma﴾ — "their hands": the dual of the genitive is used for the dual of the subject, and similar to it is ﴿fa-qad ṣaghat qulubukuma﴾ ("your hearts have indeed inclined"), where the dual of the second term was sufficient instead of the dual of the first. By "the two hands" are meant the two right hands, as shown by ʿAbd Allah's reading: "the male thieves and the female thieves, cut off their right hands" (*fa-qta'u aymanahum*).

The thief in the sacred law is one who steals from a protected place (*min al-ḥirz*). The amputation is at the wrist (*al-rusgh*). According to the Khawarij it is at the shoulder (*al-mankib*). The amount that makes amputation obligatory is ten dirhams according to Abu Hanifa; according to Malik and al-Shafi'i, may God have mercy on them, it is a quarter of a dinar. From al-Hasan (it is) a dirham. And in his admonitions: "Beware of cutting your hand for a dirham."

﴿jaza'an wa nakalan﴾ — "as a recompense and as an exemplary punishment," two objects of purpose (*maf'ul lahuma*).

﴿fa-man taba min ba'di zulmihi wa aslaḥa fa-inna Allaha yatubu 'alayhi﴾ — "Whoever repents after his wrongdoing": after his theft; "and amends (his conduct)": by freeing himself from liabilities; "then God will turn to him": and will remove from him the punishment of the Hereafter. As for the amputation, repentance does not remove it according to Abu Hanifa and his companions; according to al-Shafi'i in one of his two opinions, it removes it.

﴿Allaha ya'dhdhibu man yasha'u wa yaghfiru li-man yasha'u﴾ — "God punishes whom He wills and forgives whom He wills": whom wisdom requires to be punished, and whom He forgives, of the persistent and the repentant. It is said: the prescribed penalty for the enemy alien (*al-harbi*) who steals is dropped by repentance, so that he may be more inclined toward Islam and further from being repelled from it; but it is not dropped for a Muslim, [[His saying "and it is not dropped for a Muslim": perhaps "and it is not dropped" or "and repentance does not drop it." (ʿ)]] because in its enforcement is the welfare of the believers and life, as in ﴿and for you in retaliation there is life﴾.

If you say: why did he put punishment before forgiveness? I say: because the theft preceded the repentance, and punishment was set against it.

[[Al-Zamakhshari said: "If you say, why did he put punishment before forgiveness...?" Ahmad (Ibn al-Munayyir) says: this is based on the view that the forgiven are the repentant, and the punished are the thieves. He does not make forgiveness dependent on will except with the condition of repentance, since for one who does not repent, in his view, God cannot will to forgive him; so the general statement is restricted to what was mentioned earlier. We believe that forgiveness toward an unrepentant monotheist depends on will, so that among what falls under the generality of His saying ﴿and He forgives whom He wills﴾ is the thief who has not repented. On this view, the placing of punishment first is because the context is one of warning, so it suits the placing first of what befits it of deterrents; and God knows best.]]
