I say: Sibawayh intends to distinguish these verses from the places in which the accusative is preferred, and the basis of the distinction is that where the accusative is preferred the noun is built upon the verb; but in these verses it is not built upon it, so the accusative is not required here. Sibawayh's speech continues: "The parable was only placed for the narrative mentioned after it, so he mentioned reports and stories, as if he had said: 'and among the stories is the parable of the Garden,' so it is carried on this omission, and God knows best." Likewise, "the adulteress and the adulterer": when He, Mighty is His praise, said: ﴿A surah which We have sent down and made obligatory﴾, in the list of obligations He said ﴿the adulteress and the adulterer﴾, then ﴿flog them﴾ came after the nominative had already been established in it.

I say: Sibawayh intends that the noun was not built upon the verb mentioned afterwards; rather it was built upon an earlier omitted element, and the verb came incidentally. His speech continues: "as in the line of verse:

*And a speaker of the tribe of Khawlan said: 'Marry their girl.'*

So the verb came after the implied element had governed it. Likewise ﴿And the male thief and the female thief﴾, meaning, 'and in what is obligated upon you is the male thief and the female thief,' for these nouns entered after stories and narratives."

Some people read ﴿al-sariqu wa al-sariqatu﴾ with the accusative, and it is, in Arabic, as strong as I have mentioned to you; but the common readers refused except the nominative. I say: Sibawayh means that in the accusative reading the noun is built upon the verb, not dependent on an earlier element, so the accusative is strong relative to the nominative in that the noun is built upon the verb rather than upon an earlier element. He does not mean that it is stronger than the nominative in the case where the noun depends on an earlier omitted element, for he has made clear that this removes it from the category in which the accusative is preferred. How, then, is his preference of it over that understood, when the category differs between the two readings? Preference only occurs after equality within the category: the accusative is preferred over the nominative where the noun is built upon the verb and the nominative is obligatory. I do not say it is preferable where the noun is built upon an earlier speech. Then Sibawayh confirmed this assumed element by saying that the speech occurs after stories and reports. Had it been as al-Zamakhshari supposed, Sibawayh would not have needed an assumption, but would have put it in the nominative as a subject with the imperative as its predicate, as al-Zamakhshari parsed it. So the summary on this basis is: the accusative has one way, namely building the noun upon the imperative verb; the nominative has two ways: one weak, namely the subject (*al-ibtida'*) with the speech built upon the verb, and the other strong and complete, like the accusative way, namely its being in the nominative as predicate of an omitted subject indicated by the context. Whenever two nominative possibilities conflict for us, one strong and the other weak, the reading must be taken as the strong one, as Sibawayh parsed it, may God be pleased with him. And God the Exalted knows best.

﴿fa-qta'u aydiyahuma﴾ — "then cut off their hands." He (al-Zamakhshari) says: The second possibility is that they are in the nominative as the subject (*mubtada'*), and the predicate is ﴿fa-qta'u aydiyahuma﴾, and the particle *fa'* enters because they include the meaning of a conditional, since the meaning is: "the one who stole, male, and the one who stole, female, cut off their hands," and the relative pronoun includes the meaning of the condition.

ʿIsa ibn ʿUmar read it with the accusative, and Sibawayh preferred it over the reading of the common readers because of the imperative, since "Zaydan fa-iḍribhu" ("Zayd, so strike him") is better than "Zaydun fa-iḍribhu."

﴿aydiyahuma﴾ — "their hands": the dual of the genitive is used for the dual of the subject, and similar to it is ﴿fa-qad ṣaghat qulubukuma﴾ ("your hearts have indeed inclined"), where the dual of the second term was sufficient instead of the dual of the first. By "the two hands" are meant the two right hands, as shown by ʿAbd Allah's reading: "the male thieves and the female thieves, cut off their right hands" (*fa-qta'u aymanahum*).

The thief in the sacred law is one who steals from a protected place (*min al-ḥirz*). The amputation is at the wrist (*al-rusgh*). According to the Khawarij it is at the shoulder (*al-mankib*). The amount that makes amputation obligatory is ten dirhams according to Abu Hanifa; according to Malik and al-Shafi'i, may God have mercy on them, it is a quarter of a dinar. From al-Hasan (it is) a dirham. And in his admonitions: "Beware of cutting your hand for a dirham."

﴿jaza'an wa nakalan﴾ — "as a recompense and as an exemplary punishment," two objects of purpose (*maf'ul lahuma*).

﴿fa-man taba min ba'di zulmihi wa aslaḥa fa-inna Allaha yatubu 'alayhi﴾ — "Whoever repents after his wrongdoing": after his theft; "and amends (his conduct)": by freeing himself from liabilities; "then God will turn to him": and will remove from him the punishment of the Hereafter. As for the amputation, repentance does not remove it according to Abu Hanifa and his companions; according to al-Shafi'i in one of his two opinions, it removes it.

﴿Allaha ya'dhdhibu man yasha'u wa yaghfiru li-man yasha'u﴾ — "God punishes whom He wills and forgives whom He wills": whom wisdom requires to be punished, and whom He forgives, of the persistent and the repentant. It is said: the prescribed penalty for the enemy alien (*al-harbi*) who steals is dropped by repentance, so that he may be more inclined toward Islam and further from being repelled from it; but it is not dropped for a Muslim, [[His saying "and it is not dropped for a Muslim": perhaps "and it is not dropped" or "and repentance does not drop it." (ʿ)]] because in its enforcement is the welfare of the believers and life, as in ﴿and for you in retaliation there is life﴾.

If you say: why did he put punishment before forgiveness? I say: because the theft preceded the repentance, and punishment was set against it.

[[Al-Zamakhshari said: "If you say, why did he put punishment before forgiveness...?" Ahmad (Ibn al-Munayyir) says: this is based on the view that the forgiven are the repentant, and the punished are the thieves. He does not make forgiveness dependent on will except with the condition of repentance, since for one who does not repent, in his view, God cannot will to forgive him; so the general statement is restricted to what was mentioned earlier. We believe that forgiveness toward an unrepentant monotheist depends on will, so that among what falls under the generality of His saying ﴿and He forgives whom He wills﴾ is the thief who has not repented. On this view, the placing of punishment first is because the context is one of warning, so it suits the placing first of what befits it of deterrents; and God knows best.]]

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 5, verse 41:

It was recited as *lā yaḥzunka* (with a *ḍamma* on the *yā'*), and *yusāri'ūn*. The meaning is: do not be concerned or troubled by the hastening of the hypocrites into disbelief, that is, their display of it through what appears from them of plotting against Islam and of allying themselves with the polytheists. I will surely support you against them and suffice you against their evil. It is said: "the gray hair hastened into him" (*asra'a fīhi al-shayb*) and "corruption hastened into him" (*asra'a fīhi al-fasād*), meaning that it fell upon him quickly. Likewise, their hastening into disbelief, their falling into it and their rushing headlong into it, is the swiftest of things: whenever they find an opportunity, they do not miss it. *Āmannā* is the object of *qālū*, and *bi-afwāhihim* is attached to *qālū*, not to *āmannā*. *Wa-min alladhīna hādū* is a separate clause (*munqaṭi'*) from what precedes it; it is the predicate of *sammā'ūn*, meaning: and among the Jews there are people who are *sammā'ūn* (listeners). It is permissible that it be conjoined to *min alladhīna qālū*, with *sammā'ūn* in the nominative as in "they are *sammā'ūn*." The pronoun refers to both groups, or to those who became Jews. The meaning of *sammā'ūna lil-kadhib* is: accepting what the rabbis fabricate and invent of falsehood against God and of distortion of His Book, from your saying "the king hears the words of so-and-so." From this comes the hadith: "God hears those who praise Him" (*sami'a Allāh liman ḥamidah*). *Sammā'ūna li-qawmin ākharīna lam ya'tūk* means: the Jews who did not come to the gathering of the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and who kept away from him because of the excessive hatred and extreme enmity that had overcome them; that is, they accept from the rabbis and from those people who were extreme in enmity, who cannot bear to look at you. It has also been said: the *sammā'ūn* are listening to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) in order to lie about him, by distorting what they heard from him through addition, subtraction, substitution and alteration; they listen to the Messenger of God for the sake of other people among the Jews who sent them as spies to convey to them what they had heard from him. It has also been said: the *sammā'ūn* are the Banu Qurayza, and the "other people" are the Jews of Khaybar. *Yuḥarrifūna al-kalima* means: they turn the word aside and remove it *min ba'di mawāḍi'ihi*, from its places which God, exalted is He, had placed it in, so they put it in places other than its own, after it had had its proper places. *In ūtītum hādhā al-muḥarraf al-muzāl 'an mawāḍi'ihi* means: if you are given this distorted word that has been removed from its places, *fa-khudhūhu*, then take it, and know that it is the truth and act upon it. *Wa-in lam tu'tawhu*, and if you are not given it, that is, if Muhammad has ruled against it for you, *fa-iḥdharū*, then beware of it and of him, for it is falsehood and error.

It is narrated that a nobleman from Khaybar committed adultery with a noblewoman, and both were *muḥṣan* (married), and their punishment in the Torah is stoning. They disliked stoning them because of their nobility, so they sent a group of their men to the Banu Qurayza to ask the Messenger of God (ﷺ) about this, and they said: "If Muhammad orders you to flog and blacken them (*al-taḥmīm*), [[The phrase "al-tahmīm" means blackening. In al-Sihah, "al-ḥumma" with a *ḍamma* means blackness. (ʿA.)]] then accept it; but if he orders you to stone them, then do not accept it." They also sent the two adulterers with them. He ordered them to be stoned, but they refused to act upon it. Then Gabriel said to him: "Make between you and them Ibn Ṣūriyā." So he said: "Do you know a young, beardless, fair-skinned, one-eyed man who lives in Fadak, called Ibn Ṣūriyā?" They said: "Yes, he is the most learned Jew on the face of the earth." They accepted him as an arbitrator. The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said to him: "I adjure you by God, there is no god but Him, who split the sea for Moses, raised the mountain above you, saved you and drowned the family of Pharaoh, and who sent down to you His Book, its lawful and its unlawful: do you find in it the stoning of the one who is married?" He said: "Yes." Then the lowly Jews leapt upon him. He said: "I feared that if I lied to him, a punishment would come down upon us." Then the Messenger of God (ﷺ) asked him about things that he knew from the signs of his prophethood, and he said: "I bear witness that there is no god but God, and that you are the Messenger of God, the unlettered Arab Prophet whom the messengers gave good news of." The Messenger of God (ﷺ) then ordered the two adulterers, and they were stoned near the door of his mosque. [[Ibn Ishaq recorded it in al-Maghazi: "Ibn Shihab related to me: I heard a man from Muzayna narrating to Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib from Abu Hurayra," and he mentioned it, omitting its beginning, and omitting his saying in it: "Gabriel said to him: 'Make between you and them Ibn Ṣūriyā,' so he said: 'Do you know a young, beardless, fair-skinned, one-eyed man who lives in Fadak?'" and omitting what is at its end. Likewise al-Bayhaqi recorded it in al-Dala'il from the narration of Ma'mar from al-Zuhri in full, adding the story of the king who had committed adultery among them and whom they did not stone; its origin is in the two Sahihs from the hadith of Abu Hurayra and others, in abridged form.]] *Wa-man yuridi Allāhu fitnatahu*, "and whoever God wills to be in trial": He leaves him *maftūnan*, afflicted by trial, [[Mahmud (al-Zamakhshari) said: "The meaning of 'and whoever God wills to be in trial' is: whoever He wills to leave afflicted... etc." Ahmad, may God have mercy on him, said: How he struggles, while the truth is clear! This verse, as you see it, conforms to the creed of Ahl al-Sunna (the People of the Sunna) that God, exalted is He, willed the trial for those who are afflicted, and did not will to purify their hearts from the filth of trial and the stain of disbelief. Not as the Mu'tazila (a theological school) claim, that God, exalted is He, did not will trial for anyone, willed faith and purity of heart for everyone, that what occurs of trials is contrary to His will, and that the non-occurrence of purity of hearts among the disbelievers is willed but did not happen. This verse and its like suffice them. If God had willed to purify their hearts from the stain of innovations... "Do they not then reflect upon the Qur'an, or are there locks upon their hearts?" How abominable is al-Zamakhshari's diversion of this verse from its apparent meaning by saying: "God did not will to grant them His gentle favours, knowing that His favours would not benefit them or be effective in them; exalted is God above what the wrongdoers say, a great exaltation." When God's favours are not effective and do not benefit, then whose gentle favour is beneficial and whose will is effective? And beyond God there is no hope for a person.]] *wa-khudhlānahu*, "and His abandonment": [[The phrase "left him afflicted and abandoned" is estimated on the basis that, according to the Mu'tazila, God does not will evil; but according to Ahl al-Sunna, He wills both evil and good, as is verified in its proper place. (ʿA.)]] *fa-lan tamlika lahu mina Allāhi shay'an*, "then you will not be able to avail him anything against God", that is, you cannot secure for him any of God's gentle favour and success. *Ulā'ika alladhīna lam yuridi Allāhu an yamnaḥahum min alṭāfihi mā yuṭahhiru bihi qulūbahum*, "those are the ones whom God did not will to grant from His gentle favours that which would purify their hearts, because they are not of its people, knowing that it would not benefit them or be effective in them." (*Inna alladhīna lā yu'minūna bi-āyāti Allāhi lā yahdīhimu Allāh*) ﴿Indeed, those who do not believe in the signs of God, God will not guide them﴾ (*Kayfa yahdī Allāhu qawman kafarū ba'da īmānihim*) ﴿How could God guide a people who disbelieved after their faith?﴾

For the unlawful gain (lil-suht): everything whose earnings are not permitted. It derives from sahata, meaning "to uproot," because it is stripped of blessing (mashoot al-barakah), as God Most High said: ﴿God destroys usury﴾, and usury is one category of it. It is also read as lil-suhti with the sin unstressed and stressed. The noun as-suht with a fatha on the sin is the verbal noun of sahatahu; as-suht with two fathas; and as-suht with a kasra on the sin. They used to take bribes for judgments and for making the unlawful lawful.

From al-Hasan: the judge among the Children of Israel, when one of them came to him with a bribe, would put it in his sleeve, show it to him, and speak of his need; he would be heard by him and would not look at his opponent. So he would consume the bribe and listen to falsehood.

It is related that an official returned from his post, and his people came to him. He set before them al-'arada [[His saying "he set before them al-'arada": in al-Sihah, al-'arada, with a damma: what is offered to the visitor, i.e., food from the provisions. It is said: buy an 'arada for your family, i.e., a gift or something you carry to them. (Ibn 'Abbad)]], and began to tell them what had happened to him in his work. A Bedouin among the people said: "We are, as God Most High said: ﴿listeners to falsehood, devourers of the unlawful gain﴾."

From the Prophet (ﷺ): "Every flesh that has grown from unlawful gain, the Fire is more fitting for it" [[Al-Hakim related it through Zayd ibn Arqam from Abu Bakr al-Siddiq (may Allah be pleased with him): I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: "Whoever's flesh has grown from unlawful gain, the Fire is more fitting for it." Ibn 'Adi related it in the biography of 'Abd al-Wahid ibn Zam'a and weakened it because of him. There is also a narration from Ma'mar in al-Tabarani and Ibn 'Adi within a longer hadith, in which is Yazid ibn 'Abd al-Malik al-Nawfali, who is weak.

From Hudhayfah: Ishaq ibn Rahawayh related it through the route of Kurdus, who said: "Hudhayfah delivered a sermon at al-Mada'in," and he mentioned the sermon, in which is the hadith, with the wording: "No flesh that grows from unlawful gain will enter Paradise." Al-Tabarani related it in al-Awsat through Ayyub ibn Suwayd from al-Thawri from 'Abd al-Malik ibn 'Umayr from Rib'i from Hudhayfah, with the wording: "Flesh that has grown from unlawful gain will not enter Paradise; the Fire is more fitting for it." Abu Hatim said in al-'Ilal: Ayyub ibn Suwayd erred in it; the correct version is mawquf. From Ibn 'Umar, related by al-Tabarani and al-Harithi in al-Gharib. Ibn Mardawayh in al-Gharib related it through the route of 'Umar ibn Hamzah from him; its narrators are trustworthy except that 'Umar did not hear from Ibn 'Umar. From Ibn 'Abbas, related by al-Tabarani and al-Bayhaqi through two weak routes. Al-Tirmidhi related from the hadith of Ka'b ibn 'Ujrah, in a long hadith, at its end: "O Ka'b ibn 'Ujrah, no flesh that has grown from unlawful gain will increase except that the Fire is more fitting for it." He said: hasan gharib, which we know only through this route. I asked Muhammad (al-Bukhari) about it and he considered it strange. Abu Ya'la related it through another route from Ka'b ibn 'Ujrah, and it has a witness in which Ibn Hibban related through 'Abd Allah ibn Khaythamah from 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Sabit from Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "O Ka'b ibn 'Ujrah," and he mentioned the like of it exactly. Ahmad, Ishaq, al-Bazzar, Abu Ya'la and al-Hakim related it through this route. Al-Hakim related through the route of Sa'id ibn Bashir from Qatadah from al-Hasan from 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Samurah, mentioning the like of the hadith of Ka'b ibn 'Ujrah, that the Prophet (ﷺ) addressed it to 'Abd al-Rahman. Sa'id ibn Bashir is weak.]]."

It was said: the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was given the choice, when the People of the Book came to him for judgment, between judging between them or not judging. From 'Ata', al-Nakha'i and al-Sha'bi: when they resorted to the rulers of the Muslims, if they wished they were judged, and if they wished they turned away. It was said: it is abrogated by His saying: ﴿and judge between them by what God has sent down﴾. According to Abu Hanifah (may Allah have mercy on him): if they come to us for judgment, they are held to the judgment of Islam; if a man among them commits adultery with a Muslim woman, or steals something from a Muslim, the prescribed penalty is enforced upon him. As for the people of the Hijaz, they do not hold that the prescribed penalties are enforced upon them, holding that they have been made to settle upon their polytheism, which is the greatest of crimes. They say that the Prophet (ﷺ) stoned the two Jews before the jizyah was revealed. ﴿They will not harm you at all﴾, for they would only come to him seeking the easier and lighter option for themselves, such as flogging instead of stoning. So when he turned away from them and refused to rule for them, it grieved them, they disliked his turning away from them, and they were prone to oppose and harm him. God protected him from their plot. ﴿with justice﴾: with fairness and caution, just as he judged by stoning. ﴿And how do they make you judge, when the Torah has God's judgment in it?﴾ This is an expression of wonder at their making him judge when they do not believe in him or his Book, although the ruling is stated explicitly in their own Book, which they claim to believe in. ﴿Then they turn away after that﴾: then they turn away after your judgment, refusing to accept your ruling, which agrees with what is in their Book. ﴿And those are not believers﴾ in their Book, as they claim; or, ﴿those are not perfect in faith﴾, said in mockery of them.

If you ask: ﴿in which is God's judgment﴾, what is its place in the grammar? I say: either it is in the accusative as a circumstantial clause (hal) from the Torah, which is the subject, with "with them" as its predicate; or it is in the nominative as a predicate of it, like your saying: "and with them is the Torah speaking of God's judgment"; or it has no place in the grammar and is an explanatory clause, since with them is what suffices them from seeking judgment, as you say: "With you is Zayd, who advises you and points you to what is right, so what will you do with anyone else?"

If you ask: why was "the Torah" made feminine? I say: because it is a counterpart to words like mawmah and wadudah and the like in Arabic speech.

If you ask: upon what is "then they turn away" conjoined? I say: upon "they make you judge."

God protected him from their plot. ﴿with justice﴾: with fairness and caution, just as he judged by stoning. ﴿And how do they make you judge, when the Torah has God's judgment in it?﴾ This is an expression of wonder at their making him judge when they do not believe in him or his Book, although the ruling is stated explicitly in their own Book, which they claim to believe in. ﴿Then they turn away after that﴾: then they turn away after your judgment, refusing to accept your ruling, which agrees with what is in their Book. ﴿And those are not believers﴾ in their Book, as they claim; or, ﴿those are not perfect in faith﴾, said in mockery of them.

If you ask: ﴿in which is God's judgment﴾, what is its place in the grammar? I say: either it is in the accusative as a circumstantial clause (hal) from the Torah, which is the subject, with "with them" as its predicate; or it is in the nominative as a predicate of it, like your saying: "and with them is the Torah speaking of God's judgment"; or it has no place in the grammar and is an explanatory clause, since with them is what suffices them from seeking judgment, as you say: "With you is Zayd, who advises you and points you to what is right, so what will you do with anyone else?"

If you ask: why was "the Torah" made feminine? I say: because it is a counterpart to words like mawmah and wadudah and the like in Arabic speech.

If you ask: upon what is "then they turn away" conjoined? I say: upon "they make you judge."

Of it there is guidance and light: the Torah, which guides to the truth and to justice, and which makes clear what was ambiguous of the rulings. The Prophets who submitted (alladhina aslamu) judged by it. The phrase "who submitted" is a description applied to the Prophets by way of praise, like the descriptive attributes applied to God, Exalted is He, and not for the purpose of elaboration or clarification. [[Al-Zamakhshari said: "His saying 'who submitted' is a description applied to the Prophets by way of praise... etc." Ahmad [Ibn al-Munayyir] said: What led him to take this description as praise rather than as elaboration and clarification is that the Prophets are only ever characterised by it, so mentioning prophethood entails mentioning it, and therefore he took it as praise. But this is open to question, for praise is generally given through the particular attributes by which the one praised is distinguished from others.

Islam is a general matter that encompasses the nations of the Prophets and their followers just as it encompasses the Prophets themselves. Do you not see that it is not fitting, in praising a Prophet, to restrict oneself to saying that he was a Muslim man, since the least of his followers is also like that? The correct view, and God knows best, is that an attribute may be mentioned for its greatness in itself, and to exalt it when it is ascribed to a great person, just as it may be a way of exalting the one it describes. The upshot is that just as the one described by a great attribute may be magnified, the attribute may be magnified by the greatness of the one described. Along this manner the Prophets' description with righteousness went in His saying, exalted is He: "And We gave him the good news of Isaac, a Prophet among the righteous" (37:112), and similar verses, exalting the degree of righteousness, since it is made an attribute of the Prophets, and as an incitement for ordinary people to strive to attain its qualities. Likewise it was said regarding His saying, exalted is He: "Those who bear the Throne and those around it glorify their Lord with praise and believe in Him and ask forgiveness for those who believe" (40:7). He reports of the honoured angels that they have faith, exalting the rank of faith and inciting mankind to enter it so that they may equal the honoured angels in this attribute. Otherwise it is well known that the angels are only believers. For this reason He said, "and they ask forgiveness for those who believe", meaning from mankind, because of the established right of brotherhood in faith between the two groups. So too, God knows best, the description of the Prophets in this verse with Islam went in exalting it.

Indeed, the one who spoke well in describing the nobles, and the poet in praising him, peace and blessings be upon him, said:

"If I praise Muhammad in my poem, then my poem has been praised by Muhammad."

Islam, although it is among the noblest attributes, since its sum is knowledge of God, Exalted is He, of what is due to Him, what is impossible for Him and what is permissible regarding Him, prophethood is nonetheless more noble and more exalted, because it includes the generality of Islam together with special gifts that expression cannot contain. So if we do not go to the benefit mentioned, in mentioning Islam after prophethood in the context of praise, we would depart from the familiar rule of eloquence in the Noble Book and in the eloquent speech of the Arabs, which is ascent from the lower to the higher, not descent in reverse. Do you not see how Abu al-Tayyib deviated from this path in his saying:

"A sun whose forenoon is a crescent moon for its night, a pearl whose sea-bed is its chrysolite."

He descended from the sun to the crescent, and from the pearl to the chrysolite, in the context of praise, so tongues chewed on the honour of his eloquence and tore the hide of his phrasing. So we must reflect on the miraculous verses, so that our understanding clings to the hem of their loftiness in the eloquence known for them. And God is the granter of success to what is right.]], like the attributes applied to the Eternal, glory be to Him. Its application is intended as an allusion against the Jews, that they are estranged from the religion of Islam, which is the religion of all the Prophets, past and present, and that Judaism stands far apart from it.

His saying, "who submitted, for those who are Jews", is a proclamation of this. "And the rabbis and the scholars" — the ascetics and the learned from the progeny of Aaron, who adhered to the way of the Prophets and kept away from the religion of the Jews — "by what they were entrusted with of the Book of God": by what their prophets asked them to preserve of the Torah, that is, because their prophets asked them to keep it from alteration and distortion.

The "min" in "of the Book of God" is explanatory. "And they were witnesses to it": watchers over it, lest it be altered. The meaning is that the Prophets, between Moses and Jesus, and there were a thousand prophets between them, judged by the rulings of the Torah, and Jesus, for those who are Jews, would make them follow the rulings of the Torah and not allow them to deviate from it, just as the Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, made them submit to the ruling on stoning and humbled their noses, and refused them what they desired of flogging. Likewise the rabbis, the scholars and the Muslims ruled by reason of what their prophets had entrusted them with of the Book of God and by applying its rulings, and by reason of their being witnesses over it.

It is permissible that the pronoun in "they were entrusted" refers to the Prophets, the rabbis and the scholars all together, and that the entrusting is from God, that is, God charged them with preserving it and with being witnesses over it. "So do not fear people": a prohibition to the rulers against fearing other than God in their judgements, and against compromising in them, [[His saying "and compromising in them" — in al-Sihah: al-mudahana is like al-musana'a, and al-idhan is the same. (Ayn)]] and against carrying them out contrary to what they were commanded of justice, out of fear of an oppressive sultan or dread of harming someone among relatives and friends. "And do not sell My signs for a small price": do not exchange or barter God's signs and rulings for a small price, which is bribery, the seeking of rank, or the pleasing of people, just as the rabbis of the Jews distorted the Book of God and changed its rulings out of desire for this world and seeking leadership, and so they perished. "And whoever does not judge by what God has sent down", disdaining it, "those are the disbelievers": the disbelievers, the wrongdoers and the defiantly disobedient. This is a description of them for their extreme obstinacy in disbelief, since they wronged God's signs by treating them with contempt, and rebelled by judging by other than them.

It is reported from Ibn Abbas, may God be pleased with him and his father: that the disbelievers, the wrongdoers and the defiantly disobedient are the People of the Book.

And from him: "What a people you are! What is sweet is for you, and whatever is bitter belongs to the People of the Book. Whoever denies God's ruling is a disbeliever; whoever does not judge by it while acknowledging it is a wrongdoer and defiantly disobedient." And from al-Sha'bi: these verses concern the people of Islam, the wrongdoers are the Jews, and the defiantly disobedient are the Christians. And from Ibn Mas'ud: it is general, applying to the Jews and others.

And from Hudhayfa: "You are the nation most similar in manner to the Children of Israel. You will surely follow their path step by step and feather by feather [[His saying "feather by feather" — al-qudhdha is the feather of an arrow. (Ayn)]], except that I do not know whether you will worship the calf or not."

In Ubayy's codex: "And Allah sent down upon the Children of Israel therein." And in it: "And that the wounds are retaliation." All the conjoined items were read both in the accusative and in the nominative. The nominative is by way of coordination with the position of "an-nafs" (the soul), since the meaning is "and We prescribed for them the soul for the soul," either because "kataba" (prescribed) is treated like "qala" (said), or because the sentence "an-nafs bi-n-nafs" is itself something that can be the object of prescribing, just as it can be the object of reading. You say: "I wrote, 'al-hamdu lillah' (praise be to Allah)," and "I recited a surah which We sent down."

For this reason al-Zajjaj said: had it been read "inna an-nafs bi-n-nafs" with the kasra, it would have been correct. Or it is a resumption (istiʼnaf, a new independent clause).

The meaning: We made obligatory upon them therein that the soul is taken for the soul, that is, killed in return for it if one kills it without right; and likewise the eye is gouged out for the eye, the nose is cut off for the nose, the ear is cut off for the ear, and the tooth is pulled out for the tooth; and "the wounds are retaliation" (qisas, i.e., subject to qisas), meaning that in which retaliation is possible and equality can be known. From Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with them both: they used not to kill a man for a woman, so this was revealed. ﴿But whoever forgoes it as charity﴾ — that is, the rightful party forgoes the retaliation and pardons it — ﴿it is an expiation for him﴾: so giving it up as charity is an expiation for the one who gives it, and Allah removes from his bad deeds what the balance requires, like His other acts of obedience. From ʿAbdullah ibn ʿAmr: it wipes away from him of his sins an amount equal to what he has given as charity. It was also said: "it is an expiation for the offender": if the owner of the right overlooks it, what was due from him falls away. In Ubayy's reading: "it is an expiation for him," meaning the charity of the forgiver is his expiation, i.e., the expiation that he deserves, of which nothing is diminished; and this is an exaltation of what he has done, like His saying (exalted is He): ﴿then his reward is upon Allah﴾, and an encouragement to pardon.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 5, verses 46–47:

"Qafaytuhu" is like "aqabtuhu": when you follow him. Then it is said "qafaytuhu bi-fulan" and "aqabtuhu bihi," so you make it transitive to the second object by adding the preposition bi-. If you ask: where is the first object in the verse? I say: it is omitted, and the adverbial phrase ﴿ʿala athārihim﴾ (upon their traces) takes its place, because when he is made to follow after him upon his trace, he has in fact been made to follow him. The pronoun in "athārihim" refers to the prophets in His words: ﴿by which the prophets who submitted [to Allah] judged﴾.

Al-Hasan recited "al-injīl" with a fatha on the hamza. If this is authentically transmitted from him, then it is because it is a foreign (aʿjamī) word which, by its foreignness, left the rules of Arabic morphology (zunāt al-ʿarabiyya), just as Hābīl and Ājar did. ﴿Musaddiqan﴾ is a conjunct of the place of ﴿fihi hudan﴾ (in it is guidance), whose place is accusative as a circumstantial state (ḥāl). ﴿Hudan wa-mawʿiẓatan﴾ may be accusative as circumstantial states, like His words ﴿musaddiqan﴾, and they may be accusative as objects of purpose (mafʿūl lahu), like His words ﴿wa-liyaḥkum﴾, as if it were said: "And for guidance and admonition We gave him the Injil, and for judging by what Allah revealed in it of rulings." If you ask: if you arrange ﴿hudan wa-mawʿiẓatan﴾ in the same series as ﴿musaddiqan﴾, what do you make of His words ﴿wa-liyaḥkum﴾? I say: I treat it as I treated guidance and admonition when I made them objects of purpose, so I estimate: "and that the people of the Injil judge by what Allah revealed, We gave him it." It has been read ﴿wa-liyaḥkum﴾ in the imperative form, meaning "and We said: let him judge." And it is reported in the reading of Ubayy: ﴿wa-an liyaḥkum﴾, with the addition of "an" before the imperative, on the basis that "an" is a relative particle joined to the imperative, as when you say "amartuhu bi-an qum" (I commanded him to stand). It is as if it were said: "And We gave him the Injil, and commanded that the people of the Injil judge."

It has been said: Jesus, peace be upon him, was bound by the rulings in the Torah, because the Injil consists of admonitions and deterrents and its rulings are few. But the apparent meaning of His words ﴿And let the people of the Injil judge by what Allah revealed in it﴾ refutes this, and likewise His words ﴿For each of you We appointed a law and a way﴾. Yet it is permissible for someone to say that the meaning is: "and let them judge by what Allah revealed in it, namely the obligation to act upon the rulings of the Torah."

**Question:** What is the difference between the two definite articles in His words ﴿And We have sent down to you the Book﴾ (*al-kitab*) and ﴿confirming what is before it of the Book﴾ (*al-kitab*)?

**Answer:** The first is the definiteness of *al-ʿahd* (definiteness by prior reference, "the known one"), because it refers to the Qur'an. The second is the definiteness of *al-jins* (the generic definite, denoting the class), because it refers to the genus of revealed books.

It may also be said that the first is *al-ʿahd*, because the word does not denote whatever falls under the name "book" in the absolute sense, but a specific known type of it: that which was sent down from heaven other than the Qur'an.

﴿And a guardian (*muhayminan*) and a witness over the other scriptures﴾, because it testifies to their soundness and preservation.

It was also recited as ﴿*wa-muhayminan ʿalayhi*﴾ with a *fatha* on the *mim* (*qira'at*, a variant recitation). That means: it is the one over which (*ʿalayhi*) guardianship is exercised, in that it was preserved from alteration and corruption, as He said: ﴿falsehood cannot approach it from before it or behind it﴾. The one over which Allah, mighty and majestic, exercised guardianship is either the Qur'an, or the guardians (*al-huffaz*) in every land. Had a single letter, vowel, or diacritic been altered, everyone would have noticed it, and they would have recoiled, rejecting and denying it.

**Grammar:** *Wa-la tattabiʿ* (﴿and do not follow﴾) is construed as implying the meaning of *wa-la tanharif* ("and do not deviate"). That is why it takes *ʿan* (from). It is as if it were said: "Do not deviate from the truth that has come to you, following their desires."

﴿For each of you, O people, We have made a law (*shirʿa*), a way (*minhaj*)﴾: *shirʿa* means a law. Yaḥyā ibn Wathhab recited *shin* with a *fatha* (*shareʿa*). *Minhaj* means a clear path in religion along which you proceed.

It is said: this is evidence that we are not bound by the laws of those before us.

﴿He would have made you one nation﴾, a single community agreed upon one law, or "a people of one nation," meaning one religion without disagreement. ﴿But He intends to test you in what He has given you﴾ of the differing laws: will you act upon them, submitting and believing that they are benefits which differ according to circumstances and times, acknowledging that Allah did not intend their differences except for what wisdom required? Or will you follow doubts and neglect action?

﴿So race to the good deeds﴾: hasten toward them and compete with one another to reach them.

﴿To Allah is your return﴾: this is a resumptive clause (*istiʾnaf*) carrying the sense of a reason for the command to race toward good deeds.

﴿And He will inform you﴾, that is, He will tell you, so that you have no doubt, about the decisive recompense that distinguishes between the one of you who is right and the one who is wrong, and between the one who acts and the one who neglects action.

**Question:** On what is "and that you judge between them" (وَأَنِ احْكُمْ بَيْنَهُمْ) coordinated?

**Answer:** It is coordinated (*ma'tuf*, grammatically conjoined) with "the Book" (الْكِتابَ) in His saying ﴿And We have sent down to you the Book﴾. It is as if it were said: "And We have sent down to you that you judge..." The particle "*an*" (أن) is connected to the imperative because the imperative is a verb like other verbs. It is also permissible that it be coordinated with "with the truth" (بِالْحَقِّ), meaning: "We sent it down with the truth, and [We sent it down] that you judge."

﴿And beware lest they tempt you away from part of what Allah has sent down to you﴾, that is, lest they mislead you away from it and cause you to slip from it. This is because Ka'b ibn Usayd, Abdullah ibn Suriya and Shas ibn Qays, who were rabbis (*ahbar*, scholars) of the Jews, said: "Come, let us go to Muhammad and tempt him away from his religion." They said: "O Muhammad, you know that we are the rabbis of the Jews, and if we follow you, all the Jews will follow us and will not oppose us. Between us and our people there is a dispute, so we will bring it before you, and you will judge in our favour against them. We will believe in you and affirm you." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) refused this, and so it was revealed.

﴿Then if they turn away﴾ from judgement by what Allah has sent down to you and desire something other than it, ﴿know that Allah only wants to afflict them for some of their sins﴾. He means the sin of turning away from the judgement of Allah and desiring its opposite. He placed "for some of their sins" (بِبَعْضِ ذُنُوبِهِمْ) in the place of that, and intended that they have many sins, numerous in count, and that this sin, despite its magnitude, is one of them, a single one among them. This vagueness (*ibham*) is to magnify the act of turning away and their excess in committing it.

Similar to "some" (البعض) in this speech is what is in the verse of Labid:

*"Leaving places behind is my way when I am not content with them,*
*or the appointed death binds some souls."*

From the Mu'allaqa of Labid ibn Rabi'a. He says: I often leave places behind when I am not pleased to remain in them, or [death] binds and holds back some souls, meaning himself, "their appointed death," that is, the death decreed for them. So when I am content with a place, or death holds me there, how could I leave it? So his saying "yartabit" (يَرْتَبِطْ) is in the jussive (*majzum*), coordinated with the jussive preceding it. It has been said that "or" (أو) means "except" (إلا), but its proper case would then be the accusative. Perhaps he made it quiescent (*sakkan*) out of necessity. Just as tanwin (التنوين, the nunation marking indefiniteness) conveys the meaning of magnification, so too everything that involves vagueness, like partitiveness here, [conveys magnification]. So he expressed himself by "some souls," indicating magnification.

[Indeed, he may even have claimed that it is all souls, as hyperbole.]

He meant himself, and he intended to exalt his status by this vagueness, as if he said: "A great soul, and a soul of what a soul!" Just as indefiniteness (*tankir*) conveys the meaning of greatness (*takbir*), which is the meaning of partitiveness, so too when [the text] states "some" explicitly...

﴿And indeed, many of the people are defiantly disobedient﴾, that is, rebellious in disbelief and transgressing in it, meaning that turning away from the judgement of Allah is a great rebellion and transgression in disbelief.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 5, verse 50:

As for "afa-ḥukma l-jāhiliyyati yabghūn" (﴿Do they then desire the judgment of the Time of Ignorance?﴾), there are two interpretations. The first: the Qurayza and the Nadir asked him to judge according to what the people of the Jahiliyya used to judge, namely distinguishing between the slain (in blood-money). It is narrated that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to them, "The slain are equal (bawā')," but the Banu l-Nadir said, "We do not accept that," and so this was revealed. [[I have not found it in this form; but in Ibn Abi Shayba, by way of al-Sha'bi, he said: There was fighting between two Arab tribes, and he mentioned a story in which: they referred to the Prophet (ﷺ), and he said: "The slain are bawā'," meaning equal.]] The second: it is an address to the Jews by describing them as People of the Book and knowledge, while they desire the judgment of the Jahili creed, which is whim and ignorance, and does not proceed from a Book nor return to a revelation from Allah the Exalted. It is reported from al-Hasan: this is general, concerning everyone who desires other than the judgment of Allah. "Judgment is of two kinds: judgment with knowledge, which is the judgment of Allah, and judgment with ignorance, which is the judgment of Satan." Tawus was asked about a man who favours some of his children over others, and he recited this verse.

It has been read as "tabghūn" (with the second person) and "yabghūn" (with the third person). Al-Sulami read "afa-ḥukmu l-jāhiliyyati yabghūn" with ḥukm in the nominative as the subject (mubtada'), and yabghūn as the predicate (khabar), with the returning pronoun omitted from it, just as it is omitted from the relative clause in "a-hādhā lladhī ba'atha llāhu rasūlan" (﴿Is this the one whom Allah has sent as a messenger?﴾), and from the qualifier in "al-nāsu rajulān: rajulun ahanta, wa rajulun akramta" (﴿People are of two kinds: a man you have humiliated and a man you have honoured﴾), and from the circumstantial clause in "marartu bi-Hindin yaḍribu Zaydun" (﴿I passed by Hind, while Zayd was striking her﴾). Qatada read "afa-ḥukma l-jāhiliyyati" (with the accusative), meaning that this judgment they desire is one given by the Najran serpent, or its like among the judges of the Jahiliyya; they wished, in their foolishness, that Muhammad, the Seal of the Prophets, should be a judge like those judges. The lam in His words "li-qawmin yūqinūn" (﴿for a people who have certainty﴾) is explanatory, like the lam in "hayta laka" (﴿Come on, for you﴾); that is, this address and this question are for a people who have certainty, for they are the ones who are certain that there is no one more just than Allah, nor any better judge than Him.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 5, verses 51–53:

"Do not take them as allies" (﴿لَا تَتَّخِذُوهُمْ أَوْلِيَاءَ﴾), meaning: do not take them as helpers whom you seek help from, nor as companions, nor as close friends, nor as those with whom you associate in the manner of believers. Then he gives the reason for the prohibition with his words: ﴿بَعْضُهُمْ أَوْلِيَاءُ بَعْضٍ﴾ ("Some of them are allies of others"), meaning: some of them befriend only others, because of the unity of their religion and their gathering in disbelief. So, for one whose religion differs from theirs, there is no (share) in their friendship. And ﴿وَمَنْ يَتَوَلَّهُمْ مِنْكُمْ فَإِنَّهُ مِنْهُمْ﴾ ("Whoever of you takes them as allies, then he is one of them"), meaning: he is among them, and his ruling is their ruling. This is a severe warning from God and an emphasis on the obligation to keep away from and withdraw from those who differ in religion, as the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Do not let your fires be visible to each other" [[Related by Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi and al-Nasa'i from the hadith of Jarir: "The Messenger of God (ﷺ) sent a military expedition to Khath'am, and some people sought refuge by prostrating (in the presence of the enemy)..." and in it: he said, "I am free of every Muslim who lives among the polytheists." They said, "Why?" He said, "Do not let your fires be visible to each other." Abu Mu'awiya transmitted it connected, from Isma'il, from Qays, from him. Others among the companions of Isma'il transmitted it as mursal (with a missing link, i.e. without the companion), such as Abdah ibn Sulayman, Waki', Hushaym and Marwan. Hajjaj ibn Artat followed him in transmitting it connected from Isma'il, but Hajjaj is weak. Al-Bukhari and others preferred the mursal version. Hafs ibn Ghiyath opposed all of them, transmitting it from Isma'il, from Qays, from Khalid ibn al-Walid. Related by al-Tabarani.]] From this is the saying of Umar, may God be pleased with him, to Abu Musa regarding his Christian scribe: "Do not honour them, since God has humiliated them; do not trust them, since God has deemed them treacherous; do not bring them close, since God has distanced them." It is also read as "man yartadda" and "wa-man yartadd" (with two dals), and this is in the Imam (the 'Uthmanic codex). It is one of the unseen matters that the Qur'an reported before they occurred. It has also been said: The apostates were eleven groups. Three were in the time of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): Banu Mudlij, whose leader was Dhu al-Khimar, who is al-Aswad al-‘Ansi. He was a soothsayer who claimed prophethood in Yemen and seized its lands, and he expelled the governors of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). So the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) wrote to Mu'adh ibn Jabal and to the leaders of Yemen. Allah destroyed him at the hands of Fayruz al-Daylami, who attacked his house and killed him. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) informed them of his killing on the night he was killed, so the Muslims rejoiced, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) passed away the next day. News of it reached them at the end of Rabi' al-Awwal. [[He said: The apostates were eleven groups: three in the time of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and seven in the time of Abu Bakr (may Allah be pleased with him) and one in the time of ‘Umar. The ones in the time of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) were Banu Mudlij, whose leader was Dhu al-Khimar, who is al-Aswad al-‘Ansi. I say: The statement "al-Aswad" mentioned is not from Banu Mudlij. Rather, Banu Mudlij are a people from Banu Kinana ibn Mudar, brothers of Quraysh, and al-Aswad mentioned was in Yemen. His people were Banu ‘Ansi, with an unpointed ‘ain, then an unpointed sin after the nun. Al-Zamakhshari said: al-Aswad mentioned was a soothsayer who claimed prophethood in Yemen and seized its lands and expelled the governors of the Prophet (ﷺ). So the Prophet (ﷺ) wrote to Mu'adh ibn Jabal and to the leaders of Yemen, and Allah destroyed him at the hands of Fayruz al-Daylami, who killed him. The Prophet (ﷺ) informed of his killing on the night he was killed, so the Muslims rejoiced at that. The Prophet (ﷺ) passed away the next day, at the end of Rabi' al-Awwal. I say: In this statement there is more than one confusion. His saying "he seized the lands of Yemen and expelled the governors of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)" apparently requires that none of them remained there, and this is not the case. Rather, some of them remained in their state, including a group of the emigrants: Ibn Abi Umayya, and with him all the coasts. Mu'adh ibn Jabal and others among the governors of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) were also in Yemen, on its coasts. Al-‘Ansi only seized Sana'a and some mountainous regions. Al-Zamakhshari himself refuted his own statement when he said: He (ﷺ) wrote to Mu'adh ibn Jabal and to the leaders of Yemen. But the reconciliation between his two statements is that he meant the expulsion of the governors of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) whom he fought, so the meaning is the expulsion of some of them, not all of them. His saying "the Prophet (ﷺ) passed away the next day" means the morning of his informing of al-Aswad's killing. There is something to examine in this, and its aspect will come. The story of al-Aswad al-‘Ansi has been related in full by all who wrote on the ridda (apostasy), such as Ibn Ishaq, al-Waqidi, and Sayf ibn ‘Umar, and Sumayya? No, rather: and Sayf ibn ‘Umar, and Sawda ibn al-Furat. It was also related by al-Hakim in al-Iklil and by al-Bayhaqi in al-Dala'il. Al-Waqidi said: The name of al-Aswad was Dhu al-Khimar. Others said: His name was ‘Ahla, and his title was Dhu al-Khimar, because he used to cast a veil over his face and murmur. He had two devils: one called Sahiq and the other Bashiq. Al-Waqidi said: al-Aswad took control of Najran and stayed there for six months. Then he went out with six hundred men who followed him to Sana'a, and he besieged the Asawira (cavalrymen) among them, Badhan, Fayruz, and Dadawayh, along with others. They had embraced Islam and sent word of their Islam through Furwa ibn Musayk al-Muradi. The two sides fought until al-Aswad prevailed and killed a group of them. He gave a group the choice between leaving Sana'a for another land, settling there and paying the kharaj tax on them, and becoming his slaves. Al-Aswad chose the wife of Badhan, al-Marzubana, for himself, and she was beautiful. He used to drink wine and lie with her, and would not perform ghusl or pray. Al-Marzubana disliked him and corresponded with the Asawira, among whom was Fayruz, and they arranged to meet her in the garden at the time when al-Aswad would be drunk. Fayruz and Dadawayh and Qays ibn Maksuh entered upon him while he was drunk. Al-Marzubana said to Fayruz, who was the youngest of them in age: Here is the man for you. Fayruz said: I had forgotten my sword in my panic. So he fell upon al-Aswad and choked him until he turned his face to his back. Then his two companions entered and cut off his head. The Asawira gathered at the gate of the city, killing the followers of al-‘Ansi. The rest of the story is long, but we have abridged it. An-Nasa'i related from the hadith of ‘Abd Allah ibn Fayruz al-Daylami, from his father, who said: "I came to the Prophet (ﷺ) with the head of al-Aswad al-‘Ansi." ‘Abd al-Haqq said: Nothing authentic has been related in this chapter. Ibn al-Qattan responded to him that the chain of an-Nasa'i is sound, and what has come, that the report of his killing came right after the death of the Prophet (ﷺ), does not contradict it, because the report of an-Nasa'i does not explicitly state that he reached the Prophet (ﷺ). Indeed, in the narration of at-Tabari there is an addition that indicates that.

And Banu Hanifa, the people of Musaylima [[Al-Zamakhshari's statement: Banu Hanifa in al-Yamama, and their leader was Musaylima. Al-Waqidi related through the route of Habib ibn ‘Umayr al-Ansari, who said: Musaylima ibn Habib had claimed prophethood during the lifetime of the Prophet (ﷺ), and he said to his people: O assembly of Banu Hanifa, what made Quraysh more worthy of prophethood than you, when they are not more numerous than you nor better equipped? By Allah, your lands are wider than theirs, and Gabriel descends upon me as he descends upon Muhammad. Al-Rajjal ibn ‘Unfuwa testified for him that Muhammad had made Musaylima a partner in the matter. They asked him, and he testified. Musaylima recited to them a Qur'an that he claimed: "Glorify the name of your Lord, the Most High, who made easy the pregnant woman; He brought forth from her a living soul from between the womb and the membrane; some of them are cast into the dust, and some live to an appointed term and an end. Allah knows the secret and what is more hidden, and nothing of the matter of the Hereafter and the first is hidden from Him." The people of al-Yamama pledged allegiance to him. When the delegations of the Arabs came to the Prophet (ﷺ) after the conquest, Musaylima came in the delegation of Banu Hanifa, and he began saying: If Muhammad makes the matter mine after him, I will follow him. He came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and asked him to make him a partner in the matter and to make the caliphate his after him, but he refused. Then the delegation of Banu Hanifa showed Islam, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) gave them gifts like those given to delegations, and Musaylima returned with them, manifesting prophethood. Al-Rajjal ibn ‘Unfuwa testified for him that Muhammad had made him a partner in the matter. Musaylima persisted in his misguidance until the caliphate of Abu Bakr, when his followers increased. Abu Bakr sent an army to him with a company of the Companions. They met at al-Yamama and fought a fierce battle from sunrise until the afternoon prayer. Killing and wounds multiplied on both sides, and the Muslims suffered a setback. Then the emigrants and the Ansar regrouped and pushed Banu Hanifa back with a mighty push, until they forced them into a garden in which Musaylima was, and they took refuge in it. They closed the gate, and the Muslims besieged them. Abu Dujana said to them: Throw me up onto the wall until I climb to the top of the garden. They did, and he dropped down upon them and killed some of them when he opened the gate of the garden; he himself was killed. The Muslims entered the garden, and they killed them. When the fighting reached Musaylima, ‘Abd Allah ibn Zayd al-Ansari struck him, and Wahshi ibn Harb threw his spear at him, so they both shared in killing him.]] who claimed prophethood. He wrote to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): From Musaylima, the Messenger of Allah, to Muhammad, the Messenger of Allah. To proceed: the earth is half mine and half yours. He (ﷺ) replied: "From Muhammad, the Messenger of Allah, to Musaylima the liar. To proceed: the earth belongs to Allah; He gives it as inheritance to whomever He wills of His servants, and the good end is for the righteous." Abu Bakr (may Allah be pleased with him) fought him with the armies of the Muslims, and he was killed at the hands of Wahshi, the slayer of Hamza. Wahshi used to say: I killed the best of people in the Jahiliyya and the worst of people in Islam, meaning in my pre-Islamic time and my Islam.

Banu Asad, the people of Tulayha ibn Khuwaylid, who claimed prophethood. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) sent Khalid [[His saying "Khalid" in Abu al-Sa'ud is "Abu Bakr." End quote. (ع)]] against him, and he fled after the battle to Syria, then he embraced Islam and his Islam was good. Seven groups were in the time of Abu Bakr (may Allah be pleased with him): Fazara, the people of ‘Uyayna ibn Hisn; Ghatafan, the people of Qurra ibn Salama al-Qushayri; Banu Sulaym, the people of al-Fujaa'a ibn ‘Abd Ya Layl; Banu Yarbu', the people of Malik ibn Nuwayra; part of Tamim, the people of Sajah bint al-Mundhir, the prophetess who married herself to Musaylima the liar, and concerning her Abu al-‘Ala al-Ma'arri says in the book "Istaghfir wa-listaghfiri":

Sajah became a leader, and Musaylima allied with her,
a liar among the people of this world, and a liar.

[[By Abu al-‘Ala al-Masri. "Amat" with shadda means: she became a leader among Banu Hanifa and claimed prophethood. It is also narrated with a long vowel and without shadda, meaning she became an unmarried woman, and she was the daughter of al-Mundhir. "Wafaha" means Musaylima agreed with her, for he married her, and he too was claiming prophethood. After his killing, she repented and her Islam was good.]]

And Kinda, the people of al-Ash'ath ibn Qays; and Banu Bakr ibn Wa'il in Bahrayn, the people of al-Hutam ibn Zayd. Allah sufficed them through Abu Bakr (may Allah be pleased with him). One group in the time of ‘Umar (may Allah be pleased with him): Ghassan, the people of Jabala ibn al-Ayham. [[His saying "nusrathu al-lutma" (the slap aided him)? Perhaps it is "al-luteima," which is the caravan carrying perfume and the merchants' goods. Verify.]] He was sent to the lands of the Romans after his Islam, and "Allah will bring forth a people" was revealed. When it was revealed, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) pointed to Abu Musa al-Ash'ari and said: "These are his people." [[Ibn Abi Shayba, Ishaq, al-Hakim, al-Tabarani, and al-Tabari related it through the route of Simak ibn Harb, from ‘Iyad al-Ash'ari, who said: When this verse was revealed, and so on. al-Bayhaqi related it in al-Dala'il through another route from Simak, from ‘Iyad, from Abu Musa, who said: I recited in the presence of the Prophet (ﷺ) "Allah will bring forth a people," the verse. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Your people, O Abu Musa, the people of Yemen."]] It has also been said that they were two thousand of Nakha', five thousand of Kinda and Bajila, and three thousand from the scattered people. [[His saying "from the scattered people" in al-Sihah: "the courtyard of the house" is what extends from its sides, and the plural is afniya. It is said: he is from the scattered people, if it is not known from whom he is. End quote.]] They fought on the day of al-Qadisiyya. It has also been said: they are the Ansar. It has been said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was asked about them, and he struck the shoulder of Salman and said: "This one and his people." Then he said: "If faith were hung from the Pleiades, men from the sons of Persia would reach it." [[He related it thus, and this is a mistake from him. This statement was only in the verse of Friday prayer, through the route of Abu al-‘Aytha from Abu Hurayra, and it is agreed upon. In the verse of fighting, al-Tirmidhi related it through the route of al-‘Ala' ibn ‘Abd al-Rahman, from his father, from Abu Hurayra (may Allah be pleased with him).]]

﴿He loves them and they love Him﴾: the love of servants for their Lord is obedience to Him and seeking His pleasure, and that they not do what brings His wrath. [[Mahmud said: "The love of servants for their Lord is obedience to Him and seeking His pleasure, and that they not do what brings His wrath and punishment. The love of Allah for His servants is that He rewards them with the best reward for their obedience, honors them, praises them, and is pleased with them. As for what the most ignorant of people believe, and their enemies of knowledge and its people, and the most hateful to the Shari'a and the worst in path, even if their path is something among the ignorant and foolish like them, namely the fabricated, self-affecting sect of the ṣūfiyya from wool, and what they hold of love, passion, and singing on their chairs, may Allah ruin them, and in their dances, may Allah void them, with verses of love poetry about beardless youths whom they call martyrs, and their swoons, of which the swoon of Moses on the day the mountain was crushed is nothing. Exalted is Allah far above that. And among their sayings: just as He loves them in His essence, so they love His essence, for the pronoun returns to the essence, not to the attributes and qualities." End of his words. Ahmad said: There is no doubt that interpreting the servant's love for Allah as obedience to Him is contrary to the apparent meaning, and it is one of the figurative usages in which the cause is named for the effect, and a figurative usage from which one does not turn away from the literal meaning except after its impossibility. So let the real meaning of love be examined linguistically by the rules, to see whether it is established for the servant and related to Allah, the Exalted, or not. Love linguistically is the inclination of the one who has it toward a pleasurable thing. The pleasures that give rise to love are divided into what is perceived by the senses, such as the pleasure of taste in food, the pleasure of seeing and touching beautiful forms, the pleasure of smell in fragrant scents, and the pleasure of hearing in pleasant melodies; and into pleasures perceived by the intellect, such as the pleasure of status, leadership, knowledge, and what runs in this manner. It is thus established that among the pleasures that give rise to love are some perceived only by the intellect and not by the senses. Then love necessarily varies according to the variation of what gives rise to it. So the pleasure of a man's leadership over the people of a village is not like his pleasure in ruling over considerable regions.

And if love varies according to the variation of its inspirations, then the pleasures of knowledge also vary according to the variation of the known things. There is nothing more perfect or more beautiful than the true Worshipped One, so the pleasure obtained in knowing Him, the Exalted, and knowing His majesty and perfection, will be greater, and the love arising from it will be more possible. When this love is obtained, it moves one to acts of obedience and agreement. Thus it is established that the servant's love is possible, indeed actual in every believer, and it is among the necessities and conditions of faith. People vary in it according to the variation of their faith. Since this is so, it is necessary to interpret the servant's love for Allah according to its literal linguistic meaning, and acts of obedience and agreement are like its result and distinct from it.]]

Have you not seen the Bedouin who asked about the Hour, and the Prophet (ﷺ) said to him, "What have you prepared for it?" He said, "I have not prepared great deeds, but I love Allah and His Messenger." The Prophet (ﷺ) said, "You will be with whom you love." This hadith clearly shows that love for Allah is understood as something other than deeds and the observance of acts of obedience, because the Bedouin negated deeds and affirmed love, and the Prophet (ﷺ) approved of that. Then, if it is established that the servant's love for Allah, exalted is He, is to be taken in its literal linguistic sense, then love in the language, when it becomes intense, is called *ʿishq* (passionate love). Whoever's love for Allah, exalted is He, becomes intense, and whose intensity shows in its effects, such as filling his times with the remembrance of Him and obedience to Him, there is no objection to calling his love *ʿishq*, since *ʿishq* is nothing but love reaching its utmost degree.

I have intended by this section only to clarify the truth and to stand up for the beloved servants of Allah, exalted is He, against al-Zamakhshari. He mixed the worthless with the valuable in his speech. He spoke in the manner you have heard, with gross disparagement of the Sufis (*al-mutasawwifa*), without careful verification, and attributed to them things that no one who has any sense would commit, and which would not even be accepted from beasts, let alone from distinguished people. It does not follow that when a group takes this name, having usurped it from its rightful people, and then commits what is reported of them that contradicts the true state of those who bear the name, the righteous must be held to account for the wrongdoing of the wicked: ﴿no bearer of burdens shall bear the burden of another﴾. This is like how some people have attached themselves to the scholars of religion, calling themselves the People of Justice and Monotheism (*Ahl al-ʿAdl wa al-Tawhid*), and then cast off restraint, denied the attributes of Allah, exalted is He, His decree and His measure, and said, "The matter is newly begun." They attributed to themselves a share of creation and claimed to act and to make. It is therefore not permissible for us to disparage the scholars of the foundations of religion (*uṣūl al-dīn*) in general, because some have been attached to them who cannot be prevented from claiming their title. ﴿Allah does not burden a soul beyond its capacity﴾.

There is no doubt that among people there are those who deny that the servant's love for Allah can be conceived except as obedience to Him and nothing more, and this is the view al-Zamakhshari leans toward. We have already explained and clarified how this can be conceived. Those who acknowledge that this can be conceived and established attribute the deniers to ignorance, so they deny it, just as a child denies that there is any pleasure beyond play, when there is pleasure in intercourse or other things. Someone absorbed in appetites and infatuated with women assumes there is no pleasure beyond that, such as leadership, status or the like. Every group is dazzled by those above it and thinks they are occupied with nothing of value. Al-Ghazali said: "Those who love Allah say to whoever denies this to them: If you mock us, then we mock you as you mock us."

And His love for His servants means that He rewards them with the best reward for their obedience, honours them, praises them and is pleased with them. As for what the most ignorant of people believe, and those most hostile to knowledge and its people, most loathing of the Sharia and worst in their way, although their way is considered something by people like them among the ignorant and foolish, namely the sect fabricated and feigned from wool (*al-sūf*), and what they profess of love and passion, and their singing on their chairs, may Allah ruin them, and their dancing, may Allah nullify them, with verses of love poetry said about beardless youths whom they call "martyrs," and their swoons, compared to which the swoon of Moses at the crumbling of the mountain is nothing, exalted is Allah far above that by a great elevation. Among their sayings: "Just as He loves them with His essence, so they love His essence, for the pronoun refers to the essence and not to the attributes and qualities." And among them: "Love has a condition, which is that the intoxications of love overtake one; if that does not happen, there is no reality in it."

If you say: Where is the pronoun returning from the consequent (*jawāb*) of the condition to the noun that contains the meaning of the condition? I say: It is omitted, and its meaning is: "Allah will bring a people in their place," or "a people other than them," or something similar. ﴿humble toward the believers﴾: *adhillah* is the plural of *dhalīl*. As for *dhalūl*, its plural is *dhulul*. Whoever claims it is from *dhull*, which is the opposite of difficulty, has overlooked that *dhalūl* does not take the plural *adhillah*.

If you say: Why was it not said *adhillatan lil-mu'minīn aʿizzatan ʿalā al-kāfirīn* ("humble toward the believers, mighty over the disbelievers")? I say: There are two aspects to it. The first is that *dhull* is taken to include the meaning of tenderness and compassion, as if it were said: "showing compassion toward them with humility and modesty." The second is that they, despite their nobility, high rank and superiority over the believers, lower their wings to them. A similar example is His saying: ﴿harsh against the disbelievers, merciful among themselves﴾. It has also been read as *adhillatan* and *aʿizzatan* in the accusative as circumstantial states (*ḥāl*).

﴿and they do not fear the blame of any blamer﴾: The *wāw* may be a circumstantial *wāw*, meaning that they strive while their state in striving is different from the state of the hypocrites, for the hypocrites were allied with the Jews, may Allah curse them. When they went out in the army of the believers, they feared their Jewish allies, so they would not do anything for which they knew they would be blamed by them. But the believers used to strive for the sake of Allah's face and never feared the blame of any blamer. The *wāw* may also be a conjunction, meaning that among their characteristics is striving in the way of Allah, and that they are firm in their religion. When they undertake any matter of religion, such as denouncing an evil or enjoining what is good, they proceed in it like heated nails, and no speaker's words, no objector's opposition, and no blamer's blame terrifies them. It is hard for an opponent to bear their earnestness in denouncing and their firmness in their affair. *Lawmah* means one instance of blame, and in it, and in its indefiniteness, there are two kinds of emphasis, as if it were said: "They fear nothing at all from the blame of any of the blamers."

﴿That is the bounty of Allah, He gives it to whom He wills﴾: "That" refers to what has been described of the people: love, humility, might, striving, and the absence of fear of blame. *Yu'tīhi* means: He grants it to whom He wills, namely whoever He knows has a share of it. ﴿Allah is All-Embracing, All-Knowing﴾: *wāsiʿ* means abundant in bounties and graces, and *ʿalīm* means knowing of those who deserve them.

After the prohibition on allying with those who must be opposed, He mentions those whose alliance is obligatory, with His words ﴿Your only ally is Allah, and His Messenger, and those who believe﴾. The meaning of "innama" (only, exclusively) is that the alliance is obligatory and restricted to them.

If you ask: he mentioned a group, so why was it not said "Your allies are only..."? I answer: the original sentence is "Your only ally is Allah." Guardianship was attributed to Allah in the primary sense, and then the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and the believers were included in the same affirmation of it in a secondary sense. Had it been said, "Your allies are only Allah, His Messenger, and those who believe," the sentence would have had no primary and secondary element. In the recitation of Abdullah (ibn Mas'ud), it is "innama mawlakum" (Your only master is...).

If you ask: what is the grammatical position of ﴿those who establish prayer﴾? I answer: it is in the nominative as a substitute (badal) for "those who believe," or it is in the sense of "they are those who establish prayer." It may also be in the accusative as a term of praise. In it there is a distinction of the sincere believers from those who believe outwardly while hypocrites, or whose hearts agree with their tongues but who are negligent in deeds.

﴿while they bow﴾: the "waw" here is for the circumstantial clause (hal), meaning they perform that in the state of bowing, which is humility, submission, and lowliness before Allah, when they pray and when they give zakat. It has also been said that it is a circumstantial clause for those who give zakat, meaning they give it while bowing in prayer. It was revealed concerning Ali, may Allah ennoble his face, when a beggar asked him while he was bowing in his prayer, so he gave him his ring.

[[I say: The words from "as if he" to "like it" are from the author of al-Kashshaf. Ibn Abi Hatim narrated it through Salama ibn Kuhayl, who said: he gave me his ring while he was bowing, so this was revealed: "Your only ally is Allah and His Messenger." Ibn Mardawayh has it through the narration of Sufyan al-Thawri, from Ibn Sinan, from al-Dahhak, from Ibn Abbas, who said: Ali was standing praying, when a beggar passed by while he was bowing, so he gave him his ring, and this was revealed. Al-Hakim, in his book on the sciences of hadith, narrated through the narration of Isa ibn Abdullah ibn Umar ibn Ali, who said: My father narrated to us, from his father, from his grandfather, from Ali ibn Abi Talib, who said: This verse was revealed, "Your only ally is Allah and His Messenger," and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) entered the mosque while the people were praying, some standing, some bowing, and some prostrating. A beggar came, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to him: "Has anyone given you anything?" He said: "No, except this bowing man," meaning Ali, "who gave me his ring." Al-Tabarani narrated it in al-Awsat in the biography of Muhammad ibn Ali al-Sa'igh. In Ibn Mardawayh's collection, through the hadith of Ammar ibn Yasir, who said: A beggar stood before Ali while he was standing in his prayer... (the hadith). Its chain includes Khalid ibn Yazid al-Umari, who is abandoned (matruk) in hadith. Al-Tha'labi narrated it from the hadith of Abu Dhar at length, but its chain is invalid.]]

It was as if the ring was loose on his little finger, so he did not exert much effort to remove it, which would have spoiled his prayer by such an act.

If you ask: how is it valid that this applies to Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, when the wording is in the plural? I answer: it was expressed in the plural form, even though the cause was one man, so that people would be eager to do the like of his act and obtain the like of his reward, and to alert that the disposition of the believers must be at this height of eagerness for righteousness and kindness and attentiveness to the poor, so that if a matter arises for them that does not accept delay ["does not accept delay" may be "does not allow" (la yuf'al)] while they are in prayer, they do not postpone it until they finish it.

**So ﴿indeed, the party of Allah﴾ is an instance of placing the apparent noun in the position of the pronoun.** [Al-Zamakhshari said: "This is from placing the apparent noun in the position of the pronoun, and its meaning is..." etc.] Ahmad (Ibn al-Munayyir) said: Its counterpart is the verse ﴿Indeed, the losers are those who lost themselves and their families on the Day of Resurrection. Unquestionably, the wrongdoers will be in lasting punishment.﴾ Here ﴿the wrongdoers﴾ is placed in the position of the pronoun referring to the first group, in order to add the attribute of wrongdoing to their loss.

Its meaning is: they are the victorious. However, by this they have made themselves signs, because they are the party of Allah. The root of *hizb* (party) is a people who gather for a matter that concerns them. It is possible that by *hizb Allah* he means the Messenger and the believers. The meaning would then be: whoever takes them as allies has allied himself with the party of Allah and sought support from one who cannot be overcome.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 5, verses 57–58:

It is narrated that Rifa'a ibn Zayd and Suwayd ibn al-Harith had outwardly professed Islam and then became hypocrites (munafiqun), and some of the Muslims used to befriend them, so the verse was revealed. The meaning is that their taking your religion as a mockery and a game does not merit being met with your taking them as allies (awliya'); rather, it merits being met with hatred (al-baghda'), detestation (al-shana') and renunciation (al-munabadha). The mockers are singled out from the People of the Book and the disbelievers, even though the People of the Book are among the disbelievers, by restricting the term "disbelievers" (al-kuffar) to the polytheists (al-mushrikin). The evidence for this is the reading of Ibn Mas'ud: "and from those who associated partners" (wa min al-ladhina ashraku). It has also been read as "wa al-kuffar" in the accusative and the genitive (wa al-kuffari). The genitive reading is supported by the reading of Ubayy:

"and from the disbelievers" (wa min al-kuffar). "And fear God" (wa-attaqu Allah) in befriending the disbelievers and other matters, "if you are truly believers" (in kuntum mu'minin haqqan), because true faith (al-iman haqqan) rejects befriending the enemies of the religion. "They have taken them" (ittakhadhuha): the pronoun refers to the prayer (al-salah) or to the call (al-munada). It is said that a certain Christian man in Medina, whenever he heard the muezzin say "I bear witness that Muhammad is the Messenger of God," would say: "Burn the liar." One night his servant girl brought fire, while he was asleep, and a spark flew from it into the house, so the house burned, and he burned with his household. [[Al-Tabari related it from the narration of Asbat from al-Suddi concerning His words, "and when you call to prayer they take it as mockery and play," he said: "A certain man from the Christians ..." and then mentioned it.]] It is also said: in it is evidence that the adhan is established by the text of the Book, not by dream alone. "They do not reason" (la ya'qilun) because their play and mockery are acts of fools and ignorant people, so it is as if they had no intellect.
