Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 5, verse 59:

Al-Hasan read *hal tanqimūna* (هل تنقمون) with a fatha on the qaf. The eloquent (fasih) reading is with a kasra. The meaning is: "Do you blame us and object to us for nothing except our belief in the Books that were sent down, all of them, and that most of you are defiantly disobedient (fasiqun)?"

If you ask: on what is the clause *wa anna aktharakum fasiqun* (وَأَنَّ أَكْثَرَكُمْ فاسِقُونَ) coordinated? I say: there are several possibilities.

One is that it is coordinated with *anna amanna* (أَنْ آمَنَّا), meaning: "And you do not object to us except for combining our belief with your rebellion and your departure from belief, as if it were said: 'And you do not object to us except your opposition, in that we entered the religion of Islam while you are outside of it.'"

It is also permissible that it be on the assumption of an omitted genitive (muḍāf), meaning: "and the belief that you are defiantly disobedient."

Another is that it is coordinated with the genitive (majrur) [preceding it], meaning: "And you do not object to us except the belief in God and in what was sent down, and in the fact that most of you are defiantly disobedient."

It is also permissible that the *waw* means "with" (ma'a), meaning: "And you do not object to us except the belief along with the fact that most of you are defiantly disobedient."

It is also permissible that it be a causal clause (ta'lil) coordinated with an omitted causal clause, as if it were said: "And you do not object to us except the belief because of your lack of fairness, your defiant disobedience, and your following of desires." Al-Hasan's explanation supports this: "It is because of your defiant disobedience that you found fault with us for this."

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 5, verses 60–61:

It is related that a group of Jews came to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and asked him about which of the messengers he believed in. He said: "Do you believe in God and what has been sent down to us," up to His words, ﴿and we are submitting to Him﴾. When they heard the mention of Jesus (peace be upon him), they said: "We know of no people with less share in this world and the Hereafter than you, and no religion worse than your religion." [[Al-Wahidi reported it in *al-Asbab* (Reasons for Revelation), and al-Wasit (also) from Ibn Abbas with this wording. Al-Tabari reported it through Ibn Ishaq: "Muhammad ibn Abi Muhammad, mawla of Zayd ibn Thabit, told me: Sa'id or Ikrimah told me, from Ibn Abbas, may God be pleased with them both, who said: A group of Jews came to the Messenger of God (ﷺ), among them Abu Yasir ibn Akhtab and Rafi' ibn Abi Rafi', and Azar and Azar's two sons, Aziz and Azar." It is also said that they asked him about which of the messengers he believed in, and he mentioned something similar. In it: "When Jesus was mentioned, they denied his prophethood and said: We do not believe in Jesus, nor in anyone who believed in him."]] Then this was revealed.

**The commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 5, verse 64:**

"The tightening of the hand and its outstretching are a metaphor (majaz) for stinginess and generosity." [Al-Zamakhshari said: "The tightening of the hand and its outstretching are a metaphor for stinginess and generosity..." etc. Ahmad (Ibn al-Munayyir) said: The point of using this metaphor is to depict an abstract reality in a sensory image that usually accompanies it. Nothing is more firmly fixed in the mind than sensory images. Since generosity and stinginess are two meanings that cannot be perceived by the senses, and they are accompanied by two images that can be perceived by the senses, namely the outstretching of the hand for generosity and its gripping for stinginess, he expressed them by their accompanying images, for the benefit of clarification and of moving from abstract things to tangible ones. And God knows best.]

From this usage is His saying ﴿And do not make your hand chained to your neck, nor extend it fully outstretched﴾. The one who speaks this does not intend to affirm a hand, a chain, or an outstretching. In his mind there is no difference between this statement and what is used figuratively in its place, because both are two expressions following upon one reality. Indeed, one uses it of a king who never gives any gift and withholds only by a gesture, without using a hand, outstretching it, or gripping it. And if someone with a hand cut off at the shoulder gave a lavish gift, they would say: "How openhanded he is with his bounty!" because outstretching and gripping the hand are two expressions that occur alternately [Note: "occurred alternately" – perhaps "mu'aqibatayn," in the sense of "alternating"] for stinginess and generosity. They have used both even where a hand is not valid, as in the verse:

*The hill was showered by the outstretched pair of hands, with a heavy downpour,*
*Its high ground and its low ground gave thanks for its bounty.*

["Jada al-hima" means it rained upon it. "Basṭu al-yadayn" is the subject; its original form is a verbal noun used to mean the outstretched, the opposite of the contracted. It is also narrated as "sabṭu," with the sin first, as an attributive adjective like "ḍakhm," meaning the flowing and extended, a kinaya (metonymy) for the generous, just as one whose hands are contracted is a kinaya for the miser. So the cloud is likened to a generous person by way of implicit metaphor (al-makniyya), and affirming the two hands is a takhyil (imaginative evocation). The talʿa is high ground; the wahda is low ground. The upper and lower parts of the hill are likened to seekers of provision, and their giving thanks is a takhyil. Al-nadā means giving, a tarshīḥ (supporting element) for the first. It is also permissible that it is literal, not meaning giving. It is also permissible that the thanks is a takhyil for the first as well. He says: the cloud rained upon the land of al-Hima in Egypt abundantly, so it grew and blossomed. This is the meaning of its giving thanks. It is also permissible that the high ground and low ground are metonymies for their inhabitants who dwell in them.]

Labid also gave the north wind a hand, in his saying:

*When the wind-cold's reins were in the north wind's hand...*

["And a morning of wind has uncovered, and a cold: when it has come to the left hand, its reins." This is from Labid's Mu'allaqa. He says: many a morning of wind has been uncovered, meaning its gloom was uncovered from the people. It is narrated as "qad wazaʿat," meaning restrained and held back. Many a morning of cold, with a kasra or damma, meaning a severe chill, whose chill it also uncovered. Uncovering is specific to the perceptible, so it is borrowed for the intelligible, from the distress of hunger and cold, by way of explicit metaphor (tasrīḥiyya). It is also permissible that removing the wind and cold from the people is a kinaya for bringing them into his tent to honour them. He likened the morning to a mount which has a rein, or he likened the cold to that. He likened the north wind, which is a kind of wind, to a rider who leads that mount, by way of implicit metaphor. The rein is a takhyil for the first, and the hand for the second. It is not necessary that the likened thing have a real counterpart to what the likened-to has, according to the preferred view, such as the hand and the rein here. The meaning is that the north wind at times makes the morning dusty and cold, and at other times not. Or at times it scatters dust and cold in one direction, and at other times in another.]

It is also said: "Despair spread its two palms upon my chest," so we made for despair, which is a meaning and not a concrete thing, two palms.

Whoever has not looked into the science of rhetoric (ʿilm al-bayān) will be blind to the clear path of truth in interpreting such verses as this, and will not escape the hand of the critic when he toys with it. But if you say: it is established that their saying ﴿The hand of God is chained﴾ is an expression for stinginess [He returned to his words. He said: "If you say, it is established that their saying 'the hand of God is chained' is an expression for stinginess..." etc. Ahmad said: He has diminished the excellence he presented in this section by what this question and answer contain of the corrupt principle that it is impossible for God to desire from His servants anything He has forbidden them, and on that basis he built the impossibility that He would curse them with stinginess, because He did not will it from them, and it is impossible that He would will it from them. So he gave this text an interpretation and clung to falsehoods. The truth is that God curses them with stinginess, and His cursing is an expression for His creating miserliness in their hearts and gripping in their hands. He is the Caller and the Creator; there is no creator but Him. He creates stinginess for them, and He is exalted above it: ﴿He is not questioned about what He does, but they will be questioned﴾. Would that al-Zamakhshari had spoken of the Qur'an's exegesis only from the standpoint of rhetoric, for in it he is the most skilled of knights; none can match him in its field, and none disputes with him in its exposition.]. What then will you make of His saying ﴿Their hands were chained﴾? It must correspond to what precedes it, otherwise the speech would be discordant and depart from its course. I say: it is permissible that its meaning is a supplication against them with stinginess and misery, and for this reason they were the most miserly and wretched of God's creatures. A similar example is the verse of al-Ashtar:

*I remained alone and deviated from the heights, and I met my guests with a frowning face.*
*If I do not raid the son of Harb with a raid, it will never be free of the plundering of souls.*

[This is from al-Ashtar al-Nakhaʿi. The first verse is in the form of a report, but its intent is a performative supplication against himself with stinginess. It is also permissible that it is of the type of conditional linked to the impossible. "Wafr" means abundant wealth; it is narrated as "I remained alone," meaning my tribe perished or I was far from it. "Inḥirāf" means distancing from the edge of a perceptible thing, just as "ʿulā" is specific to perceptibles. So it is permissible that he borrowed "inḥirāf" for deviation from something and turning away from it, by way of explicit metaphor, and "ʿulā" is a tarshīḥ. It is possible he borrowed "ʿulā" for noble qualities, and "inḥirāf" is a tarshīḥ. His words "with a frowning face" mean a frowning man, and in it there is the sense of tajrīd (abstraction). "If I do not raid" with a damma on the shin is a conditional whose answer is indicated by what precedes it, meaning: if I do not stir up war against the son of Harb, Muʿawiya ibn Sakhr ibn Harb, such that it comes to him from every direction. It is narrated as "against the son of Hind." "Will never be free" is a description of "raid." "Plundering of souls" means seizing spirits by killing or capturing persons. It is narrated as "destruction of souls," meaning their annihilation. In the speech there is idmāj (embedding), in that the threat to Muʿawiya contains praise of himself for generosity, so that stinginess in his view is among the greatest calamities and the most severe shame, to the point that he attached it to the impossible, thereby conveying its impossibility.]

It is also permissible that it is a supplication against them with the literal chaining of hands, so that they are bound in this world as captives and in the Hereafter tormented with the chains of Hell. The antithesis (ṭibāq) is in the wording and in consideration of the original metaphor, as you say: "May God's Sabb (cursing) cut off his tail," meaning cut him off, because sabb originally means cutting. If you say: how is it permissible for God to curse them with what is ugly, namely stinginess and misery? I say: what is meant is a supplication with abandonment (khidhlān), by which their hearts are hardened, so that they increase in stinginess upon their stinginess and in misery upon their misery. Or it is by what results from stinginess and misery, namely the adhesion of shame to them and the evil reputation that disgraces them and tears their honour to pieces. If you say: why is the hand made dual in His saying ﴿But His two hands are outstretched﴾, when it is singular in their saying ﴿The hand of God﴾? [He returned to his words. He said: "If you say, why was the hand made dual in 'His two hands are outstretched,' when it is singular in their saying 'the hand of God'..." etc. Ahmad said: Since what is customary in giving is that it occurs with one of the two hands, namely the right, and since the prevailing belief among the Jews – may they be cursed – was corporealism (al-jismiyya), their expression came to refer to the single hand from which giving is familiar. So God made clear their falsehood in both matters: in attributing stinginess and in restricting it to the single hand, condescending to their belief in corporealism, by ascribing to His essence the attribute of generosity expressed by outstretching, and by attributing it to both hands together, because both of His hands are right hands, as is reported in the hadith, as an indication of the negation of corporealism. For if they were established, God is exalted above them, one hand would be right and the other left by necessity. When He affirmed that both are right, He negated corporealism and attributed generosity to both of them, not as it is attributed in the observable world to the right hand alone, since the other is left and is not a locus of honour. And God knows best.] I say: so that the rejection of their saying and its denial might be more eloquent and more indicative of establishing for Him the utmost extent of bounty and the negation of stinginess from Him. For the utmost that the generous one gives from his own wealth is to give with both his hands together, so the metaphor was built upon that. It is also recited as "wa-luʿinū" with a sukūn on the ʿayn. And in the codex of ʿAbdullah it reads: "Rather, His hands are outstretched."

It is said: "His hand is outstretched with goodness," and similarly "a shaḥḥ gait" and "a ṣarḥ she-camel," [He says: "shaḥḥ" in the Ṣiḥāḥ: "al-shaḥshaḥa" is swift flight, and "a shaḥshaḥ qaṭāt" means swift sandgrouse. So perhaps shaḥḥ is similar to it. Also in it: "al-ṣarḥ," with a vowel, means the pure of everything. (ʿ)] which "spends as He wills." It is an emphasis for the attribute of generosity, and an indication that He spends only according to the requirement of wisdom and benefit.

It is narrated that God, blessed and exalted, had extended provision to the Jews until they became among the people with the most wealth. When they disobeyed God regarding Muhammad (ﷺ) and denied him, God restrained the abundance He had extended to them. At that point Finḥāṣ ibn ʿĀzūrāʾ said: "The hand of God is chained," and the others approved his words and joined him in it. ﴿And surely it will increase﴾, meaning they will increase upon the revelation of the Qur'an, out of envy, in persistence of denial and disbelief in the signs of God. ﴿And We have cast among them enmity and hatred﴾, so their speech is always divergent, their hearts scattered, no agreement or support occurring among them. ﴿Whenever they kindle a fire for war, God extinguishes it﴾: whenever they wished to fight someone, they were defeated and subdued, and no victory from God ever arose for them over anyone, and Islam came to them while they were under the rule of the Magians. It has also been said: they opposed the judgement of the Torah, so God sent Nebuchadnezzar against them; then they corrupted, so God sent against them Phocas the Roman; then they corrupted, so God sent against them the Magians; then they corrupted, so God sent against them the Muslims. It has also been said: whenever they fought the Messenger of God (ﷺ), he was victorious over them. It is related from Qatada, may God be pleased with him, that one does not meet Jews in any town without finding them among the most abject of people. ﴿And they strive﴾, that is, they exert themselves in plotting against Islam and in erasing the mention of the Messenger of God (ﷺ) from their books.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 5, verses 65–66:

﴿Had the People of the Book, along with what We have counted of their misdeeds, believed in the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and in what he brought, and joined their belief with taqwa (God-consciousness, a condition for attaining faith's success), We would have expiated their misdeeds from them and not held them accountable for them, and We would have admitted them with the Muslims into the Garden.﴾ In this there is an announcement of the magnitude of the sins of the Jews and Christians and the abundance of their misdeeds, and an indication of the vastness of Allah the Exalted's mercy and His opening the door of repentance (tawbah) to every sinner, however great his sins and however far they reach, and that faith alone does not save [[Mahmud said: "In this there is evidence that faith alone does not save... etc." Ahmad (Ibn al-Munayyir) said: He seizes the opportunity from the apparent meaning of this verse and makes it evidence for his principle that mere faith does not save from eternal abiding in the Fire until taqwa is added to it, because Allah the Exalted made the combination in this verse a condition for expiation and for entering the Garden. Its apparent meaning is that, unless the two are combined, neither expiation nor entry into the Garden occurs. But how could that be, when there is consensus and agreement between the two groups, the People of Sunnah and the Mu'tazilah, that mere faith erases what came before it and wipes it out, as the text has stated? So if we suppose the one who enters faith dies immediately after entering it, he would be like the day his mother bore him, with unanimous agreement that he is one whose sins are expiated and who is judged to enter the Garden. This shows that the combination of the two matters is not a condition. This holds if taqwa means the deeds.

If taqwa is taken in its original sense of fear of Allah the Mighty and Majestic, then this meaning applies to every believer, even if he has committed major sins.

In that case, Zamakhshari's purpose is not achieved. This is nothing but insistence and obstinacy in opposing the belief derived from the words of the Messenger (peace and blessings be upon him): "Whoever says 'There is no god but Allah' enters the Garden, even if he committed adultery or theft." He repeated it several times, then said: "even if Abu Dhar's nose is rubbed in the dust," when Abu Dhar (may Allah be pleased with him) questioned him about it. And we say: "Even if the noses of the Qadariyyah (those who deny divine predestination) are rubbed in the dust."]] Yet it is not fortunate except when accompanied by taqwa, as al-Hasan said: "This is the pole, so where are the ropes?"

﴿And if they had upheld the Torah and the Gospel﴾: they would have established their rulings and their limits, and what they contain of the description of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), ﴿and what was sent down to them﴾ from the rest of Allah's books, because they are obligated to believe in all of them, so it is as if they were sent down to them. It was said: it refers to the Qur'an. ﴿He would have granted them abundant provision, and they had been struck by drought.﴾ His saying ﴿they would have eaten from above them and from beneath their feet﴾ is an expression of abundance. It has three interpretations: that He would pour upon them the blessings of heaven and the blessings of the earth; that He would multiply fruitful trees and profitable crops; and that He would provide them with gardens of luscious fruit, so that they would pick what hangs down (tadalla) from the tops of the trees and gather what falls to the ground beneath their feet. [[His saying "what hangs down" means: what droops and dangles. Cited from al-Sihah. (ʿ)]]

﴿Among them is a moderate community﴾: a group whose state is that of [[His saying "amam" means: little. Cited from al-Sihah. (ʿ)]] enmity toward the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). It was said: they are the believing group, ʿAbd Allah ibn Salam and his companions, and forty-eight Christians. ﴿And evil is what they do﴾ carries the sense of wonder, as if it were said: "And many of them, how evil their deeds are!" It was also said: they are Kaʿb ibn al-Ashraf and his companions, and the Romans.

﴿Had the People of the Book, along with what We have counted of their misdeeds, believed in the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and in what he brought, and joined their belief with taqwa (God-consciousness, a condition for attaining faith's success), We would have expiated their misdeeds from them and not held them accountable for them, and We would have admitted them with the Muslims into the Garden.﴾ In this there is an announcement of the magnitude of the sins of the Jews and Christians and the abundance of their misdeeds, and an indication of the vastness of Allah the Exalted's mercy and His opening the door of repentance (tawbah) to every sinner, however great his sins and however far they reach, and that faith alone does not save [[Mahmud said: "In this there is evidence that faith alone does not save... etc." Ahmad (Ibn al-Munayyir) said: He seizes the opportunity from the apparent meaning of this verse and makes it evidence for his principle that mere faith does not save from eternal abiding in the Fire until taqwa is added to it, because Allah the Exalted made the combination in this verse a condition for expiation and for entering the Garden. [[His saying "what hangs down" means: what droops and dangles. Cited from al-Sihah. (ʿ)]]

﴿Among them is a moderate community﴾: a group whose state is that of [[His saying "amam" means: little. Cited from al-Sihah. (ʿ)]] enmity toward the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). Proclaim what has been revealed to you (بلغ ما أنزل إليك): all that has been revealed to you, and whatever has been sent down to you, without being concerned about anyone in proclaiming it. [[Mahmud said: "Its meaning is: proclaim without concern in proclaiming it to anyone, and without fear that some harm will befall you." (وَإِنْ لَمْ تَفْعَلْ) means:

"And if you do not proclaim all of it as you were commanded, then you have not conveyed His message (فَما بَلَّغْتَ رِسالَتَهُ). Thus you have not then proclaimed what you were charged with of conveying the message, and you have not conveyed any part of it at all. That is because no part of it is more deserving of being conveyed than another. So, if you omit conveying part of it, it is as though you had neglected conveying all of it, just as one who believes in some of it is like one who does not believe in all of it, since each part conveys what the others convey. Given that they are thus, they are in the judgment of a single thing, and a single thing is not one that is conveyed and not conveyed, or believed in and not believed in." Then he said: "If you ask, how is the occurrence of his words (فَما بَلَّغْتَ رِسالَتَهُ) as the consequent of the condition valid? I say: there are two aspects to it. The first is that if he does not carry out the command of God to convey the messages and conceals them all, it is as though he had not been sent as a messenger, which is a shameful matter whose shamefulness is clear. So it is said: 'If you do not convey even the least of it, even if it is a single word, you are like one who commits the shameful act of concealing all of it,' just as the killing of a soul is magnified by His words: (فَكَأَنَّما قَتَلَ النَّاسَ جَمِيعاً) [Whoever kills a soul... it is as if he had killed all mankind]. The second is that it means: 'If you do not do it, then you will receive what the concealment of all the revelation requires of punishment,' so the cause is placed in the position of the effect, and this is supported by the words of the Prophet, peace be upon him: 'God revealed to me: if you do not convey My messages, I will punish you.'" (وَاللَّهُ يَعْصِمُكَ) is a promise from God of protection and safeguarding. The meaning: God guarantees you protection from your enemies, so what excuse do you have for being wary of them? If you ask: where is the guarantee of protection when he was wounded in the face on the day of Uhud and his front tooth was broken, peace be upon him? I say: the meaning is that He protects him from being killed. And in it: he must endure everything short of death for the sake of God. How severe is the burden on the prophets, peace be upon them. It was also said: it was revealed after the day of Uhud, and "the people" refers to the disbelievers, as is indicated by His words: (إِنَّ اللَّهَ لا يَهْدِي الْقَوْمَ الْكافِرِينَ), and its meaning is that He does not enable them to do what they want to bring upon you of destruction. It is related from Anas: The Messenger of God, peace be upon him, used to be guarded until this was revealed, then he put his head out of a leather tent and said: "Disperse, O people, for God has protected me from people."]]

You are not upon anything, i.e., not upon a religion that is counted as valid, so as to be called "something," given its corruption and invalidity. Just as you say, "This is nothing," meaning to belittle it and diminish its standing. And among their proverbs: "less than nothing." ﴿So do not grieve﴾ over them, i.e., do not feel sorrow for them because of the increase in their rebellion and disbelief, for the harm of that returns to them, not to you, and among the believers there is sufficiency without them.

**Al-Sabi'un** (the Sabians) is in the nominative case as a subject (mubtada'), and its predicate is omitted. The intended construction is that the omitted predicate follows, after the parts of the clause introduced by *inna* (indeed), its noun and its predicate. The sense is: "Indeed, those who believe, and those who are Jews, and the Christians, their ruling is such-and-such, and the Sabians likewise." Sibawayh cited a line of verse as evidence for this:

*"And if not, then know that we and you*
*are rebels (bughah) for as long as we remain in dissension (shiqaq)."*

[[Mahmud said: "In it, *al-Sabi'un* is in the nominative as a subject, and its predicate is omitted... etc." Ahmad said: He is right. The objection does not arise under this interpretation. But there is a real objection to be raised, which is this: If the Sabians were put in the accusative and coordinated, as Ibn Kathir read it, that would also have conveyed their inclusion among those who are forgiven. Mentioning them before the Christians would have conveyed, as the nominative does, that these Sabians, who are the most deeply immersed in disbelief, are forgiven. So what is to be assumed about the Christians? The sentence would then be a single eloquent and concise clause, with the coordination being of individual items. Why, then, did it shift to the nominative and make the sentence two clauses? Does it have any advantage over the accusative and individual coordination? The answer to this question is that if it were put in the accusative and coordinated, it would not convey the particular distinction of this category, since all the categories are coordinated with one another by individual coordination. This category is one of them, and the predicate concerning them is one. But with the nominative it is cut off from individual coordination, and the remaining categories are specified by the predicate they are coordinated with. The predicate of this separate category stands alone, as if to say, for example, "and the Sabians likewise." It thus comes across as if it is analogized with the remaining categories and appended to them, being in this position, because after the categories it has been established that they are eligible for acceptance of repentance. They are therefore worthy of being made subordinate and secondary, being likened to those who are more firmly established than them by this predicate. The benefit of placing the omitted subject before the predicate, so that the omitted subject sits between the two parts, is that it points more clearly to the omitted predicate than mentioning it after the sentence is complete. And God knows best.]] (The predicate is omitted.) The intention behind the omission is a postponement (ta'khir) relative to what falls under the scope of *inna* in its noun and predicate, as if it were said: "Indeed, those who believe, and those who are Jews, and the Christians, their ruling is such-and-such, and the Sabians likewise." Sibawayh cited as evidence for this the line of verse:

*"And if not, then know that we and you are rebels for as long as we remain in dissension."*

That is: "Know that we are rebels, and you likewise." If you say: "Why not claim that its nominative case is for coordination with the position (mahall) of *inna* and its noun?" I reply: That is not valid before the predicate is completed. You do not say: "Indeed Zayd and 'Amr are departing (munṭaliqan)." If you say: "Why is it not valid, when the intention is postponement, so that it is as if you had said: 'Indeed Zayd is departing, and 'Amr'?" I reply: Because if I put it in the nominative, I would be putting it in the nominative by coordination with the position of *inna* and its noun, and the governing element for both their positions is the inchoative (ibtida'). Therefore, the same element must govern the predicate, because the inchoative encompasses both parts in its operation, just as *inna* encompasses them in its operation. So if you put *al-Sabi'un*, with postponement intended, in the nominative by the inchoative, while you have put the predicate in the nominative by *anna*, you would be applying two different governing elements to both. If you say: "The coordinated word *wa-al-Sabi'un* must have a coordinated-upon item; what is it?" I reply: It, together with its omitted predicate, is a clause coordinated with the clause of His words, ﴿Indeed those who believe﴾, and so on. It has no position of its own, just as the clause it is coordinated with has none. If you say: "Placing something before its place serves a purpose; what is the purpose of this fronting?" I reply: Its purpose is to draw attention to the fact that the Sabians are forgiven if faith and righteous deeds are genuinely found in them, so what is to be assumed about others? That is because the Sabians are the clearest of those enumerated in misguidance and the most extreme in error. They were only named Sabians because they "turned away" (sabaʼu) from all religions, meaning they departed from them. Just as the poet placed his words "and you" first, to draw attention to the fact that the addressees, from among his people, are more deeply described as rebels, he hastened to mention them before the predicate "rebels," so that his people would not enter into rebellion before them, despite their being more deeply immersed in it and firmer in it. If you say: "If it had been said, 'and the Sabians and you,' fronting would have been achieved," I reply: If it had been said in that way, there would be no fronting in it at all, because nothing is displaced from its place. Fronting and postponement are said only of what has been moved, not of what remains in its place.

The structure of this clause is that of a parenthetical insertion (i'tiraḍ) within the speech. If you say: "How did He say *alladhina amanu* (those who believe), and then say *man amana* (whoever believes)?" I reply: There are two interpretations. The first is that *alladhina amanu* refers to those who believed with their tongues, namely the hypocrites, while *man amana* refers to those who held firm in faith, were upright, and were not troubled by doubt about it. If you say: "What is the position of *man amana*?" I reply: It may be in the nominative as an inchoative, with its predicate being ﴿so no fear shall be upon them﴾, the *fa'* (so) serving because the subject contains the sense of a condition, and then the whole clause is the predicate of *inna*. Or it may be in the accusative as a substitution (badal) from the subject of *inna* and what is coordinated with it, or from the coordinated-upon item. If you say: "Then where is the resumptive pronoun referring back to the subject of *inna*?" I reply: It is omitted, its estimated form being *man amana minhum* (whoever of them believes), as it occurs in another passage.

It has been read as *wa-al-Sabiyyun* with a clear *ya'* (yā'), which results from softening the hamza, like the reading of those who read *yastahziyun* (they mock) and *al-Sabun*. It derives from *ṣabawtu*, because they "inclined" (ṣabaw) to following desire and appetites in their religion, and did not follow the proofs of reason and revelation. In the reading of Ubayy, may God be pleased with him, it is *wa-al-Sabi'in* in the accusative, and Ibn Kathir read it so. 'Abd Allah (Ibn Mas'ud) read: ﴿O you who believe, and those who are Jews, and the Sabians...﴾.

We certainly took the covenant of the Children of Israel to worship none but God, and We sent to them messengers, so that they might hold them to account for what they do and what they abandon in their religion. Every time a messenger came to them with what their souls do not desire, (the clause "every time a messenger came to them" is a conditional clause functioning as an attribute of "messengers," the returning pronoun being omitted, i.e. "a messenger from among them") with that which opposes their desires and contradicts their appetites, of the hardships of obligation and the practice of the sacred laws, [the Qadi, Mahmud al-Zamakhshari, said:] "If you ask: where is the answer (jawab) to the conditional?" [Ahmad (Ibn al-Munayyir) said: What indicates that the answer is omitted is that it appears explicitly in the other verse, its twin, the saying of God Most High: ﴿Is it, whenever a messenger comes to you with what your souls do not desire, that you wax arrogant, so that you denied a group and kill a group?﴾ Here His saying ﴿you wax arrogant﴾ serves as the answer, then their arrogance and their treatment of the prophets is explained by killing some and denying others. Had al-Zamakhshari here supplied the omitted answer in the same form as what is stated in its twin verse, saying: "And We sent to them messengers; every time a messenger came to them with what their souls do not desire, they waxed arrogant," it would have been better, since the like of it indicates it.] Indeed, His saying ﴿a group they denied, and a group they kill﴾ stands in place of the answer, because one messenger cannot be two groups, and because it is not good to say: "If you honour my brother, your brother honours [you]?" I say: It is omitted, indicated by His saying ﴿a group they denied, and a group they kill﴾, as if it were said: "Every time a messenger from among them came to them, they opposed him," and His saying ﴿a group they denied﴾ is a new statement in answer to one who says: "How did they treat their messengers?" If you ask: why was one of the two verbs put in the past tense (māḍī) and the other in the present (muḍāriʿ)? I say: "yaqtulūn" (they kill) is used to narrate a past situation in the present, to express the horror of killing and to bring that dreadful state vividly before the mind, so as to wonder at it. [Ahmad said: Or it may be a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) in its real sense, because they were plotting around killing Muhammad, may the best of prayers and peace be upon him. This interpretation has been given for the twin of this verse in al-Baqarah.] The reason why the present-tense form requires presenting the action, rather than the past tense, has already been explained, and illustrated by His saying: ﴿Do you not see that God sends down water from the sky, so the earth becomes green?﴾ Here "tuṣbiḥu" (becomes) is used instead of "aṣbaḥat" (became), to depict the state and to make it present in the hearer's mind. From the same usage is the line of poetry:

"That I have met the ghoul, as it approached, with a shape like a sheet, a level ground..."

"So I seized it and struck it, and it fell prostrate, upon its hands and jaws."

Its like is abundant, and God knows best.

It is read "an lā yakūna" (that there would not be) in the accusative, as the apparent reading. And it is read in the nominative, with "an" being the lightened form of the heavy "inna," whose original was "annahu lā yakūnu fitnatun," the "an" was lightened and the pronoun of the matter (ḍamīr al-shaʾn) was omitted.

**Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf, "The Unveiler") on Surah 5, verse 71:**

If you ask: how does the verb of supposing (ḥasiba) come to govern *anna*, which is used for affirmation? The answer: their supposing, because of its firmness in their hearts, was treated as knowledge. If you ask: then where are the two objects of *ḥasiba*? The answer: what the clause of *anna* and *inna* contains, of predicate and subject, stands in place of the two objects. The meaning: "And the Children of Israel supposed that no trial from God would befall them", that is, affliction and punishment in this world and the Hereafter. So they became blind to the religion and deaf when they worshipped the calf. Then they repented of worshipping the calf, so ﴿God turned to them in forgiveness﴾. Then they became blind and deaf again, a second time, by their demand for the impossible, which is not conceivable regarding the attributes of God, namely [[the phrase "namely the vision" (al-ru'yah): the Mu'tazila (the rationalist school) deemed it impossible, while Ahl al-Sunnah (the Sunni school) permitted it, as verified in its proper place. (ʿ)]] the vision. ﴿Then they became blind and deaf﴾, and it was read: "ʿamū wa-ṣammū" with a *ḍamma*, on the assumption that God blinded them and made them deaf, that is, struck them and afflicted them with blindness and deafness, just as one says "I struck him with the *nayzak*" when one strikes him, [[the phrase "with the nayzak": this is the short spear, a Persian word arabicized, originally *nayzah*, whose *hāʾ* was replaced by *kāf*. So it is in the margin, and it is originally in the Ṣiḥāḥ. (ʿ)]] and "I knelt on him" (rakabtuhu) when one strikes him with one's knee. ﴿Many of them﴾ is a substitute for the pronoun, or it is based on their saying "the fleas ate me" (akalūnī al-barāghīth), or it is the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: those are many of them.

Isa (peace be upon him) did not distinguish himself from them in being a created servant nurtured by the Lord, like them. This is an argument against the Christians: "Indeed, whoever associates others with Allah in worship, or in what is specific to Him of His attributes or actions, then Allah has forbidden him Paradise, which is the abode of those who affirm Allah's oneness (al-muwahhidin)." That is, He has forbidden him its entry and prevented him from it, just as the forbidden is kept from what is forbidden to him. "And the wrongdoers will have no helpers." This is from the words of Allah, indicating that they wronged [[His saying "indicating that they wronged" is perhaps meant in the sense of "that they"; (ʿ).]] and deviated from the path of truth in what they said about Isa (peace be upon him). Therefore He did not support them in it, nor did He lend His support to their statement, rejecting and denying it, even though they were thereby magnifying him and elevating his station. Or it is from the words of Isa (peace be upon him), in the sense: "No one will help you in what you say, nor will anyone support you in it, because it is impossible and far from reason." Or: "No helper will help you in the Hereafter against the punishment of Allah."

"من" in His saying وَما مِنْ إِلهٍ إِلَّا إِلهٌ واحِدٌ, ﴿There is no god except One God﴾, is for comprehensiveness (istighraq, the inclusion of every individual of a category). It has the same force as "لا" in the phrase used for negating the genus in your saying (لا إله إلا الله), "There is no god but Allah." The meaning is: there is no god at all in existence except a god described by oneness, who has no second, and that is Allah alone, without partner.

"من" in His saying لَيَمَسَّنَّ الَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا مِنْهُمْ, ﴿Surely a painful punishment will afflict those of them who disbelieve﴾, is explanatory (lil-bayan), like the "من" in His saying Exalted is He: ﴿So avoid the abomination of the idols﴾. If you say: why was it not said "لَيَمَسَّنَّكُمْ مِنَّا عَذابٌ أَلِيمٌ" (a painful punishment will afflict you from us)? I say: placing the apparent noun in the place of the pronoun has a benefit, namely the repetition of the testimony against them as disbelievers in His saying ﴿Certainly they have disbelieved who said﴾. The explanatory "من" has another benefit, which is to inform, in the explanation of "الَّذِينَ كَفَرُوا مِنْهُمْ", that they are situated in disbelief.

The meaning is: a painful punishment will afflict only those of the Christians who disbelieve. "أَلِيمٌ" means a punishment of a severely painful kind. It is like when you say: "Give me twenty of the garments," meaning garments specifically, and not other kinds that twenty could include. It is also permissible for "من" to be partitive (lil-tab'id), meaning: a painful punishment will afflict those among them who remained upon disbelief, because many of them repented from Christianity. ﴿Will they not then repent?﴾, that is, will they not repent after this repeated testimony against them as disbelievers? This severe threat is an admonition for what they are upon, and it contains a wonder at their persistence. ﴿And Allah is Forgiving, Merciful﴾, He forgives these people if they repent, and others as well.

﴿The Messenger was no more than a messenger; messengers had passed away before him﴾. The phrase "قَدْ خَلَتْ مِنْ قَبْلِهِ الرُّسُلُ" is a description of "رسول" (messenger), meaning: he is only a messenger of the same kind as the messengers who passed away before him, who came with signs from Allah just as they came with the like of them. For example, he healed the leper and raised the dead by his hand; Moses turned his staff into a serpent that moves swiftly, split the sea with it, and obliterated [[The phrase "and obliterated upon the hand of Moses" is perhaps "and obliterated the wealth of Pharaoh and his people upon the hand of ... etc. (ʿ)]]. And if his creation was without a father, then Adam was created without a father or a mother. ﴿And his mother was a truthful woman﴾, meaning: his mother too was nothing but a truthful woman, like some women who affirmed the prophets and believed in them. Their station is nothing but the station of two humans: one a prophet, the other a companion. So from where has their matter become confused for you, so that you have described them with what no other prophets and their companions were described with, even though there is no distinction or difference between them and those others in any respect?

Then he explicitly stated their distance from what was attributed to them in His saying ﴿They both used to eat food﴾, because whoever needs to be nourished by food and what follows from it of digestion and elimination is only a body composed of bone, flesh, veins, nerves, humours and temperaments, together with desire and craving [[The phrase "craving" in the Sihah: "al-qaram" with a vowel: intensity of desire for meat. (ʿ)]], and other things indicating that he is a made, composed, and managed thing like other bodies. ﴿See how We make the signs clear to them, then see how they are turned away﴾, that is, the evident proofs, the manifest indications of the falsehood of their claim. ﴿How are they turned away?﴾, that is, how are they diverted from listening to the truth and reflecting upon it?

If you say: what is the meaning of the delay (tarakhi) in His saying "ثُمَّ انظر" (then see)? [[Mahmud said: "If you say, what is the meaning of the delay in His saying 'then see'..." Ahmad said: and from this are (ثُمَّ أَنْتُمْ هؤُلاءِ تَقْتُلُونَ أَنْفُسَكُمْ) and His saying (فَقُتِلَ كَيْفَ قَدَّرَ ثُمَّ قُتِلَ كَيْفَ قَدَّرَ), and in all these places it is transferred from temporal delay to figurative delay in ranks.]] I say: its meaning is between two wonders, meaning that He made the signs clear to them in a wondrous manner, and that their turning away from them is more wondrous than that.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 5, verse 76:

"What does not possess" (ما لا يَمْلِكُ) refers to Jesus, i.e., something that is not able to harm you with the like of the harm that God inflicts upon you through calamities and afflictions in your persons and your wealth, nor able to benefit you with the like of the benefit that He bestows upon you through bodily health, abundance and fertility. And since all that human beings are able to do of harm and benefit is by God's empowerment and enablement, it is as though he possesses nothing of it. This is a decisive proof that his status contradicts lordship (al-rububiyyah), since He has made him unable to inflict harm or bring benefit.

The attribute of the Lord is that He be capable of everything, such that no object of power escapes His power. ﴿And God is the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing﴾ is connected to "Do you worship" (أتعبدون), i.e., do you associate partners with God and not fear Him, while He is the One who hears what you say and knows what you believe. Or, "Do you worship what is powerless, while God is the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing," meaning the One from whom it is correct that He hears every thing heard and knows every thing known; and He would not be like this unless He were living and capable.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 5, verse 77:

﴿غَيْرَ الْحَقِّ﴾ is a qualifier of the verbal noun (maṣdar, i.e. "exaggeration"), meaning: do not exaggerate in your religion an exaggeration [that is] other than the truth. [[Mahmud said: "Its meaning is: do not exaggerate in your religion an exaggeration that is false... etc." Ahmad said: By the people of justice and monotheism he means the Mu'tazila, and by their exaggeration which is true in his view, he means that they exaggerated in monotheism, so they denied the divine attributes, and they exaggerated in [the doctrine of] justice ('adl), so they negated most acts, indeed all of them, from being created by God the Exalted, because they [supposedly] involve corruption, and because God the Exalted punishes for what is ugly among them, and justice, in their view, is that He does not punish for an act that He created. This is their exaggeration in justice, and as you see, it is a corruption of monotheism, because they made every created animal a creator. The Christians exaggerated and so associated three [gods], and the Mu'tazila, as you have seen, associated every person, indeed non-human beings, in the creation that is specific to the Lord. By the people of innovation and desires, al-Zamakhshari means all besides the group mentioned, and by their false exaggeration he means affirming attributes for God the Exalted and affirming His unity in truth, to the extent that there is no creator besides Him and no creation except by His power. He is pleased with his own sect and his brethren, and remains silent about mention of others. We say: O God, be pleased with the one who is most worthy of Your pleasure among the sects. This is also a supplication without disagreement. And God is the Granter of success.]] That is, [an exaggeration that is] false, because exaggeration in religion is of two kinds: a true exaggeration, which is to investigate its realities and search out its most remote meanings, and to strive to obtain its proofs, as the theologians of the people of justice and monotheism do, may God be pleased with them; and a false exaggeration, which is to go beyond the truth and overstep it by turning away from the evidences and following doubtful analogies, as the people of desires and innovation do.

﴿قَدْ ضَلُّوا مِنْ قَبْلُ﴾ [They had already gone astray before]: their leaders in Christianity, who were in error before the mission of the Prophet (ﷺ).

﴿وَأَضَلُّوا كَثِيراً﴾ [and led many astray]: those who followed them in the doctrine of the Trinity.

﴿وَضَلُّوا عَنْ سَواءِ السَّبِيلِ﴾ [and went astray from the right way]: when the Messenger of God (ﷺ) was sent, they denied him, envied him, and rebelled against him.

God sent His curse upon them in the Psalms through the tongue of Dawud (David), and in the Gospel through the tongue of Isa (Jesus). It is said that the people of Ayla, when they transgressed on the Sabbath, Dawud (peace be upon him) said: "O Allah, curse them and make them a sign," and so they were transformed into apes. And when the companions of Isa (peace be upon him) disbelieved after the Table (al-Ma'idah), Isa (peace be upon him) said: "O Allah, punish whoever disbelieved after eating from the Table with a punishment You have not inflicted upon anyone among the worlds, and curse them as You cursed the companions of the Sabbath." So they became swine, and they were five thousand men, with no women or children among them.

﴿That was because they disobeyed and transgressed﴾: that is, that dreadful curse which was the cause of the transformation was not for anything other than disobedience and transgression. Then he explained disobedience and transgression with His words: ﴿they did not forbid one another from any wrong they committed﴾, that is, they did not forbid one another from any wrongdoing that they did. Then He said: ﴿Evil indeed was what they used to do﴾, as a expression of wonder at the badness of their deed, emphasizing this with an oath. So, alas for the Muslims in their turning away from the matter of forbidding wrongdoing, and their scant heedfulness toward it, as if it were not part of the religion of Islam at all, despite their recitation of the words of Allah and the emphatic statements on this subject in it.

If you ask: how did the abandonment of forbidding wrong come to be explained as "disobedience and transgression"? I answer: because Allah the Exalted commanded forbidding wrong, so neglecting it was disobedience, and it is transgression, because forbidding wrong is a restraint against corruption, so abandoning it is its opposite.

If you ask: what is the meaning of describing the wrong as ﴿they committed﴾, when forbidding cannot come after the act?

I answer: its meaning is "they did not forbid one another from a wrong they committed," or "from a wrong like one they committed," or "from a wrong they intended to commit," just as you see the signs of plunging into wickedness and its tools being prepared and readied, and so it is denounced. It is also permissible to mean: "they do not refrain or abstain from a wrong they committed, rather they persist in it and continue to do it." It is said: "tanahā 'an al-amr" and "intahā 'anhu" when one refrains from it and leaves it.

﴿You see many of them making friends with those who disbelieve﴾: they are the hypocrites among the People of the Book, who were allied with the polytheists and befriended them. ﴿Evil indeed is what their souls have sent forward for them, that Allah became wrathful toward them﴾: the object of the censure is "that Allah became wrathful toward them," and its place is in the nominative case, as if it were said: "Evil indeed is what they have sent forward to the Hereafter: the wrath of Allah upon them." The meaning is: what necessitates the wrath of Allah. ﴿And if they had believed in Allah, in the Prophet, and in what was revealed to him, they would not have taken them as allies﴾: that is, the allegiance to the polytheists is by itself sufficient proof of their hypocrisy, and that their faith is not faith. ﴿But many of them are defiant transgressors﴾: rebellious in their disbelief and hypocrisy.

It was also said that its meaning is: "And if they had believed in Allah and Musa as they claim, they would not have taken the polytheists as allies, just as the Muslims did not take them as allies."

I answer: because Allah the Exalted commanded forbidding wrong, so neglecting it was disobedience, and it is transgression, because forbidding wrong is a restraint against corruption, so abandoning it is its opposite.

If you ask: what is the meaning of describing the wrong as ﴿they committed﴾, when forbidding cannot come after the act?

I answer: its meaning is "they did not forbid one another from a wrong they committed," or "from a wrong like one they committed," or "from a wrong they intended to commit," just as you see the signs of plunging into wickedness and its tools being prepared and readied, and so it is denounced. It is also permissible to mean: "they do not refrain or abstain from a wrong they committed, rather they persist in it and continue to do it." It is said: "tanahā 'an al-amr" and "intahā 'anhu" when one refrains from it and leaves it.

…and the gentleness of the Christians' disposition, the ease with which they yield, and their inclination toward Islam. It is narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ): "No two Jews sat with a Muslim except that they plotted to kill him." In this there is clear evidence that learning is the most beneficial thing, the most guiding to goodness, and the surest path to success, even to the point of [its benefit reaching] the priests. Likewise, concern for the Hereafter and speaking of the final outcome is [beneficial], even if it comes from a monk, and freedom from pride is [praiseworthy], even if it comes from a Christian.

Allah described them as tender-hearted and as weeping when they hear the Qur'an. This is like what is related about al-Najashi (the Negus), may Allah be pleased with him, who said to Ja'far ibn Abi Talib when the emigrants to Abyssinia had gathered in his assembly, while the polytheists, who had been cursed, were urging him against them and seeking to harm them in his presence: "Is there in your book any mention of Maryam?" Ja'far said: "There is a surah named after her." He recited it up to the words ﴿That is Jesus, son of Maryam﴾, and recited Surah Ta-Ha up to the words ﴿And has the story of Musa reached you?﴾. Then al-Najashi wept. [I have not found it. I think the author of al-Kashshaf mentioned it in meaning from the account of Ja'far ibn Abi Talib with 'Amr ibn al-'As, when the Quraysh sent their gift to al-Najashi to have Ja'far and his companions handed over to them. The meaning mentioned is present in it, except for the recitation of Ta-Ha. It was reported by Ibn Ishaq in al-Maghazi, from the route of Ibn Hibban, from the hadith of Umm Salamah. They entered upon the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and he recited Ya-Sin to them. They wept and recognized the truth. So this was revealed, and there was also revealed concerning them ﴿Those to whom We gave the Book before it, they believe in it﴾." Ibn Mardawayh also reported it by another route from Qays.]

And likewise did his people who came as a delegation to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), who were seventy men, when the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) recited Surah Ya-Sin to them, and they wept.

I say: It is connected to "enmity" and "affection," [meaning that] the enmity of the Jews, which is specific to the believers, is the most intense and most evident of enmities, and the affection of the Christians, which is specific to the believers, is the nearest of affections, the least in existence and the easiest to obtain. Describing the Jews with enmity and the Christians with affection indicates a difference, and then He described the enmity and the affection as the strongest and the nearest.

If you ask: What is the meaning of His words ﴿You see their eyes overflowing with tears﴾? [The author resumed his speech. He said: "If you ask what is the meaning of His words ﴿You see their eyes overflowing with tears…﴾ etc." Ahmad said: This expression is among the most eloquent and the most complete, and it has three levels. The first: "His eye overflowed with tears," and this is the original form. The second is derived from it, namely the saying of the speaker: "His eyes overflowed with tears," transferring the verb to the eye as a metaphor and an intensification, and then drawing attention to the original and literal sense by putting what was the subject into the accusative of specification (tamyiz). The third contains this transference mentioned, and it is the one found in the verse, except that it is more eloquent than the second, by omitting what draws attention to the original and by not putting the specification in the accusative, presenting it in the form of a causal clause. And Allah knows best. The statement with a causal clause is further from the original than with the specification because the specification in such a usage has become established as the original subject, as in: "Zayd's sweat flowed (tasabbaba Zayd 'araqan)," "'Amr's fat burst out (tafaqa'a 'Amr shahman)," "the head ignited with white hair (ishta'al al-ra's shayban)," and "the earth gushed forth springs (tafajjarat al-ard 'uyunan)." When you say "his eye overflowed with tears (fada'at 'aynuhu dam'an)," the original is understood from such usage customarily. But a causal clause is not known to carry that. Do you not see that you say "his eye overflowed because of the remembrance of Allah," just as you say "his eye overflowed with tears," yet the causal clause does not convey what the specification conveys? And Allah is the Granter of success.]

I say: Its meaning is that they fill with tears until they overflow, because "fayd" (overflowing) means that a vessel or something else is filled until what is in it spills over from its sides. So the word "fayd," which comes from being full, has been placed in the position of "imtila'" (being full). This is the usage of stating the effect in place of the cause. Or it is intended as an intensification in describing them as weeping, so their eyes are made as if they overflow by themselves, that is, flow with tears because of weeping, from your saying "his eye wept tears (dama'at 'aynuhu dam'an)."

If you ask: What is the difference between "min" and "min" in His words ﴿from what they have recognized of the truth﴾? I say: The first [min] indicates the starting point, since the overflow of tears began and arose from recognizing the truth, and was because of it and caused by it. The second [min] clarifies the relative clause "what they recognized." It may also carry the sense of partition, meaning that they recognized part of the truth, and this moved them to weep and affected them deeply. How much more so when they recognize all of it, recite the Qur'an, and comprehend the Sunnah?

[It is read "tara a'yunahum" (you see their eyes) in the passive voice.]

﴿Our Lord, we have believed, so register us among the witnesses.﴾ The meaning is the initiation of faith and entering into it, ﴿with the community of Muhammad (ﷺ), who are witnesses over all other nations on the Day of Resurrection﴾, as in His words ﴿that you may be witnesses over the people﴾. They said this because they found their mention in the Gospel in that way.

﴿And what is [the matter] with us that we do not believe in Allah…﴾ This is a rhetorical denial, expressing that faith is absent although its requirement is present, namely the hope that Allah would bless them with the companionship of the righteous. It was also said: When they returned to their people, they blamed them, and they answered them with this. Or they meant: "What is the matter with us that we do not believe in Allah alone," because they were Trinitarians, and that is not belief in Allah.

The place of ﴿we do not believe﴾ is in the accusative as a circumstantial clause (hal), meaning "not believing," as in your saying "mā laka qā'iman" (what is with you standing?). The wāw in ﴿and we hope﴾ is the wāw of circumstance.

If you ask: What governs the first and second circumstantial clauses? I say: The governing element of the first is the meaning of the verb contained in the lām, as if it were said: "What has happened to us, not believing?" And the second has the meaning of this verb, but restricted by the first circumstance, because if you removed the first and said "What is with us and we hope," it would not be a complete sentence. It is permissible for "and we hope" to be a circumstantial clause of "we do not believe," meaning that they rebuked themselves for not affirming the oneness of Allah while hoping at the same time to be companions of the righteous. It is also permissible for it to be coordinated with "we do not believe," with the meaning: "What is with us that we combine Trinitarianism with hoping for the companionship of the righteous?" Or with the meaning: "What is with us that we do not combine them by entering Islam, since the disbeliever should not hope for the companionship of the righteous."

[It is read "tara a'yunahum" (you see their eyes) in the passive voice.]

﴿Our Lord, we have believed, so register us among the witnesses.﴾ The meaning is the initiation of faith and entering into it, ﴿with the community of Muhammad (ﷺ), who are witnesses over all other nations on the Day of Resurrection﴾, as in His words ﴿that you may be witnesses over the people﴾. ﴿Our Lord, we have believed, so register us among the witnesses.﴾ The meaning is the initiation of faith and entering into it, ﴿with the community of Muhammad (ﷺ), who are witnesses over all other nations on the Day of Resurrection﴾, as in His words ﴿that you may be witnesses over the people﴾. They said this because they found their mention in the Gospel in that way.

﴿And what is [the matter] with us that we do not believe in Allah…﴾ This is a rhetorical denial, expressing that faith is absent although its requirement is present, namely the hope that Allah would bless them with the companionship of the righteous. It was also said: When they returned to their people, they blamed them, and they answered them with this. Or they meant: "What is the matter with us that we do not believe in Allah alone," because they were Trinitarians, and that is not belief in Allah.

The place of ﴿we do not believe﴾ is in the accusative as a circumstantial clause (hal), meaning "not believing," as in your saying "mā laka qā'iman" (what is with you standing?). The wāw in ﴿and we hope﴾ is the wāw of circumstance.

If you ask: What governs the first and second circumstantial clauses? I say: The governing element of the first is the meaning of the verb contained in the lām, as if it were said: "What has happened to us, not believing?" And the second has the meaning of this verb, but restricted by the first circumstance, because if you removed the first and said "What is with us and we hope," it would not be a complete sentence. It is permissible for "and we hope" to be a circumstantial clause of "we do not believe," meaning that they rebuked themselves for not affirming the oneness of Allah while hoping at the same time to be companions of the righteous. It is also permissible for it to be coordinated with "we do not believe," with the meaning: "What is with us that we combine Trinitarianism with hoping for the companionship of the righteous?" Or with the meaning: "What is with us that we do not combine them by entering Islam, since the disbeliever should not hope for the companionship of the righteous."

Al-Hasan read: ﴿So Allah rewarded them for what they said﴾, meaning for what they uttered out of sincere belief and devotion, as in your saying "this is the saying of so-and-so," that is, his belief and what he holds to.

**Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on Surah 5, verses 87–88:**

﴿Good things that Allah has made lawful for you﴾: what is good and pleasant among the lawful. The meaning of ﴿do not forbid﴾ is: do not withhold them from yourselves as if prohibiting them. Or it means: do not say, "We have forbidden them to ourselves," out of exaggeration in resolving to abandon them, through asceticism (tazahhud) and austerity (taqashshuf).[[On his words "taqashshufan": in al-Ṣiḥāḥ (the lexicon of al-Jawhari), "qashf" (with kasra) means "qashfan" when the sun or poverty has scorched and changed a person. The "mutaqashshif" is one who sustains himself on bare food and a patched cloak. (ʿ)]]

It is related that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) once described the Resurrection to his Companions, and he exaggerated and elaborated on the warning. They were moved and gathered in the house of ʿUthman ibn Maẓʿun, and they agreed that they would remain fasting and standing in prayer, that they would not sleep on beds, would not eat meat or fat, would not approach women or perfume, would renounce the world, would wear coarse woolen garments (masūḥ),[[On his words "wa-yalbisū al-masūḥ": al-masūḥ are coarse garments from which sacks for straw are made. Stated in al-Ṣiḥāḥ, under the root l-b-s.]] would wander about the earth, and would castrate themselves. When this reached the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), he said to them: "I was not commanded with that. Indeed, your selves have a right over you. So fast and break your fast, stand in prayer and sleep. For I stand in prayer and sleep, I fast and break my fast, I eat meat and fat, and I approach women. Whoever turns away from my Sunnah is not of me."[[Al-Wahidi mentioned this in his Asbāb (Occasions of Revelation) in this form without an isnād (chain of transmission). However, the exegetes said, and he mentioned something other than this, and al-Tabari transmitted it through al-Suddi regarding this verse, saying: "That was because the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) sat one day and admonished the people, then stood up and did not add to them beyond fear. Then some of his Companions stood up and mentioned him, in the sense of what preceded." It is drawn from several hadiths, and its origin is in the two Ṣaḥīḥs (al-Ṣaḥīḥayn, of al-Bukhari and Muslim), from ʿĀʾisha: some people among the Companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) asked his wives about his practice in private. Some of them said: "I will not eat meat." Some said: "I will not marry women." Some said: "I will not sleep on a bed." When this reached the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), he said: "What is the matter with people who say such and such? But I fast and break my fast, I sleep and I stand in prayer, I eat meat and I marry women. Whoever turns away from my Sunnah is not of me." In the two Ṣaḥīḥs, from Saʿd ibn Abi Waqqas, he said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) rejected tabattul (complete renunciation of marriage) from ʿUthman ibn Maẓʿun. Had he permitted it to him, we would have castrated ourselves." In the two Ṣaḥīḥs, from ʿAbdullah ibn ʿAmr ibn al-ʿAs, in the account of his dispute with the Prophet (ﷺ) concerning fasting and prayer, the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Fast and break your fast, stand in prayer and sleep, for your self has a right over you" — the hadith. Al-Tabari transmitted through Ibn Jurayj from Mujahid, who said: "Some men, among them ʿUthman ibn Maẓʿun and ʿAbdullah ibn ʿAmr, wanted to practice tabattul, to castrate themselves, and to wear coarse woolen garments." And through Ibn Jurayj from ʿIkrima: "ʿUthman ibn Maẓʿun, ʿAli ibn Abi Talib, Ibn Masʿud, al-Miqdad ibn al-Aswad, and Salim, the freedman of Abu Hudhayfa, along with a group of Companions, practiced tabattul. They sat in their houses, withdrew from women, wore coarse woolen garments, forbade the good food and clothing for themselves, resolved to castrate themselves, and gathered for night prayer and day fasting. Then this was revealed: ﴿O you who believe, do not forbid the good things that Allah has made lawful for you﴾ — the verse. He said: So the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) sent for them and said: 'Indeed your selves have a right over you. So fast and break your fast, pray and sleep. He is not of us who abandons our Sunnah.'"]] And it was revealed.

It is related that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to eat chicken and ḥarīsa-like dishes of fālūdhaj (a sweet made of starch, honey and butter), and he liked sweets and honey. And he said: "Indeed the believer is sweet and loves sweetness."[[This is drawn from hadiths. As for eating chicken, it is agreed upon (in al-Bukhari and Muslim) from the hadith of Abu Musa al-Ashʿari in an account of his. As for his eating fālūdhaj, al-Ḥakim transmitted it from the hadith of ʿAbdullah ibn Salam, who said: "I was with the Prophet (ﷺ) among some of his Companions when ʿUthman ibn Maẓʿun came, with a riding camel on which were two saddlebags," and he mentioned the hadith — in which it says: "Flour, butter and honey were cooked until it steamed, and then he ate." It is from the narration of al-Walid ibn Muslim from Muhammad ibn Hamza, and it is weak, and Ibn al-Jawzi declared it defective due to the weakness of al-Walid. As for "he liked sweets and honey," it is agreed upon from the hadith of Hammam from his father from ʿĀʾisha, may Allah be pleased with her. As for the last, al-Daylami mentioned it in al-Firdaws from ʿAli ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him.]]

And from Ibn Masʿud: a man said to him, "I have forbidden myself the bed," so he recited this verse and said: "Then, sit on your bed and expiate for your oath." And from al-Hasan: he was invited to a meal, and with him was Farqad al-Sabakhi and his companions. They sat at the table, and on it were various dishes of chicken cooked with fat, fālūdhaj, and other things. Farqad withdrew to one side, so al-Hasan asked: "Is he fasting?" They said: "No, but he dislikes these dishes." Al-Hasan turned to him and said: "O Farqad, do you see the saliva of bees mixed with the essence of wheat and pure butter as something a Muslim should find fault with?" And from him: it was said to him, "So-and-so does not eat fālūdhaj, and says: 'I cannot render its thanks.'" He said: "Does he drink cold water?" They said: "Yes." He said: "He is ignorant. Allah's blessing upon him in cold water is greater than His blessing upon him in fālūdhaj." And from him: Allah the Exalted disciplined His servants and perfected their discipline. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Let him who has abundance spend from his abundance﴾. Allah did not blame a people to whom He extended the world and who enjoyed it and obeyed Him, nor did He excuse a people from whom He withheld it and who disobeyed Him.

﴿And do not transgress﴾: do not exceed the limits of what Allah has made lawful for you to what He has forbidden to you. Or: do not be extravagant in consuming the good things. Or: He made the forbidding of good things a transgression and wrongdoing, so He prohibited transgression, so that the prohibition of forbidding them is included within it by a primary inclusion, since it comes right after it. Or it means: do not transgress by that.

﴿And eat of what Allah has provided for you﴾, that is, of the good sources that are called provision, ﴿lawful﴾ (ḥalālan), a state (ḥāl) qualifying what Allah has provided for you. ﴿And fear Allah﴾ is an emphasis on the exhortation to what He has commanded. He further emphasized it with His words ﴿in whom you believe﴾, because belief in Him necessitates piety in adhering to what He has commanded and in refraining from what He has forbidden.
