The commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 5, verse 89:

Al-laghw fi al-yamin (the idle oath, *al-laghw*): that which falls away and to which no ruling attaches. Scholars differ about it. From 'A'isha (may Allah be pleased with her) it is reported that she was asked about it and said: it is a man's saying, "No, by Allah; yes, by Allah" [[Reported by al-Bukhari and Malik from her hadith, without the words "she was asked." Abu Dawud related it through 'Ata' from her as both marfu' (traced back to the Prophet) and mawquf (ending with a Companion). al-Daraqutni authenticated the mawquf version.]]. This is the view of al-Shafi'i. From Mujahid: it is a man who swears about a matter, thinking it to be so, when it is not as he supposed. This is the view of Abu Hanifa (may Allah have mercy on him).

Bi-ma 'aqqadtum al-ayman (﴿for what you have bound by oaths﴾): by your binding of the oaths, that is, confirming them by intention and resolve. It is reported that al-Hasan (may Allah be pleased with him) was asked about the idle oath, and al-Farazdaq was with him. He said: "O Abu Sa'id, let me answer for you." And he said:

*"And I am not held to account for an idle word you utter,*
*when you did not intend the binding resolutions."*

[[Al-Farazdaq. It is reported that al-Hasan (may Allah be pleased with him) was asked about the idle oath, and al-Farazdaq said: "Let me answer for you, O Abu Sa'id," and recited the verse, meaning: you are not held accountable for the *laghw*, that is, the idle, fallen speech. *Ta'ammud* (تعمد) originally was *tata'ammad*, from which one of the two *ta'*s was dropped.

This is in the sense of the *istithna' munqati'* (disconnected exception). *'Aqidat al-'aza'im* (عاقدات العزائم): the firm ones. Attributing the firmness to them is a *majaz 'aqli* (rational metaphor).]]

It is also read *'aqadtum* (with the letter *qaf* lightened) and *'aqadtum* (with the *alif* after the *'ayn*). The meaning: "But He will hold you to account for what you have bound [by oaths] when you break them," so the time of the accountability is omitted, because it was known to them. Or, "for the breaking of what you have bound," so the genitive word is omitted.

*Fa-kaffaratuhu* (﴿so its expiation﴾): the expiation of its breaking. *Al-kaffarah* (expiation, *kaffarah*) is the act whose nature is to cover over a sin, that is, to conceal it.

*Min awsati ma tut'imun* (﴿from the average of what you feed﴾): from the most moderate of it, because some of them are extravagant in feeding their families and some are stingy. According to Abu Hanifa (may Allah have mercy on him), it is half a *sa'* of wheat, or a *sa'* of other grain, for each poor person, or feeding them at lunch and dinner. According to al-Shafi'i (may Allah have mercy on him), it is one *mudd* for each poor person.

Ja'far ibn Muhammad recited *ahalikum* (﴿your families﴾) with a sukun on the *ya'*. *Al-Ahali* is a collective noun for *ahl*, like *al-la'ali* for the plural of *layla*, and *al-aradi* for the plural of *ard*. And their saying *ahlun* is like their saying *ardun* with a sukun on the *ra'*. As for the sukun on the *ya'* in the accusative case, it is for lightness, as they said: "I saw Ma'dikarib," making the *ya'* like the *alif*.

*Aw kiswatuhum* (﴿or clothing them﴾): a conjunction onto the position of *min awsat* [[His words "onto the position of min awsat": this may be said to suit only the reading that follows, *aw ka-kiswatihim*. But al-Nasafi's phrasing is "a conjunction onto *it'am* or onto the position of *min awsat*." Its rationale is that *min awsat* is a substitute for *it'am*, and the substitute is what is intended in the speech. (Editor's note.)]]. It is read with a *damma* on the *kaf*, and the like of it: *qudwah* in *qudwah*, and *uswah* in *iswah*. *Al-kiswah* is a garment that covers the nakedness. From Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with him): a cloak (*'aba'ah*) sufficed on that day. From Ibn 'Umar: a waist-wrapper, or a shirt, or a cloak, or a blanket. From Mujahid: a comprehensive garment. From al-Hasan: two white garments.

Sa'id ibn al-Musayyib and al-Yamani recited *aw ka-kiswatihim* (﴿or like their clothing﴾), meaning: or like what you feed your families, whether extravagantly or stingily. You do not diminish them below the measure of their provision, but you share with them and they with you.

If you say: what is the position of the *kaf*? I say: it is in the nominative case. Its estimate is: "or their food is like their clothing," meaning: like the food of theirs, if they do not feed them the moderate amount.

*Aw tahriru raqabatin* (﴿or the freeing of a neck﴾): al-Shafi'i (may Allah have mercy on him) made faith a condition, by analogy with the expiation for killing. As for Abu Hanifa and his companions, they permitted the freeing of a slave as expiation in every expiation except the expiation for killing.

If you say: what is the meaning of *aw* (or)? I say: it gives choice, and it makes one of the three expiations obligatory in an unrestricted way; whichever of them the one expiating takes, he has done right.

*Fa-man lam yajid* (﴿but whoever does not find﴾) any one of them, then *fa-siyamu thalathati ayyamin mutatabi'at* (﴿fasting for three days consecutively﴾). According to Abu Hanifa (may Allah have mercy on him), this is by holding to the recitation of Ubayy and Ibn Mas'ud (may Allah be pleased with them): "fasting three consecutive days." From Mujahid: every fast must be consecutive except the making up of Ramadan. And one has the choice in the oath-expiation.

*Dhalika al-madhkur* (﴿that is the expiation﴾ — the referent is the thing mentioned): *kaffaratu aymanikum* (﴿the expiation of your oaths﴾). If it were said: "that is the expiation of your oaths" (*tilka*), it would be correct, meaning "those things," or because *kaffarah* is feminine. [[He said: "The one referred to is what is mentioned earlier, and if it were said ..." etc. Ahmad says: rather, in this verse there is a subtle line of argument for the validity of the expiation occurring after the oath and before the breaking of it, which is the well-known view of Malik's school. The proof is that it makes what comes after the swearing the time for the expiation recognized in the law, when it attaches *idha* (when) directly to the mere swearing.

The verse does not impose the expiation so that it could be argued that it is agreed to be due only upon breaking, and therefore that the phrase must be understood as attached to the swearing. Rather, it speaks only to the legitimacy of the expiation and its occurrence in a valid manner, since His words "that is the expiation of your oaths" do not give an obligation; they give validity and recognition. And Allah knows best. This is a defense against those who prohibited expiation before breaking absolutely, even if the oath was about something good; the three views in Malik's school are known, but the preferred view is the well-known one.]]

*Wa-ahfazu aymanakum* (﴿and guard your oaths﴾): *fa-barru fihā* (so fulfill them) and do not break them. [[He returned to his speech. He said: "And guard your oaths, that is, fulfill them ..." etc. Ahmad says: in this interpretation there is an indication that one who doubts the form of the oath, after its origin is established, is held strictly and taken by the more cautious course. So Allah guided him to guard the oath, lest the matter lead to his being bound outwardly, by way of caution, to what did not proceed from him in Allah's knowledge. An example is one who swears by divorce and forgets whether he attached it to three or left it unqualified; by the well-known view he is bound to three. It is possible that in Allah's knowledge he only swore an unqualified divorce, so he was directed to guard the oath, lest forgetfulness draw him into this severity. The "oaths" intended are every thing to which the term "oath" applies, whether it is an oath by Allah or by other than Him, which the law makes binding. And Allah knows best.]] — meaning the oaths in which breaking them is sinful, because *al-aymân* is a generic noun which may be applied to some of the genus and to all of it. It was said: guard them by expiating them. It was said: guard them however you swear by them, and do not forget them out of carelessness about them.

*Kadhalika yubayyinu Allahu lakum ayatihi* (﴿thus Allah makes clear to you His signs﴾): the signs of His law and His rulings, *la'allakum tashkurun* (﴿that you may be grateful﴾) for His favor, in that He teaches you and makes the way out of it easy for you.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 5, verses 90–91:

God emphasised the prohibition of wine and gambling in several ways [[Mahmud said: "God emphasised the prohibition of wine and gambling in several ways, among them..." etc. Ahmad (Ibn al-Munayyir) said: "It is also permissible for the pronoun to refer to *rijs* (impurity), which encompasses all that has been mentioned. And God knows best."]]. Among them is opening the sentence with *innama* (indeed/only, a restrictive particle). Among them is that He paired them with the worship of idols. From this is the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ), peace and blessings be upon him: "The drinker of wine is like the worshipper of an idol." [[Al-Bazzar narrated it from the hadith of Mujahid, from Abdullah ibn Amr, in these words. Al-Harith ibn Usama and Abu Nu'aym in *al-Hilya* narrated it from the transmission of al-Hasan, from Abdullah ibn Amr, with the same wording. In its chain is al-Khalil ibn Zakariyya, and in the preceding one is Thabit ibn Muhammad, who is in a better state than al-Khalil. Ibn Majah has it from the hadith of Abu Hurayra, with the wording "the habitual drinker of wine is like the worshipper of an idol," and its chain is good. He said: Abu Bakr ibn Abi Shayba narrated to us, Muhammad ibn Sulayman al-Isfahani narrated to us, from Suhayl, from his father, from him, with the same. Ibn Hibban narrated it from the hadith of Ibn Abbas with this wording, and said: "It seems that it refers to one who considers it lawful." In the *Musnad* of Ishaq, and from the transmission of Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz from some of his companions, the wording is: "Whoever drinks wine and dies [in that state], dies like the worshipper of an idol." Al-Tabarani in *al-Awsat* has, from the hadith of Anas, the wording: "The one who persists in wine is like the worshipper of an idol," and its chain is weak.]] Among them is that He called them *rijs* (filth), as He said, Exalted is He: ﴿So avoid the filth of the idols﴾. Among them is that He made them the work of Satan, and nothing comes from Satan except pure evil. Among them is that He commanded avoidance. Among them is that He made avoidance a means of success (*falah*), and when avoidance is success, indulgence is failure and ruin. Among them is that He mentioned the harm that results from them, which is the occurrence of enmity and hatred between the people of wine and the people of gambling [[His words "min ashab" (from the companions of) are perhaps "bayn ashab" (between the companions of). (ʿ)]], and what they lead to of barring from the remembrance of God and from observing the times of prayer. His words ﴿So will you not desist?﴾ are among the most forceful forms of prohibition, as if it were said: "There has been recited to you what they contain of kinds of distractions and obstacles; will you, with these distractions, desist? Or will you remain as you were, as though you had not been admonished or restrained?"

If you ask: To what does the pronoun in His words ﴿So avoid it﴾ refer? I say: It refers to an omitted noun that was annexed, as if it were said: "Indeed the matter of wine and gambling, or their consumption, or something similar." For this reason He said: ﴿It is an abomination from the work of Satan﴾. If you ask: Why did He group wine and gambling with the stone altars and the divining arrows at first, and then single them out at the end? I say: Because the address is to the believers, and He forbade them from what they used to indulge in, namely drinking wine and playing gambling games. He mentioned the stone altars and the divining arrows to emphasise the prohibition of wine and gambling, and to show that all of this belongs to the works of the Jahiliyya (the age of ignorance) and of the polytheists. Therefore it is obligatory to avoid all of it entirely, as if there were no difference between one who worships an idol and associates others with God in knowledge of the unseen, and one who drinks wine or gambles. Then He singled them out for mention so that it would be seen that the intended subject of mention is wine and gambling. His words ﴿and from the prayer﴾ single out the prayer from among the things mentioned, as if it were said: "And from the prayer in particular."

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 5, verses 90–91:

God emphasised the prohibition of wine and gambling in several ways [[Mahmud said: "God emphasised the prohibition of wine and gambling in several ways, among them..." etc. Ahmad (Ibn al-Munayyir) said: "It is also permissible for the pronoun to refer to *rijs* (impurity), which encompasses all that has been mentioned. And God knows best."]]. Among them is opening the sentence with *innama* (indeed/only, a restrictive particle). Among them is that He paired them with the worship of idols. From this is the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ), peace and blessings be upon him: "The drinker of wine is like the worshipper of an idol." [[Al-Bazzar narrated it from the hadith of Mujahid, from Abdullah ibn Amr, in these words. Al-Harith ibn Usama and Abu Nu'aym in *al-Hilya* narrated it from the transmission of al-Hasan, from Abdullah ibn Amr, with the same wording. Al-Tabarani in *al-Awsat* has, from the hadith of Anas, the wording: "The one who persists in wine is like the worshipper of an idol," and its chain is weak.]] Among them is that He called them *rijs* (filth), as He said, Exalted is He: ﴿So avoid the filth of the idols﴾. And beware (وَاحْذَرُوا), and be wary, fearing [God], for when they are wary, wariness leads them to guard against every evil and to do every good. It is also possible that what is meant is: beware of what is upon you concerning wine and gambling (al-maysir), or concerning abandoning obedience to God and the Messenger. ﴿But if you turn away, then know that you have not harmed the Messenger by your turning away, for the Messenger was charged only with clear delivery of the signs.﴾ Rather, you have harmed yourselves when you turned away from what you were charged with.

The commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 5, verse 93:

There is no blame upon those who believe and do righteous deeds, for what they have eaten, from the pleasant foods and the things they desire, when they fear God and refrain from what He has forbidden them of it, and believe and remain steadfast in faith and righteous deeds, and increase in them. Then they fear God and believe, then remain steadfast in piety and faith. Then they fear God and do good, then remain steadfast in refraining from sins and in perfecting their deeds. Or [it means] do good to people: give them of what God has provided you of good things.

It is said that when the prohibition of wine (khamr) was revealed, the Companions said: "O Messenger of God, what about our brothers who died while drinking wine and consuming the wealth gained through gambling (maysir)?" [Narrated by Ahmad, through the transmission of Ibn Wahb, the client of Abu Hurayrah, who said: "Wine was prohibited in three stages. When the Messenger of God (ﷺ) came to Medina, they were drinking wine and gambling. They asked the Messenger of God (ﷺ) about that, and God revealed: ﴿They ask you about wine and gambling﴾ [2:219], the verse. The people said: 'It has not been prohibited for us; He only said: in them is great sin,' so they continued to drink wine, until one day a man from the Emigrants (Muhajirun) led the Maghrib prayer and mixed up his recitation. Then God revealed: ﴿O you who believe, do not approach prayer while you are intoxicated﴾ [4:43]. So they continued drinking it, but would come to the prayer sober. Then it was revealed: ﴿O you who believe, indeed wine and gambling...﴾ [5:90], the verse. They said: 'We have ceased, O Lord.' The people said: 'O Messenger of God, there are people who were killed in the way of God, or who died on their beds, who used to drink wine and consume gambling gains, and God has made it an abomination from the work of Satan.' Then God revealed: ﴿There is no blame upon those who believe and do righteous deeds...﴾ [5:93], the verse. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: 'If it had been prohibited to them, they would have abandoned it as you have abandoned it.' Its chain is weak, for it is a transmission from Abu Ma'shar, from Abu Wahb, and Abu Ma'shar is weak."]

Al-Tabari narrated, through the chain of Ali ibn Abi Talhah from Ibn Abbas, concerning God's words ﴿There is no blame upon those who believe﴾ [5:93], the verse, that he said: "They said: 'O Messenger of God, what do you say about our brothers who died while they were drinking wine and consuming gambling gains?' So God revealed the verse."

In the agreed-upon (Muttafaq 'alayh) report from Hammad ibn Zayd, from Thabit, from Anas, who said: "I was the cupbearer of the people at the house of Abu Talhah, and their drink that day was fadikh (a drink made from crushed dates). He commanded a crier, who called out: 'Indeed wine has been prohibited!'" The hadith continues: some of the people said: "So-and-so was killed, and so-and-so and so-and-so, and it was still in their bellies," and then God revealed: ﴿There is no blame upon those who believe and do righteous deeds for what they have eaten...﴾ [5:93], the verse.

The meaning is that the believers bear no blame for whatever they have eaten of what is permissible, provided they fear God by avoiding what is forbidden, then fear Him and believe, then fear Him and do good. The sense is that those people were characterized by these qualities, as praise of them and commendation of their states in faith, piety, and goodness. An example of this is when someone is asked: "Is there any blame upon Zayd for what he did?" and you reply, knowing that the matter is permissible: "No one is blameworthy for what is permissible, if he fears God by avoiding what is forbidden and is a believer who does good," intending that Zayd is pious, a believer, and a doer of good, and that he is not held accountable for what he did.

Revealed in the year of al-Hudaybiyah. Allah tested them with game while they were in the state of ihram, and it became abundant around them, so much so that it would come upon them in their camps, and they could take it with their hands and spear it with their lances. ﴿That Allah may make evident who fears Him in the Unseen﴾

That is, that He may distinguish those who fear the punishment of Allah while He is unseen, awaited in the Hereafter, so that they refrain from the game, from those who do not fear Him and so advance upon it. ﴿So whoever transgresses after that﴾, that is, hunts after that trial, then the threat applies to him. If you ask: what is the meaning of the diminishing and belittling [[Mahmud said: "If you ask what is the meaning of the diminishing and belittling... etc." Ahmad said: This very same form has also occurred regarding great trials, in the words of the Exalted: ﴿And We will surely test you with something of fear and hunger and a loss of wealth and lives and fruits, but give good tidings to the patient﴾. There is no doubt about the greatness of these calamities and afflictions, for which the one who endures them deserves to be given good tidings, because he has endured something great. So al-Zamakhshari's statement, "He diminished and belittled it to alert that this trial is not among the great trials," is refuted by its use alongside trials agreed to be great.

And the apparent meaning, Allah knows best, is that what the wording indicates of diminishing and belittling is an alert that everything with which they are tested of these calamities is only a part of a whole in relation to the decree of Allah the Exalted, that He is capable of making what He tests them with greater and more terrifying than what occurs, and that whatever He averts from them of what is greater in His decree, He averts it only toward what is lighter and easier, out of gentleness and mercy toward them. This alert is meant to incite them to patience and to bear them to endurance. What indicates that this is the intended meaning is that the prior warning of it was only so that they would be prepared for it when it occurs, and so it also serves as an incitement to bear it, because a sudden unexpected hardship is harder, while warning of it before it occurs makes its encounter easier. The outcome of this is gentleness in the divine decree. Glory be to Allah, the Gentle with His servants. When the intelligent person reflects on the kinds of trials with which he is tested, he finds that what is averted from him of them is more, without reaching any limit. So we ask Allah for pardon, well-being, and gentleness in what is decreed.]] in His saying: ﴿with something of the game﴾? I say: He diminished and belittled it so that it is known that it is not one of the great trials by which the feet of the steadfast slip, such as being tested with the sacrifice of lives and wealth. Rather, it is similar to what the people of Aylah were tested with regarding fish hunting, and that if they did not stand firm before this, then what would their condition be before something harder than it? And Ibrahim recited: ﴿yanaluhu﴾ with the letter ya.

**Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on Surah 5, verse 95:**

*Ḥurum* (muḥrimūn, "those in the state of ihram," the plural of *ḥarām*) is like *kurdaḥ* as the plural of *raddāḥ*. Deliberateness (*al-ta'ammud*) means that he kills it while remembering his state of ihram (ritual consecration for pilgrimage), or while knowing that what he kills is something whose killing is forbidden to him. If he kills it while forgetting his ihram, or shoots at game while thinking it is not game and it turns out to be game, or aims his shot at something other than game and the arrow veers from its target and strikes game, then he is one who erred (*mukhṭi'*).

If you say: the prohibitions of ihram are equal in respect to deliberate and mistaken acts, so why is deliberateness stipulated in the verse? I say: because the occasion of the verse concerns one who acted deliberately. It is related that during the 'Umrah of al-Ḥudaybiyyah a wild ass appeared to them, and Abu al-Yusr charged at it and struck it with his spear and killed it. He was told, "You have killed game while you are in ihram," and so the verse was revealed. Also, the basic case is the deliberate act, and the mistaken act is attached to it for the sake of severity. Evidence for this is His saying, ﴿that he may taste the consequence of his deed﴾ and ﴿whoever returns, God will take retribution from him﴾. It is related from al-Zuhri: "The Book revealed (the ruling) concerning the deliberate act, and the Sunnah came concerning the mistaken act." And it is related from Sa'id ibn Jubayr: "I do not see anything in the mistaken act," taking the stipulation of deliberateness in the verse as binding.

There are two readings from al-Ḥasan regarding ﴿a recompense equal to what he killed﴾, with *jazā'* (recompense) in the nominative and *mithl* (equal) in the nominative, both together. The meaning is: upon him is a recompense that equals what he killed of the game. According to Abu Hanifa, this is the value of the game, assessed at the place where it was hunted. If its value reaches the price of a sacrificial animal, he has the choice between sacrificing from the livestock an animal whose value equals the value of the game, or buying food with its value and giving each needy person half a *ṣā'* of wheat or a *ṣā'* of something else; and if he wishes, he may fast one day for the food of each needy person. If what remains does not reach the food of a needy person, he fasts for it one day or gives it in charity. According to Muhammad and al-Shafi'i, may God have mercy on them both, the "equal" is its counterpart from the livestock; if there is no counterpart from the livestock, one turns to the view of Abu Hanifa, may God have mercy on him.

If you say: what does one who interprets "equal" as value do with His words ﴿from the livestock﴾, which is an explanation of "equal," and His words ﴿as an offering reaching the Kaaba﴾? I say: whoever makes value obligatory has granted the choice between buying with it an offering, or food, or fasting, just as God granted the choice in the verse. So His words ﴿from the livestock﴾ are an explanation of the offering bought with the value, in one of the aspects of the choice. For whoever assesses the game and buys with its value an offering and sacrifices it has indeed recompensed with an equal of what he killed from the livestock.

Moreover, the choice in the verse, between recompensing with the offering, or expiating by feeding, or by fasting, is only correct in an evident manner, without strain, when the game is assessed and, after assessment, one looks to see which of the three he chooses. But if one aims at the counterpart and makes it the sole obligation without choice, then when something has no counterpart it is assessed, and then one chooses between feeding and fasting, and this departs from what is in the verse. Do you not see His saying, ﴿or as expiation, the feeding of needy persons, or the equivalent of that in fasting﴾, how He granted the choice among the three things, and there is no way to that except through assessment?

'Abd Allah (ibn Mas'ud) read: ﴿then its recompense is the like of what he killed﴾. It is also read: ﴿a recompense the like of what he killed﴾ with the genitive (idafah). Its origin is: ﴿a recompense the like of what he killed,﴾ with *mithl* in the accusative, meaning: upon him is that he should recompense the like of what he killed; then it was made genitive, as you say, "I marvelled at the striking of Zayd." Al-Sulami read it in its original form. Muhammad ibn Muqatil read ﴿a recompense the like of what he killed﴾ with both in the accusative, meaning: let him recompense a recompense the like of what he killed.

al-Ḥasan read *min al-na'am* (from the livestock) with the 'ayn sukūn, finding the vowel heavy on a guttural letter, so he made it quiescent.

﴿Judged by it, the like of what he killed, two just men from among you﴾: two just men from among the Muslims. They said: in this is evidence that "the like" means value, because assessment requires consideration and effort, unlike visible things.

It is related from Qabisah that he hit a gazelle while in ihram, and he asked 'Umar, and he consulted 'Abd al-Raḥmān ibn 'Awf, then 'Umar ordered him to slaughter a sheep. Qabisah said to his companion: "By God, the Commander of the Faithful did not know until he asked someone else." So 'Umar came upon him, striking him with a whip, and said: "Do you belittle the giving of rulings and kill game while you are in ihram? God, may He be exalted, said: ﴿judged by it two just men from among you﴾. I am 'Umar, and this is 'Abd al-Raḥmān." [[Narrated by 'Abd al-Razzaq from Ma'mar from 'Abd al-Malik ibn 'Umayr, and he mentioned it. The addition at its end is in it.]]

Muhammad ibn Ja'far read *dhū 'adlin minkum* (singular), intending "judged by it by one who is just among you," and did not intend the singularity of the number.

It has been said that *hadyan* (as an offering) is intended as a circumstantial accusative (*ḥāl*) from *jazā'* (recompense) for the one who described it as "the like," because the description specified it and brought it closer to definiteness; or it is an apposition (*badal*) from *mithl* for the one who put it in the accusative, or from its place for the one who put it in the genitive. It is permissible for it to be in the accusative as a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in *bihi* (by it).

*Hadyan* is described by *bāligh al-Ka'bah* (reaching the Kaaba) because its annexation (*iḍāfah*) is not genuine. The meaning of its reaching the Kaaba is that it be slaughtered in the Sacred Precinct (*al-Ḥaram*). As for giving it in charity, it may be done wherever you wish according to Abu Hanifa, while according to al-Shafi'i it must be in the Sacred Precinct.

If you say: with what does the one who puts *jazā'* in the accusative make *kaffārah* (expiation) nominative? I say: he makes it the predicate of an omitted subject, as if it were said: "or the obligation upon him is expiation." Or he supposes: "upon him is that he recompense a recompense, or an expiation," and so he conjoins it to "that he recompense."

It is read: ﴿or expiation of the food of needy persons﴾ with the genitive annexation. This annexation is explanatory, as if it were said: "or expiation of food for needy persons," like your saying "a ring of silver," meaning "a ring made of silver." Al-A'raj read: ﴿or expiation, food of needy persons.﴾ He made it singular because it occupies the place of explanation, so the singular sufficed as indicating the genus.

It is read: ﴿or the equivalent of that﴾ with the 'ayn in kasra. The difference between them is that *'adl* (with fatha) is what is equal to a thing from a different kind, like fasting and feeding. *'Idl* (with kasra) is what is equal to it in quantity; from this comes *'idlā al-ḥiml* (the two equal loads), because each of them is equal to the other until they are balanced. It is as if the fatha form is a name given by way of the verbal noun, and the kasra form has the sense of the object, like *al-dhibḥ* (the slaughter, slaughtered thing) and similar, and similar to them *al-ḥiml* and *al-ḥimil* (load, carried thing).

﴿That﴾ refers to the food. ﴿Fasting﴾ is a specification (*tamyīz*) for *'adl*, like your saying, "I have a man like him." The choice in this matter belongs to the one who killed the game according to Abu Hanifa and Abu Yusuf. According to Muhammad, it belongs to the two judges.

﴿That he may taste﴾ is connected to His saying ﴿then a recompense﴾, meaning: upon him is that he recompense or expiate, so that he may taste the evil outcome of his violating the sanctity of ihram. *Al-wabāl* is the disliked thing and the harm that one suffers in the consequence of an evil deed, because of its heaviness upon him, like His saying, ﴿So We seized him with a heavy seizing (akhdhan wabīlan)﴾, meaning heavy. And a *ṭa'ām wabīl* is a food that weighs upon the stomach so that it is not digested.

﴿God has pardoned what has passed﴾ of the game during the state of ihram, before you consulted the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and asked him about its permissibility. It has been said: "what has passed for you of it in the pre-Islamic period," because they were bound by the laws of those before them, and game was forbidden in them.

﴿And whoever returns﴾ to killing game while in ihram after the prohibition has been revealed, ﴿God will take retribution from him.﴾ *Yantaqim* (will take retribution) is the predicate of an omitted subject, its supposed form being: "so He takes retribution from him," and for this reason the *fā'* (so) entered. A similar example is ﴿whoever believes in his Lord, then he does not fear﴾, meaning: He takes retribution from him in the Hereafter.

There is disagreement concerning whether expiation is obligatory upon the one who returns. According to 'Aṭa', Ibrahim, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, and al-Ḥasan, it is obligatory, and this is the view of the majority of scholars. According to Ibn 'Abbas and Shurayh, there is no expiation upon him, adhering to the apparent meaning, and that He did not mention expiation here.

**Ṣayd al-baḥr** (game of the sea): the sea's catches, both what is eaten and what is not. **Wa ṭaʿāmuhu** (and its food): what is fed from its game. The meaning is: Allah has made lawful to you the use of everything that is caught in the sea. [Note: "a statement 'bi-jamīʿ mā yuṣād fī al-baḥr' (with everything that is caught in the sea)" is perhaps from… (ʿ)]. He has also made lawful to you the eating of what is edible from it, which is fish alone, according to Abu Hanifa. According to Ibn Abi Layla, it is everything that is caught from it. On his reading, the interpretation of the verse is: "Lawful to you is the game of the sea's animals, and that you feed it as **mataʿan lakum** (an object of purpose, *maf'ul lahu*), meaning: lawful to you as a provision for you." In the matter of the object of purpose, this is like the Almighty's words, ﴿And We gave him Isaac and Jacob as an extra gift﴾, in the matter of the circumstantial accusative (*ḥāl*), because His words **mataʿan lakum** are an object of purpose specific to the food, just as **nāfilatan** (as an extra gift) is a circumstantial accusative specific to Jacob. That is, lawful to you is its food as a provision for you: [you may] eat it fresh (**ṭariyyan**), and for your travellers (**sayyāratikum**) to take it as provision dried (**qadīdan**), just as Musa, peace be upon him, took a fish with him on his journey to al-Khidr, peace be upon him.

It is also read **wa ṭaʿmuhu** (its food, singular).

**Ṣayd al-barr** (game of the land): what is hunted on land, meaning what breeds there, even if it lives in water at some times, such as waterfowl according to Abu Hanifa. Scholars differed about it. **Qāla Maḥmūd** ("Maḥmūd said," i.e. al-Zamakhshari): "There is a difference about the intended meaning of the prohibition…" Aḥmad [ibn al-Munayyir] said: Restricting the general wording of the verse is necessary on both positions, because Malik, may Allah be pleased with him, permits eating the game of the land for one in a state of ihram if a lawful person hunted it for himself or for a lawful person. So, according to his school, the restriction of the general must also be restricted. The most that can be said is that the restricted scope on Abu Hanifa's school is greater than on Malik's school, because Malik permits eating what a lawful person hunted on behalf of the one in ihram, as is reported from him. So it exceeds Malik's school in this case. And Allah knows best.

Some scholars prohibited for the one in ihram everything that falls under the name of game. This is the view of ʿAmr ibn ʿAbbas. Narrated from Abu Hurayra, ʿAṭāʾ, Mujahid, and Saʿid ibn Jubayr: they permitted the one in ihram to eat what a lawful person hunted, even if it was hunted for his sake, provided he did not direct him to it or point it out. Likewise, what was slaughtered before his ihram. This is the school of Abu Hanifa and his companions, may Allah have mercy on them. According to Malik, al-Shafiʿi, and Ahmad, may Allah have mercy on them, it is not permitted to him what was hunted for his sake.

If you say: What does Abu Hanifa do with the general wording "game of the land"? I say: Abu Hanifa, may Allah have mercy on him, took the implied meaning (*mafhūm*) from the words ﴿And the game of the land is forbidden to you as long as you are in ihram﴾, because its apparent meaning is the game of those in ihram, not the game of others, since they are the ones addressed. It is as if it were said: "What you hunt on land is forbidden to you," so what others hunt is excluded, and what they hunted while not in ihram. The Almighty's words support this: ﴿O you who believe, do not kill game while you are in ihram﴾.

Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with him, read: "And the game of the land is forbidden to you," meaning Allah, Mighty and Majestic, is the one who forbids it. It is also read **mā dumtum** with a kasra on the dal, according to those who say **dāma yadāmu** (to last).

The Sacred House, the Sacred Month, the offering and the garlands.

Al-Bayt al-Haram (the Sacred House) is an explicative apposition (ʿatf bayān) placed for the sake of praise, not for the sake of clarification, just as a qualifier sometimes comes in this manner. ﴿Allah made the Ka'bah, the Sacred House, a means of standing for mankind﴾ — qiyaman lil-nas: i'tāshan lahum (a revival and uplifting for them).

[[Al-Zamakhshari said: "The meaning of qiyaman lil-nas is: a revival for them in the matter of their religion and their worldly life ... etc." Ahmad (Ibn al-Munayyir) said: In this verse there is something that rules out two of the three interpretations mentioned in his statement at the beginning of this surah (﴿Do not violate the rites of Allah, nor the sacred month, nor the offerings, nor the garlands﴾). The interpretation of the garlands as they are literally understood, and the interpretation that diverts the "violation" to its places on the one wearing them — like His saying (﴿and not display their adornment except what appears thereof﴾), meaning the places of adornment, and the prohibition of violating the garlands resembles it, as if He said: "Do not violate their garlands, let alone them" — is impossible in this verse, because it came in the context of bestowing favour through what Allah made a means of standing for people among these enumerated matters. He has specified the favour concerning the camels in His saying (﴿And the camels — We have made them for you among the rites of Allah; in them is good for you ...﴾), the verse. It is not fitting for the context of favour to move from the higher to the lower, such that the favour falls on the one wearing the garland and then on the garlands. Rather, that is fitting in the context of prohibition: that it moves from prohibiting the higher to intensifying by prohibiting the lower. As for the other interpretation — that the garlands remain in their literal sense and the prohibited violation is directed to them literally, i.e., "do not approach the garlands and do not benefit from them," as the Prophet ﷺ said: "Hang their garlands on their blood and leave the people free to them" — it is also impossible for the same reason that rules out the previous one. As for the third interpretation — that it refers to the owners of the garlands — it is fitting for both, so it is necessary to adopt it. For this reason al-Zamakhshari did not mention the equality in this verse. The reason it is suitable and apparent in both: the purpose in the context of prohibition is to single it out for mention and specify it with the prohibition, after it had been included with others in the prohibition, so it is as if it were prohibited for its particularity twice. The purpose in the context of favour is also that — repeating the favour concerning it while included in the generality and specified by mention. Also, it is fitting in the context of favour to ascend from the lower to the higher, unlike the prohibition. And Allah knows best.]] In the matter of their religion and their worldly life, and an upholding of their aims and purposes in their livelihood and their hereafter, because there is accomplished for them the matter of their Hajj and their ʿUmrah, their trade, and various kinds of their benefits. It is related from ʿAṭāʾ ibn Abi Rabah: "If they left it for a single year, they would not be given respite and would not be delayed."

Wal-shahr al-haram (the Sacred Month): the month in which the Hajj is performed, which is Dhu al-Hijjah, because of its distinction among the months by the holding of the pilgrimage season in it, a matter Allah the Exalted has made known. It was said that what is meant is the category of the sacred months.

Wal-hady wal-qala'id (the offering and the garlands): the garlanded [offerings] in particular, namely the camels, because the reward in them is greater and the splendour of the Hajj is more apparent with them.

Dhalika (That) is a reference either to the making of the Ka'bah a means of standing for mankind, or to what was mentioned of preserving the sanctity of the state of ihram by abstaining from hunting and other things.

﴿That you may know that Allah knows whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth, and that Allah is Knower of all things﴾ — knowing what benefits you and what uplifts you, of what He has commanded you and charged you with. ﴿Severe in punishment﴾ for whoever violates His sanctities; ﴿Forgiving and Merciful﴾ toward whoever observes them.

The distance between the corrupt and the good is great in the sight of God, the Exalted. [Mahmud said: "The distance between the corrupt and the good is great in the sight of God..." etc.] Ahmad, may God have mercy on him, said: It has been established by the Sharia that most of the people of Paradise are from this community. The Qadariyya have acknowledged that they (the Qadariyya) are few in it, and an anomaly in comparison with those who are other than them among the sects. The matter is in this position. They also believe that they are the saved sect, promised Paradise and no others, since everyone other than them, despite their corrupt greed, is destined to abide in the Fire with the disbelievers. Accordingly, this small, anomalous sect would be most of the people of Paradise. Far be it from God that this should persist in the mind of an intelligent, discerning person who is aware of what has been transmitted in the traditions (al-sunan) that refute and reject this corrupt assumption.

Who are the Mu'tazila, that their greed should extend to this limit? And this inference that al-Zamakhshari drew, that what is meant by "the good" is this Mu'tazili group, is of the same kind as the claim that what is meant in God's saying ﴿Had we listened or reasoned, we would not have been among the companions of the Blaze﴾ is the People of Hadith and the People of Opinion (Ahl al-Ra'y), meaning the truth. He was harsh in his interpretation of this verse against whoever said that, and considered it an innovation, yet he has innovated something close to it in his taking "the good" in this verse to mean the Mu'tazili group. Indeed, by God, it is worse than that statement, because he took "the corrupt" to mean those other than them among the Sunni sects. We seek refuge in God from that, and we disavow his audacity against the predecessors and the successors.

Even if it is near to you, do not be impressed by the abundance of the corrupt so that you prefer it for its multitude over the few good things. For what you imagine as virtue in abundance does not compensate for the deficiency in the corrupt and the loss of the good. This applies generally to lawful and unlawful wealth, righteous and wicked deeds, sound and corrupt doctrines, and excellent and inferior people. ﴿So fear God﴾ and prefer the good, though it be little, over the corrupt, though it be much. It is fitting that this verse be used to slap in the faces of the Mujbira (al-Mujbira, the determinists) (1) when they boast of numbers, as it is said:

"Boast of Sa'd, for Sa'd is numerous,
but do not expect from Sa'd fulfilment or victory."

[Sa'd is the name of a tribe. The meaning: there is no benefit in them except increasing the army's numbers; they do not fulfil what they promised of victory, nor do they give victory without a promise. It is possible that what is meant is fulfilment of the right of bravery, and "victory" is an explanation. In the repetition of the name there is a kind of mockery.]

And as it is said:

"Let not the mass of their multitude overwhelm you,
for most of them, indeed all of them, are cattle."

[These lines are by Abu Tammam: "No remnant of most of these people remains that imagination can grasp, except these figures and visible bodies, mere forms before the intellects. So do not be alarmed by the multitude of their number, for most of them are like cattle, indeed all of them are so, having no planning for matters of war." "Dahamahu al-amr" means the matter overtook him, bewildered him, and closed the door of opinion upon him. "Al-dahma'" means the great, dense crowd, from "al-dahma," which is darkness and blackness.]

It was said: it was revealed concerning the pilgrims of al-Yamama, when the Muslims wished to attack them, and they were forbidden to attack them even though they were polytheists.

(1) Al-Mujbira: those who hold the doctrine of compulsion (jabr), here meant as Ahl al-Sunna, as glossed in the commentary.

The conditional clause and the clause it coordinates with, namely His saying ﴿If it is made known to you, it will distress you﴾ and ﴿And if you ask about them when the Qur'an is being revealed, it will be made known to you﴾, are a description of the things (ashya'). The meaning: do not multiply your questions to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) to the point that you ask him about burdensome obligations which, if he gives you a ruling on them and imposes them on you, will grieve you, weigh upon you, and make you regret having asked about them. This is like what is related: that Suraqah ibn Malik or ʿUkkashah ibn Mihsan said:

"O Messenger of Allah, is the Hajj obligatory upon us every year?" The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) turned away from him until he repeated his question three times. He (ﷺ) said: "Woe to you! What will assure you that I would not say yes? By Allah, if I had said yes, it would have become obligatory, and if it had become obligatory you would not have been able to fulfil it, and if you had left it you would have disbelieved. So leave me as I leave you, for those before you were destroyed through their excessive questioning and their disputing with their prophets. When I command you to do something, do of it what you are able, and when I forbid you from something, avoid it."

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 5, verse 103:

The people of the Jahiliyya (the age of ignorance before Islam) used to do this: when a she-camel gave birth to five offspring, with the last one being male, they would slit her ear (baḥḥara, from baḥīra), that is, split it, and they forbade riding her. She was not kept away from water or pasture, and if a weary traveller met her, he would not ride her. Her name was the baḥīra.

A man would say: "If I return from my journey or recover from my illness, then my she-camel is sā'iba (set free)," and he would make her like the baḥīra in forbidding any benefit from her. It was also said: when a man freed a slave, he would say, "He is sā'iba; there is no blood-money (ʿaql) between them and no inheritance." When a sheep gave birth to a female, it belonged to them; if it gave birth to a male, it was for their gods. If it gave birth to a male and a female, they said, "It has joined its brother," and they did not slaughter the male for their gods. When a stallion sired ten offspring, they said, "Its back has been protected (ḥumiya)," so it was not ridden, not burdened, and not kept from water or pasture.

The meaning of "ma jaʿala" (﴿Allah has not appointed﴾) is that God did not legislate that, nor did He command baḥr, taswīb, or anything else of the kind. But by their forbidding what they forbade, ﴿they invent lies against Allah﴾, ﴿and most of them do not understand﴾. They do not attribute the prohibition to God until they fabricate, but they follow their elders in forbidding these things.

The waw in His saying ﴿أَوَلَوْ كانَ آباؤُهُمْ﴾ is the waw of circumstance (waw al-hal), into which the interrogative hamzah of denunciation (hamzat al-inkar) has entered. Its implied sense is: "Would you suppose they follow it even though their fathers ﴿did not know anything, nor were they guided﴾?" The meaning is that following (al-iqtida') is only valid when one follows a knowledgeable person who is guided, and his being guided is known only through proof (al-hujjah).

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 5, verse 105:

The believers' souls would waste away in grief over the obstinate and stubborn disbelievers, wishing that they would enter Islam. So it was said to them: ﴿Look to your own souls﴾, meaning: [concern yourselves with] the reform of your own souls and the guiding of them along the paths of guidance, and ﴿the one who has strayed cannot harm you if you are [rightly] guided﴾. This is like what the Mighty and Majestic said to His Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him): ﴿So let not your soul waste away in grief over them﴾ [35:8]. Likewise, whoever grieves over the sinfulness of the wicked and their transgressions, and never ceases to mention their faults and their evils, is also addressed by this verse. The intended meaning is not the abandonment of enjoining good and forbidding evil, for whoever abandons them while able to do so is not guided; rather, this is part of the misguidance that the verse distinguishes between them and it. It is narrated from Ibn Mas'ud that this verse was recited in his presence, and he said: "This is not its time (the sentence 'it is not its time' is probably referring to the admonition understood from the context). Today it is accepted. But soon a time will come when you will command and it will not be accepted from you; then ﴿look to your own souls﴾." So on this reading it is a consolation for one who commands and forbids but is not heeded, and an extension of excuse for him. It is also narrated from him: "This is not the time of its interpretation." It was asked: "When, then?" He said: "When there is set before it the sword, the whip, and the prison."

It is narrated from Abu Tha'laba al-Khushani that he was asked about this, and he said to the questioner: "You have asked one who knows. I asked the Messenger of Allah (peace and blessings be upon him) about it, and he said: 'Enjoin good and forbid evil, until you see a miserly greed obeyed, a desire followed, this world preferred, and every person of opinion pleased with his own opinion; then [look to] yourself and leave the affairs of the common people. For behind you are days in which patience is like clutching a live coal; the one who acts among them will have the reward of fifty men who act like his deed.'"

[Narrated by the compilers of the Sunan except al-Nasa'i, from the narration of Abdullah ibn al-Mubarak from Utba ibn Abi Hakim from Amr ibn Harithah al-Lakhmi from Abu Umayya al-San'ani, who said: "I came to Abu Tha'laba al-Khushani and said to him: 'How do you act regarding this verse?' He said: 'Which verse?' I said: 'The saying of the Exalted: (O you who believe, look to your own souls)...' The verse. He said: 'By Allah, you have asked one who knows. I asked the Messenger of Allah (peace and blessings be upon him), and he said: "Rather, enjoin good and forbid evil..." and he mentioned it, and said in it: "then take care of your own self and leave the common people," and said at its end: "like your deed."' Ibn al-Mubarak said: 'Someone other than Utba added to me: It was said, "O Messenger of Allah, the reward of fifty of us, or of them?" He said: "No, rather of you."' It was also narrated by Ibn Hibban, al-Hakim, Ishaq, Abu Ya'la, and al-Tabarani.]

It was said: when a man embraced Islam, they would say to him, "You have made foolish your fathers," and blame him, so this verse was revealed: ﴿Look to your own souls﴾. ["Alaykum" (look to / keep to), is among the verbs of obligation, meaning: "Keep to the reform of your own souls," and for this reason its answer is apocopated (jazm).] It is narrated from Nafi': "'Alaykum anfusakum" with a raised (rafʿ) ending. And it was read: ﴿lā yaḍurrukum﴾ [the harm will not harm you], and in this there are two possibilities: that it be a raised predicate (khabar marfu') — and the reading of Abu Haywa supports it, "lā yaḍīrukum" — and that it be a jussive answer to the command. The rāʾ was given a damma to follow the damma of the ḍād, which was transferred to it from the rāʾ that was assimilated. The original is "lā yaḍurrukum" (lā yadurrūkum). It is also possible that it is a prohibition: "wa-lā yaḍurrukum," with the ḍād vowelled with kasra or damma, from "ḍārahu yaḍīruhu" and "yaḍūruhu."

The Kashshaf of al-Zamakhshari, commentary on Surah 5, verses 106–108:

Itha "two" (ithnan) is raised as the predicate of the subject *shahadatu baynikum* ("the testimony among you"), with the implied sense: "the testimony among you is the testimony of two." Alternatively, it is the agent (*fa'il*) of *shahadatu baynikum*, with the meaning: "in what has been enjoined upon you, that two should bear witness." Al-Sha'bi read *shahadatu baynikum* with tanwin (*shahadatun baynikum*).

Al-Hasan read *shahadatan* with the accusative and tanwin, on the basis of the sense: "Let there be the testimony of two." *Idha hadara* ("when there comes") is a temporal clause governing the testimony. *Hina al-wasiyyah* ("at the time of the bequest") is a substitution (*badal*) for it. That it is a substitution indicates that making a bequest is obligatory, and that it is among the binding matters which a Muslim should not neglect or be heedless of. *Hudur al-mawt* ("the presence of death") means its approach and the appearance of the signs that the term has come.

*Minkum* ("from among you") means from among your relatives, and *min ghayrikum* ("from other than you") means from among strangers. *In antum darabtum fi al-ard* ("if you travel in the land") means: if death occurs during a journey and none of your kin is present, then call upon two strangers to witness the bequest. Relatives are given precedence because they know the circumstances of the deceased better, and what is most beneficial for him, and they are the most sincere in advising him. It is also said that *minkum* means from among the Muslims and *min ghayrikum* means from among the *ahl al-dhimma* (the protected non-Muslim subjects). It is further said that the verse is abrogated (*mansukh*, that is, its ruling has been superseded by a later ruling, *naskh*): the testimony of a *dhimmi* against a Muslim is not permitted, and it was permitted only at the beginning of Islam, owing to the scarcity of Muslims and the difficulty of finding them during travel. Makhul reported that its abrogation is by the words of God, Exalted: ﴿And call to witness two just men from among you﴾.

It is reported that Badil ibn Abi Maryam, the client (*mawla*) of Amr ibn al-As, who was one of the Emigrants (*muhajirun*), went out to Syria for trade together with Adi ibn Zayd and Tamim ibn Aws, both of whom were Christians. Badil fell ill and wrote a document containing what he had with him, placed it among his goods, and did not inform his two companions. He instructed them to deliver his goods to his family. He died, and they searched his goods and took a silver vessel containing three hundred mithqals, decorated with gold, and concealed it. The family of Badil found the document and demanded the vessel from them, but they denied it, so they were brought before the Messenger of God (ﷺ). [Al-Tirmidhi transmitted it from the narration of Ibn Ishaq, from Abu al-Nadr, who is Muhammad ibn al-Sa'ib al-Kalbi, from Badhan, meaning Abu Salih, the client of Umm Hani, from Ibn Abbas, from Tamim al-Dari, may God be pleased with them all. He related it and said: its chain is not authentic. Al-Bukhari and Abu Dawud transmitted it in abridged form.] Then the verse was revealed: ﴿You shall detain them﴾, meaning you shall stop them and hold them back for the oath, ﴿after the prayer﴾, meaning after the afternoon prayer (*salat al-asr*), because that is the time when people gather. It is reported from al-Hasan that it refers to after the afternoon or the noon prayer, because the people of the Hijaz used to sit for judgment after them.

In the narration of Badil: when this verse was revealed, the Messenger of God (ﷺ) prayed the afternoon prayer, summoned Adi and Tamim, and had them swear an oath by the pulpit. They swore, and then the vessel was found in Mecca. The people said: "We bought it from Tamim and Adi."

It is also said that the prayer here is the prayer of the *ahl al-dhimma*, who hold the afternoon prayer in high esteem.

*In irtabtum* ("if you doubt") is an interjected clause between the oath and the thing sworn to. The meaning is: if you doubt concerning their two, and suspect them, then have them swear. It is said: if by the two are meant the two witnesses, then the requirement of swearing the two witnesses has been abrogated; but if by them are meant the two executors (*wasiyyan*), then the requirement of their swearing has not been abrogated. It is reported from Ali, may God be pleased with him, that he used to have a witness or a narrator swear when he suspected them. [As for the swearing of a witness, I have not seen it. As for the swearing of a narrator, it was transmitted by the authors of the three Sunan collections, and by al-Bazzar and Ibn Hibban, from the narration of Asma' ibn al-Hakam al-Fazari, from Ali, may God be pleased with him, who said: "When I heard a hadith from the Messenger of God (ﷺ), God benefited me by it as much as He willed. And when someone from among his Companions related to me, I had him swear. If he swore to me, I believed him." He said: "Abu Bakr related to me, and Abu Bakr spoke the truth," and then the hadith. Al-Tirmidhi said: it is good, and we only know it from this route. Some transmitted this hadith as a *mawquf* (a report ending at a Companion), meaning the text without the story. Al-Bazzar said: this Asma' is unknown.]

The pronoun in *musibatun* ("calamity") refers to the oath. The pronoun in *kana* ("it be") refers to the person for whom the oath is sworn. The meaning is: we will not exchange the truthfulness of the oath by God for any worldly good, that is, we will not swear falsely for the sake of wealth, even if the person for whom we swear is a relative of ours. The sense is that this is their custom in their truthfulness and trustworthiness at all times, and that they fall under the words of God, Exalted: ﴿Be steadfast in justice, witnesses for God, even against yourselves or parents and close relatives﴾.

*Shahadata Allah* ("the testimony of God") means the testimony which God has commanded to be preserved and honored. It is reported from al-Sha'bi that he paused at *shahadah* and then began again with the prolonged *Allah* (*Allahi*), by omitting the particle of oath and compensating for it with the interrogative hamza. He also transmitted it without the prolongation, in accordance with what Sibawayh mentioned, that some speakers omit the particle of oath and do not compensate for it with the interrogative hamza, so they say: *Allahi laqad kana kadha* ("By God, it was such").

It was also read as *lamalathimin*, with the hamza omitted, its vowel transferred to the lam, and the nun of *min* assimilated into the following letter, like the line: "A companion of the tribe" (*'ada lawli*).

If you ask: what is the position of *tahbisunahuma* ("you detain them")? I answer: it is a resumption of speech, as if it were said after the condition of their uprightness: "How shall we act if we doubt them?" and it was answered: "You shall detain them."

If you ask: how did you interpret the prayer as the afternoon prayer when it is unrestricted? I answer: because it was known among them that the oath was administered after it, this removed the need for specification, just as if you said of some jurist: "When he has prayed he takes up the lesson," it would be understood that it refers to the dawn prayer. It is also permissible that the lam (in *al-salat*) be generic, and that the oath after the prayer be intended to make the prayer an aid to speaking the truth and a restraint from lying and falsehood, as in the words of God: ﴿Indeed, prayer restrains from immorality and wrongdoing﴾.

*Fa in 'uthira* ("then if it is discovered") means: if it becomes known that the two have incurred *ithm* ("sin"), that is, they committed something that made them sinful, and deserved to be described as sinners. *Fa-akharani* ("then two others") means two other witnesses, who stand in their place *min al-ladhina istahqqa 'alayhim* ("from among those against whom it was merited"), meaning from among those against whom sin was incurred. The meaning is: from among those who were wronged, namely the family and kin of the deceased.

In the story of Badil: when the treachery of the two men became apparent, two men from among his heirs swore that the vessel belonged to their companion, and that their testimony was more worthy than the testimony of the two Christians.

*Al-awliyan* ("the more worthy") means the more entitled to testify because of their kinship and their knowledge. Its raising (as *awliyani*) is as the predicate of an implied subject: "They are the two more worthy." As if it were said: "And who are they?" and the answer was: "The two more worthy." It is also said that they are a substitution (*badal*) for the pronoun in *yaqumani*, or for *akharani*.

It is also permissible that the two be raised by *istahqqa*, meaning: from among those against whom the appointing of the two more worthy among them to testify was merited, because they have knowledge of the true state of affairs.

*Al-awwalin* ("the first") was also read, as a description of *alladhina istahqqa 'alayhim*, in the genitive, or in the accusative as a commendation. The sense of *awwaliyyah* ("precedence") is precedence over the strangers in testimony, because they have more right to it.

*Al-awwalin* was also read in the dual form (*al-awwalayn*), with an accusative in the sense of commendation. Al-Hasan read *al-awwalan*, and whoever holds that the oath is returned to the claimant (*radd al-yamin 'ala al-mudda'i*) argues from this reading. Abu Hanifa and his companions do not hold this view. Their reasoning is that the heirs had claimed against the two Christians that they had committed treachery, and they swore. When their lie became apparent, they claimed that they had bought what they had concealed. The heirs denied the sale, so the oath fell upon the heirs, because they were denying the sale.

If you ask: what is the meaning of the reading of those who read *istahqqa 'alayhim al-awwalan* with the verb in the active voice, which was transmitted by Ali, Ubayy, and Ibn Abbas? I answer: its meaning is: from among the heirs, those against whom the two more worthy among them were merited for the testimony, that they should single out the two of them to stand as witnesses, and display through them the falsehood of the liars.

*Dhalika* ("that") refers to what was set forth before, the statement of the ruling, *adna an ya'tu al-shuhada'u 'ala nahwi tilka al-hadithah bil-shahadati 'ala wajiha* ("is more likely that the witnesses will bring the testimony in its proper form, like that incident"), *aw yakhafu an turadda aymanun* ("or they will fear that oaths will be returned"), meaning that the oaths of other witnesses will be returned after their own oaths, *fayaftadahu bi-zuhuri kadhibihim kama jara fi qissati Badil* ("so that they will be disgraced by the exposure of their lies, as happened in the story of Badil"). *Wasma'u* ("and listen") means listen with acceptance and submission.

The pronoun in *musibatun* ("calamity") refers to the oath. The pronoun in *kana* ("it be") refers to the person for whom the oath is sworn. The meaning is: we will not exchange the truthfulness of the oath by God for any worldly good, that is, we will not swear falsely for the sake of wealth, even if the person for whom we swear is a relative of ours. The sense is that this is their custom in their truthfulness and trustworthiness at all times, and that they fall under the words of God, Exalted: ﴿Be steadfast in justice, witnesses for God, even against yourselves or parents and close relatives﴾.

*Shahadata Allah* ("the testimony of God") means the testimony which God has commanded to be preserved and honored. It is reported from al-Sha'bi that he paused at *shahadah* and then began again with the prolonged *Allah* (*Allahi*), by omitting the particle of oath and compensating for it with the interrogative hamza. He also transmitted it without the prolongation, in accordance with what Sibawayh mentioned, that some speakers omit the particle of oath and do not compensate for it with the interrogative hamza, so they say: *Allahi laqad kana kadha* ("By God, it was such").

It was also read as *lamalathimin*, with the hamza omitted, its vowel transferred to the lam, and the nun of *min* assimilated into the following letter, like the line: "A companion of the tribe" (*'ada lawli*).

If you ask: what is the position of *tahbisunahuma* ("you detain them")? I answer: it is a resumption of speech, as if it were said after the condition of their uprightness: "How shall we act if we doubt them?" and it was answered: "You shall detain them."

If you ask: how did you interpret the prayer as the afternoon prayer when it is unrestricted? I answer: because it was known among them that the oath was administered after it, this removed the need for specification, just as if you said of some jurist: "When he has prayed he takes up the lesson," it would be understood that it refers to the dawn prayer. It is also permissible that the lam (in *al-salat*) be generic, and that the oath after the prayer be intended to make the prayer an aid to speaking the truth and a restraint from lying and falsehood, as in the words of God: ﴿Indeed, prayer restrains from immorality and wrongdoing﴾.

*Fa in 'uthira* ("then if it is discovered") means: if it becomes known that the two have incurred *ithm* ("sin"), that is, they committed something that made them sinful, and deserved to be described as sinners. *Fa-akharani* ("then two others") means two other witnesses, who stand in their place *min al-ladhina istahqqa 'alayhim* ("from among those against whom it was merited"), meaning from among those against whom sin was incurred. The meaning is: from among those who were wronged, namely the family and kin of the deceased.

In the story of Badil: when the treachery of the two men became apparent, two men from among his heirs swore that the vessel belonged to their companion, and that their testimony was more worthy than the testimony of the two Christians.

*Al-awliyan* ("the more worthy") means the more entitled to testify because of their kinship and their knowledge. Its raising (as *awliyani*) is as the predicate of an implied subject: "They are the two more worthy." As if it were said: "And who are they?" and the answer was: "The two more worthy." It is also said that they are a substitution (*badal*) for the pronoun in *yaqumani*, or for *akharani*.

It is also permissible that the two be raised by *istahqqa*, meaning: from among those against whom the appointing of the two more worthy among them to testify was merited, because they have knowledge of the true state of affairs.

*Al-awwalin* ("the first") was also read, as a description of *alladhina istahqqa 'alayhim*, in the genitive, or in the accusative as a commendation. The sense of *awwaliyyah* ("precedence") is precedence over the strangers in testimony, because they have more right to it.

*Al-awwalin* was also read in the dual form (*al-awwalayn*), with an accusative in the sense of commendation. Al-Hasan read *al-awwalan*, and whoever holds that the oath is returned to the claimant (*radd al-yamin 'ala al-mudda'i*) argues from this reading. Abu Hanifa and his companions do not hold this view. Their reasoning is that the heirs had claimed against the two Christians that they had committed treachery, and they swore. When their lie became apparent, they claimed that they had bought what they had concealed. The heirs denied the sale, so the oath fell upon the heirs, because they were denying the sale.

If you ask: what is the meaning of the reading of those who read *istahqqa 'alayhim al-awwalan* with the verb in the active voice, which was transmitted by Ali, Ubayy, and Ibn Abbas? I answer: its meaning is: from among the heirs, those against whom the two more worthy among them were merited for the testimony, that they should single out the two of them to stand as witnesses, and display through them the falsehood of the liars.

*Dhalika* ("that") refers to what was set forth before, the statement of the ruling, *adna an ya'tu al-shuhada'u 'ala nahwi tilka al-hadithah bil-shahadati 'ala wajiha* ("is more likely that the witnesses will bring the testimony in its proper form, like that incident"), *aw yakhafu an turadda aymanun* ("or they will fear that oaths will be returned"), meaning that the oaths of other witnesses will be returned after their own oaths, *fayaftadahu bi-zuhuri kadhibihim kama jara fi qissati Badil* ("so that they will be disgraced by the exposure of their lies, as happened in the story of Badil"). *Wasma'u* ("and listen") means listen with acceptance and submission.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 5, verses 109–110:

﴿Yawma yajma'u﴾ is a substitute (badal) for the accusative noun in ﴿wattaqu Allah﴾ [[Mahmud said: "﴿Yawma yajma'u﴾ is a substitute for the accusative ... etc." Ahmad (Ibn al-Munayyir) said: In that case its accusative status is that of a direct object (maf'ul bihi), not of an adverb of time (zarf), following the ruling of the noun it substitutes.]]. It is a substitution of inclusion (badal al-ishtimal), as if it were said: "Fear God on the day of their gathering." Or it is an adverb of time (zarf) for ﴿la yahdi﴾ [[He resumed his speech: "Or it is an adverb of time for ﴿la yahdi al-qawm al-fasiqin﴾ ... etc." Ahmad said: On this view too it is a direct object.]], meaning: He will not guide them to the path of Paradise on that day, as He does with others. Or it is governed by an implied ﴿udhkur﴾ (remember). Or: "on the day God gathers the Messengers, such-and-such occurred."

﴿Ma dha﴾ is in the accusative governed by ﴿ajabtum﴾ [[He resumed: "﴿Ma dha﴾ is in the accusative as the verbal noun (masdar) of ﴿ajabtum﴾, in the sense of 'what response you responded with' ... etc." Ahmad said: This kind of glorification is like the glorification through silence about the relative clause in the phrase: "It did not happen except after 'the one' and 'the other'."]], as the verbal noun of it, in the sense of: "What response did you respond with?" Had the meaning been the answer itself, it would have been said: "With what did you respond?"

If you ask: What is the purpose of their question? I say: It is a rebuke to their peoples, just as the question to the buried infant (al-mawuda) was a rebuke to the one who buried her.

If you ask: How can they say ﴿la 'ilma lana﴾ ("We have no knowledge") when they know what answer they were given? I say: They know that the purpose of the question is to rebuke their enemies, so they leave the matter to His knowledge and His encompassing awareness of what they were tested with from them [[His words "bima munu bihi minhum" mean: "what they were afflicted with." In al-Sihah, "manituhu" and "manawtuhu" mean "I tested him."]] and endured from their evil response, as a display of complaint and of seeking refuge with their Lord for vengeance upon them. That is more grievous to the disbelievers, more weakening to their resolve, more conducive to their regret, and to their being struck with remorse, when God's rebuke and the complaint of His prophets against them are combined.

An example: one of the Khawarij wrongs a particular companion of the ruler, a wrong the ruler knows and understands fully, and he resolves to avenge him against him. He brings the two together and says to him: "What did this Khariji do to you, while he knows what he did?", intending to rebuke and reprimand him. The companion replies: "You know better what was done to me," entrusting the matter to the ruler's knowledge, relying on him, displaying complaint, and magnifying what befell him at his hands.

It is also said: From the terror of that day they will be panicked and bewildered [[He resumed: "It is said: from the horror and fright they will be distracted from the answer ..." Ahmad said: Moreover, what is asked about is their response when they were called to God, not what happened afterward, which the knowledge of the Messengers does not encompass. And God knows best.]] about the answer, and then they will answer after their minds return to them, by bearing witness against their peoples.

It is also said: The meaning is that our knowledge is insignificant beside Your knowledge and submerged in it, for You are the Knower of the unseen. Whoever knows the hidden things does not have the outward things hidden from him, and among the outward things is the response of nations to their messengers. So it is as if we have no knowledge in comparison with Your knowledge.

It is also said: "We have no knowledge of what they did after us; the judgment rests only on the final outcome." How could their affair be hidden from them, when they have seen them with blackened faces, blue eyes, and rebuked?

﴿'Allam al-ghuyub﴾ has been read in the accusative [[He resumed: "﴿'Allam al-ghuyub﴾ has been read in the accusative ..." Ahmad said: This is of the type of the verse: "I am Abu al-Najm, and my poetry, my poetry." It has been mentioned before, in verses. I mentioned these three grammatical points only because they are confusing except to the skilled, and they are few.]]. The speech is complete with the words ﴿innaka anta﴾, meaning: "Indeed You are the One described by Your well-known attributes, including knowledge and other things." Then ﴿'allam al-ghuyub﴾ is in the accusative as a specification (ikhtisas), or as a vocative (nida'), or it is an attribute (sifa) of the subject of ﴿inna﴾.

﴿Idh qala Allah﴾ is a substitution for ﴿yawma yajma'u﴾. The meaning: He will rebuke the disbelievers on that day by asking the Messengers about their response, and by enumerating the great signs that appeared at their hands. They denied them and called them sorcerers. Or they exceeded the limit of belief by taking them as gods, as some of the Children of Israel said regarding the clear signs and miracles that appeared at the hand of ʿIsa (peace be upon him): ﴿This is nothing but manifest magic﴾. And some of them took him and his mother as two gods.

﴿Ayyadtuka﴾: I strengthened you. It has also been read as ﴿ayyadtuka﴾ in the form ʾafʿaltuka. ﴿Bi-ruh al-qudus﴾: with the speech by which religion is given life. He attributed it to "the Holy" (al-qudus) because it is the cause of purity from the filth of sins. The evidence for this is His saying: ﴿You speak to people in the cradle﴾, where ﴿fi al-mahd﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal), because the meaning is "You speak to them as a child," and ﴿wa-kahlan﴾ (and in maturity), except that "in the cradle" indicates a limit of childhood.

It is also said: The Holy Spirit (ruh al-qudus) is Jibril (peace be upon him), with whom He strengthened him to establish the proof.

If you ask: What is the meaning of His saying ﴿fi al-mahd wa-kahlan﴾? I say: The meaning is that you speak to them in these two states, without your speech differing between the time of childhood and the time of maturity, which is the time of the perfection of intellect and the attainment of full strength, and the limit at which prophets are sent.

﴿Al-Tawrat wa-al-Injil﴾ are singled out for mention from what the Book and wisdom encompass, because by them is meant the category of the Book and wisdom. It is also said: ﴿al-Kitab﴾ is writing, and ﴿al-Hikmah﴾ is speech that is firm and correct.

﴿Ka-hay'at al-tayr﴾: a form like the form of a bird, ﴿bi-idhni﴾: by My permission, ﴿fa-tanfukhu fiha﴾: the pronoun refers to the kaf (ka), because it is the attribute of the form which ʿIsa (peace be upon him) used to create and then breathe into. It does not refer to the form that is its annexed noun, because that form is not from his creation nor from his breathing in any respect. The same applies to the pronoun in ﴿fa-takunu﴾.

﴿Tukhriju al-mawta﴾: You bring forth the dead, bringing them out of their graves and raising them. It is said: He brought out Sam ibn Nuh, two men, a woman, and a girl.

﴿Wa-idh kafaftu Bani Isra'il ʿanka﴾: meaning the Jews, when they resolved to kill him.

It is also said: When God said to ʿIsa (peace be upon him): ﴿Remember My favor upon you﴾, he used to wear hair and eat from trees, and would not store anything for the next day, saying: "With each day comes its provision." He had no house that could be ruined, nor child who could die; wherever evening came, he spent the night there.
