I inspired the disciples: I commanded them through the tongues of the messengers. *Muslimūn* (submitting, sincere), *man aslama wajhahu lillāh*. *ʿĪsā* is in the accusative position, following the vowel of *ibn* (the son), as in your saying: *yā Zayd ibn ʿAmr*. This is the common dialect. It is also permissible for it to be marked with a *ḍamma*, as in your saying: *yā Zayd ibn ʿAmr*. The evidence for this is his saying:

*Aḥāra ibn ʿAmrin, ka-annī khimr*
*Wa-yabdū ʿalā al-marʾi mā yaʾtamir*

*Wa-lā wa-abīki ibnata al-ʿĀmirī*
*Lā yadʿī al-qawmu annī afirr*

These lines are by Imruʾ al-Qays ibn Ḥujr. It is also said that they belong to Rabīʿa ibn Jusham al-Yumnā. The *hamza* is for the vocative. *Ḥār* is a truncated form (*tarkhīm*, vocative truncation); its original form is *Ḥārith*, and it is given a *ḍamma* according to the dialect of those who do not wait for the deleted letter to return. The well-known usage is to treat it as a complete noun. Likewise, the well-known practice is also to give a *fatḥa* to the named vocative described by *ibn* followed by another proper name, following the accusative of *ibn*. It may also be given a *ḍamma*, as here, because truncation occurs only on a word ending in *ḍamma*, since a word ending in *fatḥa* by imitation is like a compound with what follows it. Truncation does not occur in the middle of a word. Also, if it were *fatḥa* and it were given a *ḍamma* in truncation, this would disturb the *fatḥa* that is brought in for harmony. *Al-khamr* (with *fatḥa* and *kasra* in the pattern *ḥadhar*) is one whose intellect has been covered by a disease that infected him. *Al-khamr* (in the pattern *sabab*) is everything that is covered by a building or trees. Then he mentions the reason for this, which is his obedience to what should not be obeyed, so he says: *and he attacks the human being in obeying him*, that is, his submission to the command of another. It is also permissible for *mā* to be a relative pronoun, meaning: what he obeys from the command of one who does not know the consequences of affairs, or from the command of his own self and desire. This is likened to one from whom aggression can properly arise, by way of metonymy (*kināya*). It is related as *wa-yabdū ʿalā al-marʾ*, meaning it overlooks him and shows him the consequence of obeying what should not be obeyed. Many recite the rhyme-ending of this verse with the heavy *tanwīn*, but al-Zajjāj and al-Sīrāfī rejected this, because it breaks the meter. Ibn Yaʿīsh considered it the *tanwīn al-tarannum* (the *tanwīn* of melodic chanting), based on the view that it is used to bring about melody, not to cut it off, so it is not restricted to open rhymes, but also includes closed rhymes, as here. The well-known form is to vocalize the letter before it with a *kasra*. Ibn al-Ḥājib preferred the *fatḥa*. Some permitted vocalizing it with what it would deserve were it not for its being sukūn. Some permitted two consecutive unvocalized letters. The entry of the negative *lā* before the oath is common and acceptable in the Arabic language, because it generally serves to reject and deny the claim of the opponent. So the implied meaning is: *that does not happen, and by the right of your father*. Had it been purely superfluous, the *wāw* in the implied meaning would have entered upon the *wāw* of the oath. It is also related with the first *wāw* omitted: meaning, *and by the right of your father, O daughter of al-ʿĀmirī, I do not flee from war at all, so no one claims it against me*. Thus denying the claim is a metonymy for denying the flight, in the most eloquent way.

Because truncation occurs only on what is given a *ḍamma*. If you say: how did they say *Can your Lord send down to us a table?* after their faith and sincerity? [Al-Zamakhsharī said: If you say: how did they say, *Can your Lord…?* after their faith and sincerity, in His saying: *And when I inspired the disciples: Believe in Me and My Messenger, they said: We believe, and bear witness that we are submitting* — I say: Allah did not describe them with faith and sincerity; He only related their claim to them. Then He followed it with His saying: *When Jesus said…*] Ibn al-Munayyir said: It has been said that the meaning of *hal yastaṭīʿu* is *hal yafʿal* (will He do?), just as you say to one who is capable of standing: *Can you stand?*, as an intensification of urging. This view is related from al-Ḥasan. Accordingly, their faith would be free from the defect of doubt about power. If the expression of the act by *istiṭāʿa* (ability) is sound, then that is, Allah knows best, from the type of expressing the effect by the cause, since ability is among the causes of bringing into existence. The opposite is expressing the will to act by the act, naming the cause, which is the will, with the name of the effect, which is the act, as in His saying: *When you rise to prayer* (mentioned at the beginning of the surah). In this fine interpretation there is support for the interpretation of Abū Ḥanīfa, who made the means (*ṭawl*) that prevents marrying a slave woman the existence of a free wife in marriage, and its absence to be that one does not own a free woman in wedlock even though he is able to do so; then the slave woman becomes permissible for him. He understood His saying: *And whoever among you cannot afford (lam yastaṭiʿ) the means to marry believing free women* as meaning: *whoever among you does not own*, and understood marriage as sexual intercourse, so he made the negated ability to own the ownership itself, as you see, so that one who is capable but does not own is considered by him to lack the means, and so he marries a slave woman. His school has been mentioned, and I used to think it unlikely that this could be an interpretation that the wording allows and usage supports, until I came upon this interpretation of al-Ḥasan. Allah knows best.] I say: Allah did not describe them with faith and sincerity; He only related their claim to them. Then He followed it with *When he said*. So their claim was false, and they were doubters. His saying *Can your Lord…?* is a statement that could not be issued by believers who venerate their Lord. Likewise, the statement of Jesus (peace be upon him) to them means: fear Allah and do not doubt His power and ability, do not propose to Him, and do not dictate the signs you desire, lest you perish if you disobey Him after them, *if you are believers*, if your claim of faith is true.

It is read: *Hal tastaṭīʿu rabbaka*, meaning: *Can you ask your Lord?*, and the meaning is: *Will you ask Him for that without any obstacle preventing you from asking Him?* *Al-Māʾida* is the table (*al-khiwān*) when food is on it. (Al-Khiwān, with a *kasra*, is that on which food is eaten; it is arabicized. His saying *from madda* [the word in the Ṣiḥāḥ is *māda al-shayʾ*, it moved; *māda al-aghṣān*, they swayed]. ) It comes from *māddah*, when one gives and provides, as if it sways toward the one who approaches it.

*And we would be among its witnesses*: we would bear witness to it before those who did not attend it among the Children of Israel, or we would be among those who witness for Allah with His oneness and for you with prophethood, devoted to it. *ʿAlayhā* is in the position of the *ḥāl* (circumstantial accusative). Their claim was for the purpose of what they mentioned, like their claim of faith and sincerity. Then a red tablecloth descended between two clouds: a cloud above it and another below it, and they were looking at it until it fell before them. Jesus (peace be upon him) wept and said: *O Allah, make me among the thankful. O Allah, make it a mercy and do not make it a punishment and a chastisement.* He said to them: *Let the best of you in deeds stand up, uncover it, mention the name of Allah over it, and eat from it.* Shamʿūn, the head of the disciples, said: *You are more deserving of that.* So Jesus stood, performed ablution, prayed, and wept. Then he uncovered the cloth and said: *In the name of Allah, the best of providers.* Suddenly there was a grilled fish, without scales or thorns, dripping fat. At its head was salt, at its tail was vinegar, and around it were various herbs except leeks. And there were five loaves of bread: on one was olives, on the second honey, on the third butter, on the fourth cheese, and on the fifth dried meat. Shamʿūn said: *O Spirit of Allah, is this from the food of this world or from the food of the Hereafter?* He said: *It is neither of them, but a thing that Allah created by His lofty power. It is also related that when they heard of the condition, which is His saying: *Whoever among you disbelieves after that, I shall surely punish him*, they said: *We do not want it,* and so it was not sent down. *Aḥāra ibn ʿAmrin, ka-annī khimr*
*Wa-yabdū ʿalā al-marʾi mā yaʾtamir*

This is likened to one from whom aggression can properly arise, by way of metonymy (*kināya*). It is related as *wa-yabdū ʿalā al-marʾ*, meaning it overlooks him and shows him the consequence of obeying what should not be obeyed. The entry of the negative *lā* before the oath is common and acceptable in the Arabic language, because it generally serves to reject and deny the claim of the opponent. Then he mentions the reason for this, which is his obedience to what should not be obeyed, so he says: *and he attacks the human being in obeying him*, that is, his submission to the command of another. It is also permissible for *mā* to be a relative pronoun, meaning: what he obeys from the command of one who does not know the consequences of affairs, or from the command of his own self and desire. This is likened to one from whom aggression can properly arise, by way of metonymy (*kināya*). It is related as *wa-yabdū ʿalā al-marʾ*, meaning it overlooks him and shows him the consequence of obeying what should not be obeyed. Many recite the rhyme-ending of this verse with the heavy *tanwīn*, but al-Zajjāj and al-Sīrāfī rejected this, because it breaks the meter. Ibn Yaʿīsh considered it the *tanwīn al-tarannum* (the *tanwīn* of melodic chanting), based on the view that it is used to bring about melody, not to cut it off, so it is not restricted to open rhymes, but also includes closed rhymes, as here. The well-known form is to vocalize the letter before it with a *kasra*. Ibn al-Ḥājib preferred the *fatḥa*. Some permitted vocalizing it with what it would deserve were it not for its being sukūn. Some permitted two consecutive unvocalized letters. The entry of the negative *lā* before the oath is common and acceptable in the Arabic language, because it generally serves to reject and deny the claim of the opponent. So the implied meaning is: *that does not happen, and by the right of your father*. Had it been purely superfluous, the *wāw* in the implied meaning would have entered upon the *wāw* of the oath. It is also related with the first *wāw* omitted: meaning, *and by the right of your father, O daughter of al-ʿĀmirī, I do not flee from war at all, so no one claims it against me*. Thus denying the claim is a metonymy for denying the flight, in the most eloquent way.

Because truncation occurs only on what is given a *ḍamma*. If you say: how did they say *Can your Lord send down to us a table?* after their faith and sincerity? [Al-Zamakhsharī said: If you say: how did they say, *Can your Lord…?* after their faith and sincerity, in His saying: *And when I inspired the disciples: Believe in Me and My Messenger, they said: We believe, and bear witness that we are submitting* — I say: Allah did not describe them with faith and sincerity; He only related their claim to them. Then He followed it with His saying: *When Jesus said…*] Ibn al-Munayyir said: It has been said that the meaning of *hal yastaṭīʿu* is *hal yafʿal* (will He do?), just as you say to one who is capable of standing: *Can you stand?*, as an intensification of urging. This view is related from al-Ḥasan. Accordingly, their faith would be free from the defect of doubt about power. If the expression of the act by *istiṭāʿa* (ability) is sound, then that is, Allah knows best, from the type of expressing the effect by the cause, since ability is among the causes of bringing into existence. In this fine interpretation there is support for the interpretation of Abū Ḥanīfa, who made the means (*ṭawl*) that prevents marrying a slave woman the existence of a free wife in marriage, and its absence to be that one does not own a free woman in wedlock even though he is able to do so; then the slave woman becomes permissible for him. He understood His saying: *And whoever among you cannot afford (lam yastaṭiʿ) the means to marry believing free women* as meaning: *whoever among you does not own*, and understood marriage as sexual intercourse, so he made the negated ability to own the ownership itself, as you see, so that one who is capable but does not own is considered by him to lack the means, and so he marries a slave woman. His school has been mentioned, and I used to think it unlikely that this could be an interpretation that the wording allows and usage supports, until I came upon this interpretation of al-Ḥasan. Allah knows best.] I say: Allah did not describe them with faith and sincerity; He only related their claim to them. Then He followed it with *When he said*. So their claim was false, and they were doubters. His saying *Can your Lord…?* is a statement that could not be issued by believers who venerate their Lord. It is read: *Hal tastaṭīʿu rabbaka*, meaning: *Can you ask your Lord?*, and the meaning is: *Will you ask Him for that without any obstacle preventing you from asking Him?* *Al-Māʾida* is the table (*al-khiwān*) when food is on it. (Al-Khiwān, with a *kasra*, is that on which food is eaten; it is arabicized. His saying *from madda* [the word in the Ṣiḥāḥ is *māda al-shayʾ*, it moved; *māda al-aghṣān*, they swayed]. ) It comes from *māddah*, when one gives and provides, as if it sways toward the one who approaches it.

*And we would be among its witnesses*: we would bear witness to it before those who did not attend it among the Children of Israel, or we would be among those who witness for Allah with His oneness and for you with prophethood, devoted to it. *ʿAlayhā* is in the position of the *ḥāl* (circumstantial accusative). Their claim was for the purpose of what they mentioned, like their claim of faith and sincerity. Jesus asked, and was answered, so that the proof would be complete against them and the punishment would be sent upon them if they opposed.

It is read: *yuʿlamu* with *yāʾ* in the passive, and *taʿlam*, and *takūn* with *tāʾ*; the pronoun refers to the hearts.

*Allāhumma*: its origin is *yā Allāh*; the vocative particle was deleted and the *mīm* was substituted for it. *Rabbanā* is a second vocative.

*Takūnu lanā ʿīdan*: meaning, the day of its descent would be a feast. It has been said: it is Sunday, and for this reason the Christians took it as a feast. It has also been said: *ʿīd* is the recurring joy, and for this reason it is said *yawm ʿīd* (a feast day), so its meaning is as if: *it would be joy and delight for us*. ʿAbd Allāh (Ibn Masʿūd) read: *takun*, as an answer to the imperative. Similar to these two is *yarthinī* and *yarithunī*.

*Li-awwalinā wa-ākhirinā*: a substitution for *lanā* by repeating the governing word, meaning: for those in our time among the people of our religion, and for those who come after us. In the reading of Zayd: *li-ūlānā wa-ukhrānā*. The feminine form is in the sense of the community and the group.

*ʿAdhāban* means *taʿdhīb* (punishment). The pronoun in *lā uʿadhdhibuhu* refers to the verbal noun. If *al-ʿadhāb* were meant as what one is punished with, then a *bāʾ* would be necessary.

It is related that when Jesus (peace be upon him) wanted to supplicate, he wore wool and said: *O Allah, send down upon us*. Then a red tablecloth descended between two clouds: a cloud above it and another below it, and they were looking at it until it fell before them. Jesus (peace be upon him) wept and said: *O Allah, make me among the thankful. O Allah, make it a mercy and do not make it a punishment and a chastisement.* He said to them: *Let the best of you in deeds stand up, uncover it, mention the name of Allah over it, and eat from it.* Shamʿūn, the head of the disciples, said: *You are more deserving of that.* So Jesus stood, performed ablution, prayed, and wept. Then he uncovered the cloth and said: *In the name of Allah, the best of providers.* Suddenly there was a grilled fish, without scales or thorns, dripping fat. It is also related that when they heard of the condition, which is His saying: *Whoever among you disbelieves after that, I shall surely punish him*, they said: *We do not want it,* and so it was not sent down. Glory be to You! It is not for me to say what I have no right to say. (Glory be to You; "It is not for me..." — the verse text is rendered as the commentary frames it.)

Let me correct that: the translation should follow the passage itself, which is a gloss on the verse (5:116), so here is the faithful rendering:

"Glory be to You! It is not for me to have... [that] there should be any associate for You. It is not for me (ما يكون لي ما ينبغي لي) to say (أن أقول) a saying (قولا) that I have no right (لا يحق لي) to say. (That is) in my self (فِي نَفْسِي), in my heart. And the meaning: You know what is known to me, and I do not know what is known to You. But (the verse) took the path of mushakalah (correspondence of expression), which is among the eloquent kinds of speech and its finest, so it was said "in Your self" (فِي نَفْسِكَ) corresponding to His saying "in my self" (فِي نَفْسِي). (The phrase) "Indeed, You are the Knower of the unseen" (إِنَّكَ أَنْتَ عَلَّامُ الْغُيُوبِ) is a confirmation of both clauses together, because what the souls harbour is among the unseen matters, and because what the Knower of the unseen knows, no one's knowledge reaches it."

Note on the rendering: the Arabic words in parentheses are the source terms, and the bracketed phrase "[that] there should be any associate" is my addition to complete the sense of the opening clause, which is not fully explicit in the source.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 5, verse 117–118:

(an) in His saying ﴿an u'budu Allah﴾ [[Mahmud said: "As for 'an' in His saying ﴿an u'budu﴾: if you take it as explanatory (mufassira), it must have something it explains..." etc. Ahmad said: Some scholars have permitted the explanatory 'an' to occur after the word of saying (lafz al-qawl), and did not restrict it to what has the same meaning. So, according to this view, it is permissible for it to occur as an explanation of the verb of saying. Al-Zamakhshari, in his Mufassal, refused its occurrence except after a verb having the sense of saying, as is his position here.]] If you take it as explanatory, it must have something it explains. What it explains is either the verb of saying or the verb of command, and both have no justification. As for the verb of saying, speech after it is quoted without a particle of explanation intervening between them. You do not say: "I did not say to them except that worship Allah," but rather: "I did not say to them except worship Allah." As for the verb of command, it is attributed to the pronoun of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic. So if you explained it as ﴿worship Allah, my Lord and your Lord﴾, it would not be correct, because Allah, exalted is He, does not say: "Worship Allah, my Lord and your Lord." If you take it as relative (mawsula) with the verb, [[His speech returns. He said: "As for the verb of command, it is attributed to the pronoun of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic..." etc. Ahmad said: This aspect is also permissible if the explanation is turned to the meaning, as if he related the meaning of Allah's saying to him in other words, as if Allah had said to him: "Command them to worship Me," or He said to them through the tongue of Jesus: "Worship Allah, the Lord of Jesus and your Lord." When Jesus, peace be upon him, related it, he said: "Worship Allah, my Lord and your Lord," so he referred to the apparent name by its pronoun, as Allah the Exalted said, relating from Moses: (He said: Its knowledge is with my Lord, in a Book. My Lord neither errs nor forgets, who made the earth for you a cradle and threaded for you therein ways, and sent down from the sky water, and We brought forth thereby pairs of various plants.) So observe how the beginning of the speech came as a relation of Moses' words, and Moses would not say "fa-akhrajna" (We brought forth) but "fa-akhraja Allah" (Allah brought forth). When Allah related it from Moses, He returned the speech to Himself, and attributed the bringing forth to His own essence in the manner of the speaker, not the relater. Likewise His saying: (They will surely say: "The Mighty, the All-Knowing created them") up to His saying: (so We revived thereby a dead land), and their parallels are many. I had previously presented something similar to this discussion at His saying, relating from the Jews: (Indeed we killed the Messiah, Jesus son of Mary, the Messenger of Allah), when al-Zamakhshari considered it unlikely that the Jews would describe him with these attributes which contradict their belief about him.]] it is either a substitute (badal) for ﴿ma amartani bihi﴾ (what You commanded me), or for the pronoun in ﴿bihi﴾ (with it). Both are not correct, because a substitute is that which takes the place of the replaced item. And one cannot say: "I did not say to them except that worship Allah," meaning "I did not say to them except His worship," because worship is not said. Likewise, if you make it a substitute for the pronoun [[His speech returns. He said: "Likewise if you make it a substitute for the pronoun, because you..." etc. Ahmad said: This also does not preclude substitution, and the author is only confronted with what he cannot deny. In his Mufassal he said the following text: "Their saying that the substitute is in the place of abandoning the first is an announcement from them of its independence in itself and its separation from the emphasis and the adjective in that both are nouns for what they follow, not that they mean the nullification and discarding of the first. Do you not see that you say: 'Zaydan ra'aytu ghulamahu rajulan salihan' (Zayd, I saw his servant, a righteous man), for if you went to the nullification of the first, your speech would not be complete." So observe how his speech in the Mufassal refutes his position. The truth is what he committed, namely rejecting the substitute in this verse, due to the necessity of dropping the first, so the relative clause would be left without the pronoun. He did not consider this measure an obstacle in the example mentioned. Moreover, if you dropped the first, the predicate would be left without the returning pronoun and the speech would not be complete. These are four aspects he rejected in the grammatical analysis of "an," and all are supported as we have shown. This dispute over this grammatical analysis is among the rare and noble points in the art of grammar and rhetoric, and champions of this field are few.]] in it (bihi), because if you put (an u'budu Allah) in the place of the pronoun, saying: "except what You commanded me with, that worship Allah," it would not be correct, since the relative clause would remain without a returning reference from its complement. If you say: "How then is it done?" [[His speech returns. He said: "If you say, how is it done? I say: the verb of saying is carried upon its meaning..." etc. Ahmad said: This interpretation is due to the expectation that the explanatory 'an' follows a verb having the sense of saying, and not an explicit saying. Carrying "saying" on "commanding" supports the other view that permits its occurrence after saying, for were it not for the semantic difference between saying and commanding, it would not be permissible to use one and intend the other.

It is strange that commanding is a category of saying, and the relation between them is only general and specific. There is nothing in this interpretation he followed except a burden with no benefit behind it. And if the Arabs refused the occurrence of the explanatory 'an' after saying, they would not have placed it after a verb that is not a saying, then expressed that verb by saying, because that is like returning to what one fled from, and they are far from that.]] I say: the verb of saying is carried on its meaning, because the meaning of ﴿ma qultu lahum illa ma amartani bihi﴾ (I did not say to them except what You commanded me with) is: "I did not command them except with what You commanded me," so that its explanation becomes ﴿an u'budu Allah rabbi wa rabbakum﴾. It is also permissible that 'an' be relative, [[His speech returns. He said: "It may be that 'an' is relative..." etc. Ahmad said: By making it an explanatory appositive (ʿatf bayan) to the pronoun rather than a substitute, he intends to avoid the assumption of dropping the first in the substitute and the relative clause being left without a returning pronoun. We have shown that this is not necessary in the substitute. ﴿And I was a witness over them, while I remained among them﴾: a watcher, like a witness over the one witnessed against, preventing them from saying that and adhering to it. ﴿But when You took me up, You were the Watcher over them﴾, restraining them from saying it through the proofs You set up for them, the clear signs You sent down to them, and the messengers You sent to them. ﴿If You punish them, they are Your servants﴾, whom You know to be disobedient, denying Your signs and rejecting Your prophets. ﴿And if You forgive them, You are the Mighty﴾, the strong, the one able to reward and to punish, ﴿the Wise﴾, who does not reward or punish except with wisdom and rightness. If you say: forgiveness does not occur for disbelievers, so how did he say: ﴿And if You forgive them﴾? [[Mahmud said: "If you say: forgiveness does not occur for disbelievers, how did He say: ﴿And if You forgive them﴾..." etc. Ahmad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: Al-Zamakhshari wavered in this place, neither going to the People of the Sunnah nor to the Qadariyya. As for the People of the Sunnah, forgiveness of a disbeliever is permissible in Allah's judgment by reason, and indeed punishing the pious sincere one is likewise not rationally impossible for Allah. Since this is so, this statement came under rational possibility, even though revelation has reported the punishment of disbelievers and their non-forgiveness. However, the report of revelation in this does not remove rational possibility. As for the Qadariyya, they claim that forgiveness of a disbeliever is rationally impossible and not permissible for Allah, because it contradicts wisdom. Therefore this verse refuted them, for if the matter were as they claim, the particle "in" used for doubt about the occurrence of an act would not have been used before an act of which there is no doubt about non-occurrence by reason; and that would be conditioning on the impossible, as in "if the crow turns white" and similar. This is not the place for it. So al-Zamakhshari's saying "then ﴿if You forgive them﴾ lacks no aspect of wisdom in forgiveness" is consistent: pardoning a criminal is rationally good, and does not fit the rules of the Sunnah, since they do not regard rational goodness, nor does it fit the whims of the Qadariyya, since they insist there is no aspect of wisdom in forgiving a disbeliever and assert its contradiction to wisdom. How then would Allah be addressed with it? It is known that Jesus, peace be upon him, disowns to Allah this unrestricted expression and the bad manners it contains, for the saying of one who addresses someone: "What did he do? He will not lack an excuse or an aspect of benefit in it" is a commonly used expression and phrase lower than the highest levels of courtesy, which a speaker uses only for one who is ordinarily below him. We ask Allah for the inspiration of courtesy and to avoid what in its offense contains the slips of ruin.]]? I say: He did not say "You forgive them," but he built the speech on "if You forgive": he said "if You punish them, You are just, because they deserve punishment," and "if You forgive them despite their disbelief, You will not lack an aspect of wisdom in forgiveness, for forgiveness is good for every criminal in reason. Indeed, whenever the crime is greater, pardoning it is better."

It is recited as "﻿هذا يوم ينفع﻿" in the nominative with an annexed noun (ʾidāfa). In the accusative it can be read in two ways: either as an adverbial of time (ẓarf) governed by "qāla" (he said), or with "hādhā" as the subject (mubtadaʾ) and the time expression as its predicate (khabar). The meaning is: what we have mentioned of the words of ʿIsā (peace be upon him) takes place on a day when it benefits. It cannot be read as a fatha (the final vowel of an indeclinable noun), as in His words ﴿يوم لا تملك نفس لنفس شيئا﴾ (the day when no soul will have power for another soul at all), because it is annexed to a declinable noun (mutamakkin). Al-Aʿmash recited "يوم ينفع" with tanwīn (nunation), as in His words ﴿واتقوا يوما لا تجزي نفس عن نفس شيئا﴾ (And guard yourselves against a day when no soul will avail another at all).

If you ask: what is the meaning of His words ﴿ينفع الصادقين صدقهم﴾ (it benefits the truthful their truthfulness)? If what is meant is their truthfulness in the Hereafter, then the Hereafter is not a place of action. And if what is meant is their truthfulness in this world, then it does not correspond to what has been reported about it, since it implies a testimony to ʿIsā (peace be upon him) concerning his truthfulness in what he answers on the Day of Resurrection? I say: its meaning is the continuous truthfulness of the truthful in both their worldly life and their Hereafter. From Qatada:

Two speakers spoke on the Day of Resurrection. As for Iblis, he said: "Indeed, Allah promised you a promise of truth" (﴿إن الله وعدكم وعد الحق﴾), so he was truthful that day, though he had been a liar before it, and his truthfulness did not benefit him. As for ʿIsā (peace be upon him), he was truthful in life and after death, so his truthfulness benefited him.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 5, verse 120:

If you say: In the heavens and the earth there are rational beings and others, so why was the masculine rational plural given precedence, such that it would be said: "and whoever is in them" (wa man fihinna)?

I answer: "mā" (what) encompasses all genera in a general way. Do you not see that when you see a figure from afar, you say: "What is it?" before you know whether it is a rational being or something else? So it is more fitting for the intended meaning to be general.

From the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "Whoever recites Surah al-Ma'idah will be given the reward of ten good deeds, ten of his sins will be erased, and ten degrees will be raised for him, according to the number of every Jew and Christian who breathes in the world." [Its chain of narration has been mentioned previously, going back to Ubayy ibn Ka'b, in the tafsir of Al ʿImran.]

The first volume is complete by the grace of Allah Most High, and it is followed, Allah willing, by the second volume, beginning with: Surah al-An'am, the second volume.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.
